choices.text: The 2019 study of 97 cities focused mainly on surface temperatures.

explanation: The text describes the cooling benefits of urban trees and then adds that trees require long-term care, so the central idea includes both the benefit and the need for maintenance.

passage.text: Urban beekeeping has moved from a niche hobby to a common feature of many cities. Rooftop hives can be found on hotels, museums, and corporate headquarters. City bees often have access to a wider variety of flowering plants than rural bees, since urban parks, gardens, and street trees bloom at different times. Beekeepers in cities also face challenges, including pollution and limited green space. Still, supporters say urban hives produce flavorful honey and help pollinate community gardens.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban beekeeping is now widespread and offers both benefits and challenges.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rooftop hives are more common than ground-level hives in cities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: City honey is superior to rural honey because city trees bloom longer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hotels and museums use beekeeping mainly to earn extra income.

explanation: The passage describes the growth of urban beekeeping, notes some benefits, and acknowledges challenges; choice A captures this overall point.

passage.text: Many people believe that all screen light interferes with sleep, but the story is more complicated. Exposure to blue light in the evening can reduce the body’s production of melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate sleep. However, the amount of blue light emitted by a typical smartphone is much smaller than the amount in sunlight. Researchers have found that factors such as the brightness of the screen, the distance from the eyes, and the duration of use matter more than the color of the light alone.

stem: According to the text, which factor is explicitly identified as more important than color of screen light in affecting sleep?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The amount of outdoor exercise during the day

choices.label: D
choices.text: The type of phone operating system

explanation: The passage says brightness, distance, and duration of use matter more than color alone; duration is one of those factors.

passage.text: Desert tortoises spend nearly all their lives underground. They dig burrows that protect them from the intense heat of the Mojave Desert and from predators. By remaining in their burrows during the hottest months, they reduce water loss and avoid the need to search for food when plants are dry. When rains do come, they emerge to drink from temporary pools and feed on annual plants. This pattern of activity allows them to survive in an environment where surface conditions are deadly for most of the year.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Desert tortoises rely on burrows to stay safe from predators in the Mojave Desert.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desert tortoises are the only animals in the Mojave Desert that can survive extreme heat.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Desert tortoises spend most of their lives searching for temporary pools of water.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Desert tortoises survive harsh desert conditions by staying underground and emerging mainly when rain arrives.

explanation: The passage explains that desert tortoises avoid heat and water loss by staying in burrows and only becoming active when rain makes surface conditions more favorable, which matches choice D.

passage.text: Volcanic lightning can occur during powerful eruptions when ash particles collide and create static electricity. Scientists study this lightning because it may help them monitor eruptions from a distance. In the hours after an eruption begins, radio sensors can detect lightning strikes even when thick ash clouds hide the volcano from view. This gives researchers an early warning that an eruption is continuing, especially at remote volcanoes where ground instruments are scarce.

stem: According to the text, why do scientists study volcanic lightning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To measure the height of ash clouds

choices.label: B
choices.text: To monitor eruptions when the volcano cannot be seen

choices.label: C
choices.text: To determine when a volcano will become dormant

choices.label: D
choices.text: To protect nearby towns from falling ash

explanation: The text says scientists study volcanic lightning because radio sensors can detect it even when ash clouds hide the volcano, helping researchers monitor eruptions from a distance.

passage.text: Many city governments once treated urban beekeeping as a nuisance, but recent changes reflect a growing appreciation for its benefits. New York and Denver, for example, have revised zoning codes to permit hives on residential rooftops. Beekeepers argue that city bees often produce more honey than rural bees because urban floral sources are more diverse and free of agricultural pesticides. Meanwhile, local food advocates value the role honeybees play in pollinating community gardens. The trend is pragmatic: cities are finding that supporting bees is not merely a hobbyist indulgence but a way to strengthen their food systems.

stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban beekeeping has gained acceptance because it can provide practical benefits to city food systems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beekeepers prefer raising hives in cities because rural bees are more vulnerable to pesticides.

choices.label: C
choices.text: New York and Denver were the first cities to legalize beekeeping on residential rooftops.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Community gardens cannot be successfully pollinated without honeybees from urban hives.

explanation: The passage traces how cities have moved from treating urban beekeeping as a nuisance to allowing it, and it links this change to concrete benefits such as honey production and pollination of community gardens. The best statement of the central idea is that urban beekeeping has gained acceptance because it offers practical advantages to city food systems.

passage.text: Slow television, or “slow TV,” consists of uninterrupted broadcasts of mundane events, such as a train journey or a fire burning for hours. Critics dismiss these programs as tedious, yet they attract devoted audiences in Norway and beyond. Researchers suggest that the genre’s appeal lies in its contrast to rapid-fire media: viewers can watch without feeling compelled to follow a plot or absorb constant information. For many, slow TV functions as ambient company, a calming backdrop for work or relaxation. The genre’s popularity thus reflects not laziness but a need for low-stakes, unhurried viewing experiences.

stem: According to the passage, the popularity of slow television is best explained as

choices.label: A
choices.text: an attempt by viewers to reduce the cost of streaming entertainment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: proof that traditional television plots are too complex for most audiences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: evidence that Norwegian viewers have fewer entertainment choices than others.

choices.label: D
choices.text: a desire for undemanding programming that can serve as a soothing background.

explanation: The passage explicitly says that researchers attribute slow TV’s appeal to its contrast with rapid-fire media and that for many viewers it functions as “a calming backdrop.” Thus the popularity is best explained as a desire for undemanding programming that can serve as a soothing background.

passage.text: Universities are increasingly offering microcredentials—short online courses that certify specific job-related skills. Some observers worry that these programs distract from the broad critical thinking expected of a traditional degree. However, advocates argue that microcredentials meet a real demand from adults who cannot commit to a four-year program but still need to update their skills. Employers, in turn, often use these certificates to screen candidates quickly. Rather than undermining higher education, microcredentials may complement it by making training more flexible and more closely tied to labor-market needs.

stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most employers now value microcredentials more than they value traditional college degrees.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Universities should replace four-year degree programs with short skill-based courses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Microcredentials can fit alongside traditional higher education by offering flexible, job-relevant training.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The main purpose of microcredentials is to help employers screen applicants more quickly.

explanation: The passage acknowledges concerns about microcredentials but ultimately presents them as complementing, not replacing, traditional higher education: they provide flexible training tied to labor-market needs. This is the central idea, so choice C is correct.

passage.text: Cloud seeding, the practice of dispersing chemicals into clouds to encourage rain, has been used for decades in drought-prone regions. Proponents point to increased snowfall in mountain basins and increased reservoir levels as evidence of its usefulness. Yet scientists caution that evaluating effectiveness is difficult: no one can know exactly how much precipitation would have fallen without intervention. They also note that seeding requires particular atmospheric conditions, so it cannot end a drought by itself. Still, many water managers regard cloud seeding as a relatively inexpensive tool among a broader set of strategies.

stem: According to the passage, which of the following is a limitation of cloud seeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It produces no measurable increase in snowfall or reservoir levels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It cannot eliminate a drought by itself.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is too expensive for most water managers to employ.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has been used only in drought-prone regions for a few years.

explanation: The passage explicitly states that cloud seeding “cannot end a drought by itself,” making B the correct answer. Choice A contradicts the passage, C misstates the passage’s claim that cloud seeding is relatively inexpensive, and D is unsupported.

passage.text: Public libraries are sometimes seen as quiet warehouses for books, but their contemporary role is more active. Many libraries host job-seeking workshops, teach digital literacy classes, and provide internet access to people who lack it at home. These services have prompted some city officials to call libraries “essential infrastructure,” as vital as roads or water lines. Librarians themselves suggest that the core mission has shifted from preserving collections to ensuring equitable access to information and opportunity. The transformation is not without costs, but it has made libraries central to community support.

stem: Which statement best captures the main idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Libraries would be more efficient if they concentrated solely on maintaining their book collections.

choices.label: B
choices.text: City officials have begun calling libraries essential infrastructure because roads and water lines are inadequate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Public libraries have become important community hubs that provide services beyond traditional book lending.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Public libraries now prioritize job-seeking workshops over all other services, including book lending.

explanation: The passage says libraries are no longer just quiet warehouses for books; they host workshops, teach digital literacy, and provide internet access. This supports C as the main idea. A, B, and D distort or contradict the passage.

passage.text: City planners often praise street trees for shade and beauty, but their benefits go deeper. Beneath pavement, tree roots break up compacted soil, improving drainage and reducing runoff after storms. A single mature canopy can intercept hundreds of gallons of rainwater. Moreover, soil around tree roots harbors microbes that filter pollutants from water seeping into groundwater. These hidden functions make street trees not merely ornamental but vital infrastructure in urban water management.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Street trees are primarily valued for the shade and beauty they provide to city residents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mature street tree can intercept hundreds of gallons of rainwater during storms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Street trees play crucial roles in urban water management because of their roots and surrounding soil.

choices.label: D
choices.text: City planners should remove pavement around street trees to improve soil drainage.

explanation: The passage builds from examples about roots, runoff, and soil microbes to a larger claim: street trees are essential infrastructure in urban water management. Choice C captures that central claim; choices A, B, and D are either a supporting detail, an inverted emphasis, or an unsupported recommendation.

passage.text: In the deep North Pacific, sponge communities thrive where other animals cannot, relying on patches of hard seafloor and slow currents that deliver food particles. Unlike shallow-water sponges, deep-sea species grow extremely slowly, with some colonies estimated to be thousands of years old. Their porous bodies also provide shelter for small crustaceans. Because their growth is so slow, any damage from bottom trawling could take centuries to reverse.

stem: According to the text, which statement about deep-sea sponge communities is true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They depend on hard seafloor and slow currents for food.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They grow faster than shallow-water sponges do.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are found only in the North Pacific Ocean.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their slow growth protects them from damage caused by bottom trawling.

explanation: The passage explicitly states that deep-sea sponge communities rely on patches of hard seafloor and slow currents that deliver food particles. Choice A is therefore correct. B reverses the stated comparison, C overstates the geographic scope, and D mistakes the consequence of slow growth for a protective effect.

passage.text: Does the language people speak shape how they think about time? Speakers of languages that use absolute spatial terms, such as 'uphill' and 'downhill,' often arrange past and future events in space according to physical landmarks rather than their own bodies. Researchers found that these speakers oriented timelines consistently no matter which way they faced, whereas speakers of relative-language oriented timelines from left to right. The results suggest that habitual spatial language can influence mental representations of abstract domains like time.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Language completely determines how people think about time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Habitual spatial language may influence how people mentally represent time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Speakers of absolute spatial terms usually cannot understand relative spatial terms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Researchers disagree about whether language affects time perception.

explanation: The passage presents research findings and concludes that habitual spatial language can influence mental representations of abstract domains such as time. Choice B captures this qualified central claim. A overstates the effect, C is unsupported, and D contradicts the passage, which reports convergent research results.

passage.text: Rare earth elements, despite their name, are not especially scarce in Earth's crust; they are difficult to separate from one another because their chemical properties are nearly identical. In permanent magnets used in electric vehicle motors, rare earths such as neodymium generate a strong magnetic field at high temperatures. Substitutes exist, but they are heavier and less efficient. Recycling these elements from electronic waste is promising, though commercial methods remain limited.

stem: According to the text, which statement about rare earth elements is true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are among the scarcest elements in Earth's crust.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are difficult to separate because their chemical properties are nearly identical.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Substitutes for them in permanent magnets are lighter and more efficient.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Commercial recycling of them from electronic waste is already widespread.

explanation: The passage explicitly says rare earths are difficult to separate from one another because their chemical properties are nearly identical. Choice B is therefore correct. A contradicts the passage, C reverses the stated comparison about substitutes, and D contradicts the claim that commercial recycling methods remain limited.

passage.text: Old maps are often treated as objective records of past geography, but historians emphasize that they were shaped by commercial, political, and religious interests. A sixteenth-century chart may exaggerate the size of a monarch's territory or decorate unexplored regions with monsters, but these features are not merely decorative. They conveyed ownership, advertised reliable routes, and encoded the mapmaker's assumptions about the world. Thus, maps are useful historical evidence precisely because they reveal what people of the time valued and feared, not just what they knew.

stem: Which choice best describes the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sixteenth-century maps are less accurate than modern maps and should not be used for navigation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mapmakers decorated unexplored regions with monsters in order to hide their ignorance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Old maps are mainly useful to historians because their decorative elements can be dated by art historians.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maps from the past are valuable historical evidence of the attitudes and assumptions of the people who made them.

explanation: The passage claims that old maps express commercial, political, and religious interests and are evidence of what people valued and feared, not just what they knew. Choice D captures that central claim. A overreaches into modern navigation, B misreads the monsters as deception, and C reduces the maps' value to dating decorative elements.

passage.text: City planners often praise urban street trees as green infrastructure that controls stormwater. Tree canopies intercept raindrops, and their roots create pathways for water to enter soil. Yet watershed-scale studies report a modest average effect, with trees reducing annual runoff by only a few percentage points. The size of the benefit changes with soil type, tree species, and how much pavement surrounds the tree. Trees therefore support urban drainage, but they cannot replace engineered stormwater systems.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Street trees are the most effective method of controlling stormwater in cities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Urban trees help manage stormwater, but their ability to do so is limited and context-dependent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Planting more street trees will eliminate the need for engineered stormwater systems.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The main benefit of urban trees is reducing the amount of pavement in a city.

explanation: The passage says trees intercept rain and increase infiltration but that studies show only a modest runoff reduction and that the benefit depends on soil, species, and pavement. It concludes that trees cannot replace engineered systems, so choice B captures the limited, context-dependent role the passage describes.

passage.text: Scholars once claimed that reading in the ancient Greco-Roman world was exclusively oral, since most surviving texts mention people reading out loud. But a careful survey of ancient sources challenges this view. A character in a fifth-century BCE play reads a letter silently on stage, and a later medical handbook advises silent reading as a way to soothe an inflamed throat. Such examples make clear that silent reading was a known practice, even if public reading aloud was more common.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ancient Greeks and Romans read silently more often than they read aloud.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The practice of silent reading developed only after public reading aloud had disappeared.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Evidence of silent reading in antiquity is limited to medical textbooks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ancient Greeks and Romans sometimes read silently, but reading aloud was more common.

explanation: The passage argues against the old view that ancient reading was exclusively oral. It gives examples of silent reading but also says public reading aloud was more common, so choice D accurately reflects the central idea.

passage.text: In debates about artificial intelligence, algorithmic transparency is often described as a simple cure for biased decisions. The reasoning is that if companies disclose how their models work, outsiders can spot discrimination and force corrections. However, transparency can fail in several ways. A model may rely on decades of historical data that already encode unjust patterns; revealing the code does not expose those patterns, let alone change them. Regulations that require disclosure can also turn into checklists that companies satisfy while leaving underlying harms in place. Transparency, in other words, is a necessary step but not a sufficient one.

stem: Which choice best captures the main idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Algorithmic transparency is more effective in theory than in practice because companies resist disclosure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regulatory checklists are more important than actually revealing how algorithms make decisions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Algorithmic transparency is valuable but does not by itself guarantee fair decisions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Requiring companies to disclose algorithms prevents biased decision-making.

explanation: The passage says transparency is often presented as a cure but then explains several ways it can fail, concluding that it is necessary but not sufficient. Choice C matches this central idea.

passage.text: After the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens, many ecologists expected a textbook sequence of recovery: hardy pioneer plants would appear first, followed by shrubs, and finally forest. In some areas, that sequence did occur. In others, recovery was much slower or took different pathways. Some plants survived the blast and spread outward from sheltered pockets, while some landscapes stayed barren for decades because the eruption had stripped away the soil. The disaster consequently became a natural experiment showing that succession is not a fixed, universal ladder but a process shaped by local conditions and chance.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The recovery at Mount St. Helens showed that ecological succession can vary widely with local conditions and chance events.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ecologists' original textbook model accurately predicted the timing of recovery at Mount St. Helens.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mount St. Helens remained permanently barren because the eruption stripped away all soil.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pioneer plants were unable to survive anywhere in the blast zone because of the heat.

explanation: The passage describes how recovery differed from the expected textbook sequence and says succession is shaped by local conditions and chance. Choice A states this central idea, while the other choices contradict or overstate the passage.

passage.text: Polymetallic nodules are potato-sized rocks scattered across the deep-ocean floor and rich in metals used in batteries. Companies propose collecting them with remotely operated vehicles that vacuum the seabed. Scientists monitoring test mining runs report that the process churns up fine sediment, creating plumes that can drift hundreds of kilometers and bury filter-feeding organisms. Nodule fields also host slow-growing sponges and worms found nowhere else; if these habitats are removed, recolonization might take millions of years. For now, the scale of these impacts is hard to predict because commercial mining has not yet begun.

stem: According to the passage, which of the following is a specific concern scientists have about collecting polymetallic nodules?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Remotely operated vehicles may not be able to reach the deep-ocean floor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sediment plumes from vacuuming the seabed could harm animals far away from the mining sites.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The nodules contain too few metals to make mining worthwhile.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sponges and worms in nodule fields are expected to recolonize within a few years.

explanation: The passage states that test mining churns up sediment plumes that can drift hundreds of kilometers and bury filter-feeding organisms, so choice B is an explicitly stated concern. The other choices either contradict the passage or are not mentioned.

passage.text: In 2019, Millport altered its zoning code to permit backyard beekeeping on residential lots under 5,000 square feet. Within two years, the number of registered hives in the city tripled. However, urban beekeeping advocates warn that the surge has outpaced the availability of flowering plants, prompting recommendations that new beekeepers plant pollinator gardens. The city council is now considering a grant program to support habitat restoration alongside hive registration.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Millport’s zoning change led to rapid growth in urban beekeeping, but the increase has raised concerns about limited bee forage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beekeeping is now the most popular hobby in Millport, and the city council wants to restrict it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The main effect of Millport’s zoning change was to reduce the number of registered hives in the city.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urban beekeepers in Millport are primarily concerned about the cost of maintaining backyard hives.

explanation: The text says the zoning change caused registered hives to triple, but advocates warn that flowering plants are now insufficient. This matches the idea that the policy led to growth while raising concerns about bee forage.

passage.text: Marine biologists once dismissed sea sponges as passive filter feeders, but symbiotic microbes inside some deep-sea sponge species perform a more active role. These microbes convert dissolved organic matter in the surrounding water into food the sponge can use. In certain sponge reefs, the study found, this microbial partnership can supply nearly 40 percent of the carbon the sponges consume. Because these reefs cover wide areas of the seafloor, researchers now classify them as significant processors of carbon in deep-ocean ecosystems.

stem: According to the text, what is one function of symbiotic microbes in some deep-sea sponges?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They enable a sponge to filter bacteria and other particles from seawater.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They convert dissolved organic matter in the water into food for the sponge.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They give sea sponges their passive, plantlike appearance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They recycle waste products produced by sponge reefs.

explanation: The passage explicitly states that symbiotic microbes convert dissolved organic matter in the surrounding water into food the sponge can use. The other choices describe roles that are either misattributed or unsupported by the text.

passage.text: In his Autobiography, Benjamin Franklin presents himself as a model of industrious self-improvement. Yet literary scholar J. A. Leo Lemay argued that this plainspoken persona is a deliberate construction. Franklin chose anecdotes and aphorisms that projected honesty, while remaining silent about episodes that would complicate the image. Lemay therefore concluded that the Autobiography should be read not as a complete confession but as a strategic self-portrait, crafted to persuade readers of Franklin’s character.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Franklin’s Autobiography is primarily a collection of traditional aphorisms and moral anecdotes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Scholars agree that the Autobiography gives a complete and accurate record of Franklin’s life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: According to Lemay, the Autobiography is a carefully designed self-presentation rather than a fully transparent account.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Franklin wrote the Autobiography mainly to demonstrate that ordinary people can succeed through honesty.

explanation: The passage presents Lemay’s view that Franklin crafted a plainspoken persona and left out episodes that would complicate his image. This supports the central idea that the Autobiography is a strategic self-portrait rather than a fully transparent account.

passage.text: After the Hobart Dam was removed from the Quenemo River in 2016, scientists monitored the river’s recovery. By 2024, migratory fish species were once again spawning upstream, and summer water temperatures downstream had dropped by nearly two degrees Celsius. But sediment that had collected behind the dam still moves downstream during heavy rains, burying parts of the floodplain under sand. For this reason, the research team calls the restoration a qualified success, not a full return to the river’s original state.

stem: According to the text, which change was observed in the Quenemo River by 2024?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All sediment behind the old dam had been flushed out to sea.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Summer water temperatures downstream had risen by nearly two degrees Celsius.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Migratory fish species had disappeared from their upstream spawning grounds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migratory fish were once again spawning upstream.

explanation: The passage states that by 2024, migratory fish species were once again spawning upstream. The other choices contradict the text or misstate the observed changes.

passage.text: Airport security waits are often experienced as longer than they objectively are. In a controlled study, passengers who stood in a steadily moving line and passengers who were stopped for the same total time gave very different estimates: the stop-and-go group believed the wait was significantly longer. Adding a countdown display for the stop-and-go group reduced reported frustration, even though the actual wait time did not change. The researchers concluded that perceived delay depends less on objective time than on visible progress and information.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: How long a security wait seems is shaped more by visible progress and information than by the actual elapsed time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A countdown display can eliminate travelers’ frustration with airport security waits.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Steadily moving security lines are always shorter in actual duration than stop-and-go lines.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Objective wait time is the strongest factor in how long travelers believe they waited.

explanation: The passage concludes that perceived delay depends less on objective time than on visible progress and information. The correct choice captures this central idea, while the others misstate or contradict the study’s findings.

passage.text: Urban soils are often described as lifeless fill, but that generalization misses a more complicated reality. Demolition and construction can leave behind compacted, nutrient-poor ground, while old gardens and vacant lots may contain deep, fertile layers enriched by decades of leaf litter and rubble. Soil scientists increasingly create block-by-block maps of these differences rather than treating the whole city as one zone. Effective greening projects, they argue, depend on identifying what kind of soil actually exists at a particular site.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban soil is generally too contaminated for large-scale greening projects to succeed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The condition of urban soil varies by location, so successful restoration must be based on local conditions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The main barrier to urban greening is a lack of accurate maps showing soil quality.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Old gardens and vacant lots are the only parts of a city where fertile soil can be found.

explanation: The text emphasizes that urban soil is not uniform and that restoration projects must account for local conditions. Choice B captures this central idea, while the other choices overstate or distort details from the passage.

passage.text: For much of the twentieth century, sleep was viewed as a time when the brain simply shut down and recovered. Research has since shown that during deep sleep the brain replays the day's events, but not indiscriminately. In experiments, people who expected a test on certain material showed stronger replay of that material than of equally recent but unimportant events. Emotional memories were also favored over neutral ones. Sleep thus acts less like a tape recorder and more like an editor, deciding which experiences deserve to be strengthened.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sleep helps the brain recover energy by temporarily shutting down neural activity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During sleep, the brain strengthens memories from the day exactly as they occurred.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Emotional events interfere with the brain's ability to choose which memories to keep.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sleep selectively strengthens certain memories rather than preserving all recent experiences equally.

explanation: The passage argues that sleep is an active process that edits memories, strengthening some experiences and not others. Choice D restates that central idea; the other choices contradict or misrepresent the passage.

passage.text: The Mexican cavefish is famous for having no eyes, but darkness itself does not cause blindness. Instead, eye loss is tied to genetic changes that also increase the number of taste buds and alter jaw structure. These traits develop together because the same genes influence multiple parts of the body. Natural selection for more effective feeding in food-scarce cave pools can therefore produce eyeless fish, since the genes that improve feeding happen to disrupt eye development as well.

stem: According to the text, what explains the loss of eyes in Mexican cavefish?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The absence of light in caves removes any need for eyes and leads directly to their degeneration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Changes in genes that improve feeding in caves also disrupt eye development.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cavefish use so much energy developing taste buds that their eyes shrink.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Predators in cave pools selectively eat fish with large eyes.

explanation: The passage explicitly states that eye loss is tied to genetic changes that also improve feeding, and that the genes disrupting eye development are selected because they aid feeding. Choice B matches this explanation.

passage.text: Vertical farms stack crops indoors under artificial lights and can use far less water and land than conventional agriculture. Yet these benefits come with a major cost: electricity needed for lighting and climate control is expensive. For low-value staple crops such as wheat, the energy cost typically exceeds the market price, making vertical farming unprofitable. High-value, perishable crops such as leafy greens and herbs, however, can bear that cost, which is why most vertical farms concentrate on them.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vertical farming is more environmentally friendly than conventional farming because it uses less water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although vertical farming saves land and water, high energy costs restrict its profitability to certain crops.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Artificial lighting is the only reason vertical farming has not replaced conventional agriculture.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Consumers prefer leafy greens and herbs over staple crops such as wheat.

explanation: The passage presents both a benefit and a drawback of vertical farming, concluding that only high-value crops can offset the high electricity costs. Choice B best captures that central idea.

passage.text: Dictionaries are sometimes imagined as official rulebooks that decide what is correct English, but dictionary editors see their task differently. They collect millions of examples of written and spoken language and record the meanings and usages they observe. If a new word appears often enough and across varied sources, editors add it, whether or not older guides approve. A dictionary entry is therefore better understood as evidence of how people use language than as a verdict on how they ought to.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dictionary editors reject new words that older guides do not approve.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dictionaries should only include words that have appeared in formal writing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dictionaries describe actual language use rather than prescribe correct usage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dictionaries are unreliable because spoken language changes too quickly.

explanation: The passage argues that dictionaries record observed usage, not official rules. Choice C matches this central idea; the other choices contradict or misstate the text.

passage.text: During sleep, the brain does not simply power down. Electroencephalogram studies show that patterns of neural activity from waking hours are replayed during slow-wave sleep, often at many times their original speed. This replay appears to strengthen the synaptic connections involved in memory. Researchers have observed that people who are deprived of slow-wave sleep after learning a skill perform notably worse on later tests than those who sleep normally, even if total sleep time is similar.

stem: Which of the following most accurately describes the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The most vivid dreams occur during slow-wave sleep.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Slow-wave sleep appears to help consolidate memories by replaying waking neural patterns.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who get less sleep than normal cannot learn new skills.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electroencephalogram studies prove that the brain is inactive during sleep.

explanation: The passage states that during slow-wave sleep the brain replays waking neural activity and that people deprived of this sleep perform worse on later tests, indicating that slow-wave sleep supports memory consolidation. A, C, and D are either unsupported or contradicted by the passage.

passage.text: After only eighteen months of operation, the Pony Express ceased activity; it had never turned a profit. Yet its place in American history is secure. The relay system, in which a single rider could cover about 75 miles before passing mail to a fresh rider, proved that a transcontinental mail route was feasible. The overland mail service that replaced it borrowed the Pony Express's relay strategy, though it was slower and less romantic.

stem: According to the passage, what did the relay system of the Pony Express demonstrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: That riders could not cover long distances without fresh horses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: That a transcontinental mail route could not be profitable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: That a transcontinental mail route was feasible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: That overland mail service should replace relay riders.

explanation: The passage explicitly says the relay system "proved that a transcontinental mail route was feasible." The other choices misstate the passage: the Pony Express was unprofitable, but that is not what the relay system demonstrated.

passage.text: Although bamboo can tower as high as a forty-story building, it is not a tree. Botanically, bamboo is a woody grass, distinguished by its hollow, jointed stems and its remarkable growth pattern. A bamboo shoot can add as much as one meter in a single day because, unlike trees, it does not grow thicker through annual rings; it emerges at full diameter and lengthens upward. This unusual combination makes bamboo useful where rapid, renewable material is needed.

stem: Which statement about bamboo's growth would best explain why the author calls it "remarkable"?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bamboo can grow as tall as a forty-story building.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bamboo is classified as a woody grass rather than a tree.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bamboo is useful as a renewable material.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A bamboo shoot can add as much as one meter in a single day.

explanation: The passage ties the word "remarkable" directly to bamboo's growth pattern, specifically noting that a shoot can add as much as one meter in a single day. The other options either are not about growth or do not match the passage's stated reason.

passage.text: Rising water temperatures trigger coral bleaching: corals expel the symbiotic algae that provide them with nutrients and color. The algae, called zooxanthellae, live inside coral tissues and supply most of the coral's energy through photosynthesis. A brief heat spike can cause bleaching, but if temperatures return to normal quickly, corals may regain algae and recover. Prolonged heat, by contrast, can lead to death. Understanding this difference is critical for predicting which reef areas may survive climate change.

stem: According to the passage, which factor most directly determines whether a bleached coral can recover?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The number of zooxanthellae it expels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: How quickly water temperatures return to normal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: How much photosynthesis the algae perform.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The depth of the reef where it lives.

explanation: The passage says that if temperatures return to normal quickly, corals may regain algae and recover, while prolonged heat can lead to death. Thus the key factor is how long temperature stress lasts, not the other details.

passage.text: The invention of photography in the nineteenth century was inseparable from chemistry. Early photographers coated glass plates with silver halide, a light-sensitive compound. Wherever light struck the plate, the silver halide darkened, creating a latent image that could be developed and fixed. This direct chemical process allowed images of extraordinary precision to be recorded for the first time. Even after digital technology replaced most film, silver-based chemical reactions remain the foundation of analog photography.

stem: According to the passage, what was the role of silver halide in early photography?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It darkened when exposed to light, forming the basis of a photographic image.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It fixed the image so it would not fade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It was the first digital recording medium.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It protected glass plates from moisture.

explanation: The passage states that silver halide darkened wherever light struck the plate, creating a latent image. Fixing was a separate later step, and silver halide was not digital or a moisture barrier.

passage.text: In many cities, street trees are often viewed as decorative, but their role goes far beyond appearance. A mature tree can intercept thousands of gallons of stormwater, reducing strain on drainage systems, and its shade lowers pavement temperatures, cutting air-conditioning demand in adjacent buildings. Moreover, neighborhoods with dense canopy report higher property values and greater resident interaction. While new plantings require initial investment, studies show that every dollar spent on tree maintenance yields several dollars in environmental and social benefits. Thus, urban forestry is more than beautification; it is essential infrastructure.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban trees are primarily decorative, but they can also help manage stormwater.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Street trees provide important environmental and social benefits and should be treated as vital urban infrastructure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Property values improve primarily because of street trees' ability to reduce air-conditioning costs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cities should invest in new tree plantings even when maintenance budgets are limited.

explanation: The passage gives multiple environmental and social benefits of street trees and concludes that urban forestry is essential infrastructure, not mere decoration.

passage.text: During deep sleep, the brain replays patterns of neural activity from waking experience, a process believed to strengthen recently formed memories. Researchers at a sleep lab found that participants who heard an odor while learning a spatial task and again during slow-wave sleep showed improved recall the next day compared with controls who received the odor only during learning. Interestingly, no benefit appeared when the odor was presented during rapid-eye-movement sleep. The researchers concluded that sensory cues can selectively reinforce memory consolidation during the specific stage of sleep associated with replay.

stem: According to the text, what did the researchers conclude?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A sensory cue can strengthen a memory when it is presented during the sleep stage in which replay occurs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Odors improve memory only when paired with spatial learning in a laboratory setting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rapid-eye-movement sleep interferes with the consolidation of memories formed during waking.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Replaying neural patterns during sleep requires two exposures to the same sensory cue.

explanation: The final sentence says sensory cues can selectively reinforce memory consolidation during the specific sleep stage associated with replay, which matches choice A.

passage.text: The earliest surviving written documents from ancient Mesopotamia are not epic poems or royal decrees but administrative records—ledgers of grain, livestock, and labor. These clay tablets rarely mention named individuals beyond officials and often use numerical signs rather than full sentences. Their apparent dullness has led some to dismiss them as archaeological trivia. Yet these records reveal how a complex society managed resources, tracked obligations, and created the bureaucratic structures that made cities possible. Their very ordinariness is what makes them historically invaluable: they document the everyday workings of the earliest state institutions.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ancient Mesopotamian tablets are too fragmentary for scholars to reconstruct royal decrees.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The earliest written Mesopotamian documents consisted mainly of royal decrees and epic poems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mesopotamian cities depended on full sentences to manage complex resources.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The apparent dullness of early administrative tablets is precisely what makes them historically important.

explanation: The passage argues that although the administrative tablets seem dull, their ordinariness makes them invaluable for understanding early state institutions.

passage.text: Mycorrhizal fungi form underground networks that connect the root systems of many plants. It was once assumed that these networks benefit only the fungi, which receive sugars from plants. In the past two decades, experiments have shown that resources such as carbon, nitrogen, and water can move between neighboring plants through these fungal links. Seedlings shaded under mature trees often receive carbon through the network, improving survival. This finding challenges the view that forest plants are solitary competitors; instead, they are linked in a dynamic exchange system in which some plants may support others under stress.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fungi receive sugars from plants, while plants receive no benefit from the fungal network.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shaded seedlings survive better than mature trees because of fungal networks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Underground fungal networks can transfer resources among plants, suggesting that forest plants are not isolated competitors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Experiments on mycorrhizal fungi have proven that nitrogen is the most important resource shared between plants.

explanation: The passage says that resources move between plants through fungal links and that this challenges the idea of plants as solitary competitors.

passage.text: In the sixteenth century, the rapid expansion of printing created pressure for more standardized spelling in English. Early printers, many of them from the European continent, introduced conventions based on their own typographic needs rather than on pronunciation. For example, the letter v was used at the beginning of words and u elsewhere, and the long s was used unless a word ended in s or s followed by f. Printers also fixed spellings for the sake of line justification, adding or removing letters to adjust line endings. These typographic choices, not gradual changes in pronunciation, explain many features of modern English spelling.

stem: According to the text, a major reason modern English spelling has certain unusual features is that

choices.label: A
choices.text: printers made spelling changes to match the pronunciation of continental Europe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the English government issued standardized spelling rules for printing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: typographic considerations led early printers to impose fixed spellings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: line justification in manuscripts encouraged scholars to spell words phonetically.

explanation: The passage states that printers introduced conventions based on typographic needs and that these typographic choices explain many features of modern English spelling.

passage.text: Urban planners increasingly use pocket forests, dense plantings of native species in areas as small as a tennis court, to address heat and flooding. Although a single pocket forest cannot absorb heavy rainfall by itself, clusterings of these mini-ecosystems across a city can lower local temperatures and slow stormwater runoff. Their benefits depend less on the size of any one planting than on how many patches a neighborhood has and whether residents can reach them.

stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pocket forests are too small to make a meaningful environmental difference in cities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Native species planted in cities require less water than nonnative species do.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The environmental value of pocket forests in cities comes mainly from their combined presence and accessibility, not from individual size.

choices.label: D
choices.text: City heat and flooding can be eliminated if every tennis-court-sized lot is converted to forest.

explanation: Although a single pocket forest has limits, the passage says clusters can lower temperatures and slow runoff; the final sentence identifies the number of patches and residents' access as key. Thus C best captures the central idea.

passage.text: Some fungi that decompose wood in forests emit a faint blue glow, a phenomenon called bioluminescence. The light is produced by an enzyme that consumes oxygen, and scientists hypothesize that it attracts nocturnal insects, which then carry fungal spores to new trees. However, laboratory experiments show that the glow intensifies when the fungus is actively breaking down wood, suggesting the light may be a by-product of metabolic activity rather than a signal.

stem: According to the text, what happens when a fungus is actively breaking down wood?

choices.label: C
choices.text: It attracts more nocturnal insects than usual.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It releases spores into the air.

explanation: The text states that laboratory experiments show the glow intensifies when the fungus is actively breaking down wood, so a brighter glow is the correct explicit detail.

passage.text: Adaptive reuse—converting obsolete factories and warehouses into housing—is often praised as a sustainable alternative to demolition. Yet preservationists caution that not every industrial building is worth saving; some have floor plans that are unsafe for residential occupancy or are located far from jobs and transit. The most successful projects, they argue, require more than nostalgia: they demand a practical match between an old structure's constraints and the current needs of a community.

stem: Which statement best summarizes the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Demolition is generally a better option than adaptive reuse for obsolete industrial buildings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Preservationists oppose most efforts to convert factories and warehouses into housing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Older industrial buildings are safer residences than buildings constructed specifically for housing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adaptive reuse succeeds only when a building's structural constraints are matched with current community needs.

explanation: The passage praises adaptive reuse conditionally: successful projects require a practical match between an old structure's constraints and current community needs, making D the central idea.

passage.text: Research on 'desirable difficulties' suggests that learning is sometimes improved when conditions are made harder, not easier. Interleaving different types of practice problems, for instance, slows initial performance but strengthens long-term retention compared to blocked practice. Yet the benefits are not automatic: if the extra difficulty is so severe that learners cannot solve the problems or receive no feedback, the strategy backfires. Difficulty, in other words, aids learning only within a zone the learner can still manage.

stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocked practice is generally more effective than interleaving because it avoids initial frustration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Introducing difficulty into practice improves learning only when the challenge remains manageable and supported.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All extra difficulty in learning situations is beneficial for long-term retention.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Learners should never be given feedback while practicing difficult problems.

explanation: The passage argues that difficulty aids learning only within a manageable zone, especially when feedback is present; B states this precisely.

passage.text: Cloud seeding involves dispersing substances such as silver iodide into clouds to encourage precipitation. Its effectiveness is difficult to measure because natural rainfall varies enormously; scientists use randomized trials and historical comparisons to isolate the seeding effect. One well-known study in Wyoming estimated that seeded winter storms produced about 5 to 15 percent additional snow, while another in Idaho found no statistically significant increase. Thus, the same technique can yield different results depending on local atmospheric conditions.

stem: According to the text, why is the effectiveness of cloud seeding difficult to measure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Silver iodide can damage the clouds it is meant to affect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Seeded winter storms in Wyoming produced no increase in snow.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Natural rainfall varies greatly, making it hard to isolate the effect of seeding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cloud seeding only works during winter months.

explanation: The passage says effectiveness is difficult to measure because natural rainfall varies enormously, which makes isolating the seeding effect hard; C is the explicit reason.

passage.text: Climate scientists often describe carbon dioxide emissions as an invisible crisis because the worst effects unfold over decades. By contrast, an oil spill produces immediate, visually striking damage. This contrast can shape public perception: dramatic disasters attract intense media coverage and prompt policy action, while gradual warming receives less urgent attention even though its cumulative consequences are far greater. Scholars argue that the slow pace of climate change makes it psychologically easy to discount, and they recommend framing environmental harm in terms of long-term human health to overcome this bias.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oil spills are more destructive to the environment than long-term carbon emissions are.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Environmental harm is judged more by how quickly it becomes visible than by its total impact.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dramatic environmental disasters are the only events that can motivate governments to act.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scholars should focus on preventing oil spills rather than on long-term climate change.

explanation: The passage contrasts immediate, visible disasters with slow-developing climate change and says the slow pace makes climate change easy to discount; thus the main idea is that visible speed, not total harm, drives perception.

passage.text: Urban trees are often celebrated for aesthetic value, but their most significant contributions are infrastructural. A mature canopy can intercept rainfall, reducing stormwater runoff and the burden on sewer systems during heavy storms. Shade from trees lowers pavement temperatures, cutting the energy demand for air conditioning in adjacent buildings. By reducing runoff and cooling cities, strategically placed trees function as green infrastructure, providing measurable economic savings that ornamental landscaping alone cannot match.

stem: Which choice best describes the central claim of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The main benefit of urban trees is that they make city streets more attractive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Trees reduce the need for air conditioning by lowering pavement temperatures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Urban trees provide practical services that can be quantified in economic terms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stormwater runoff is the most serious environmental problem faced by modern cities.

explanation: The passage says trees' most significant contributions are infrastructural, then lists runoff reduction and cooling as measurable economic savings. C states that central claim; B names only one supporting detail.

passage.text: Plants cannot change their location, so they rely on directional growth responses to cope with their environment. Phototropism, growth toward or away from light, is controlled by auxin, a hormone that redistributes to the shaded side of a stem. There, auxin promotes cell elongation, causing the stem to curve toward the light. Gravitropism, a response to gravity, also depends on auxin redistribution in roots and shoots. Together, these tropisms help sessile organisms position themselves to capture resources.

stem: According to the text, what role does auxin play in phototropism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It accumulates on the shaded side of a stem and stimulates cells there to lengthen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It prevents growth on the side of the stem that faces the light.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It causes stems to bend away from light by redistributing to the lit side.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It affects only roots and has no role in shoot responses to light.

explanation: The text explicitly states that auxin redistributes to the shaded side of a stem, where it promotes cell elongation, making A the correct detail.

passage.text: In the 1970s, many American orchestras began placing auditioning musicians behind opaque screens so that judging panels could not see them. The practice was intended to reduce bias, and studies of actual audition data showed that it increased the probability that female musicians would advance to later rounds. Yet screens do not eliminate all bias: judges can sometimes infer gender from sound alone, and other social identities may be detectable from subtle stylistic cues. The screen remains, however, an instructive example of how institutional design can counteract discrimination.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Screens eliminated gender discrimination in American orchestras.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The main purpose of orchestra screens was to improve the quality of musicians.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Screens are less useful now than they were in the 1970s.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blind auditions reduced, though did not end, bias in orchestra hiring.

explanation: The passage says screens reduced bias but "do not eliminate all bias," so D captures the qualified main idea.

passage.text: New Caledonian crows manufacture tools from plant material, shaping twigs and leaves into hooks to extract insects from crevices. In recent experiments, crows presented with novel materials readily made tools, suggesting that they can plan a sequence of actions rather than relying solely on inherited routines. The birds also modify tools in response to changing tasks, a flexibility that researchers interpret as evidence of advanced cognitive ability. However, the same behavior has not been observed to the same degree in mainland crow species, indicating that such tool use may depend on ecological pressures or social learning unique to New Caledonia.

stem: According to the text, what do the experiments with novel materials suggest about New Caledonian crows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They rely on a fixed set of inherited behaviors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They can plan actions instead of only following ready-made routines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are less flexible than mainland crow species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They refuse to use materials they have not encountered before.

explanation: The passage says novel-material experiments suggest the crows "can plan a sequence of actions rather than relying solely on inherited routines," matching B.

passage.text: Although vertical farming is often praised for using less land than conventional agriculture, its energy demands remain a serious obstacle. Most vertical farms rely on artificial lighting and climate control, and this electricity can account for more than half of operating costs. Researchers note that the technology is viable mainly for high-value crops such as herbs and leafy greens, which can command premium prices. For staple crops like wheat or rice, the energy cost makes vertical farming economically impractical on a large scale.

stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vertical farming consumes less land than conventional agriculture and is therefore environmentally beneficial overall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vertical farming is economically practical only for a limited range of crops because of its high energy costs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vertical farming will replace conventional farming for staple crops once energy costs are reduced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vertical farming relies mainly on artificial lighting and climate control, which are more efficient than sunlight.

explanation: The passage acknowledges the land advantage but emphasizes that energy demands are a serious obstacle, making vertical farming viable mainly for high-value crops and impractical for staples. This aligns with choice B.

passage.text: Citizen science projects, in which volunteers collect ecological observations, have expanded the amount of data available to researchers. However, these data are not always uniform in quality. Volunteers may identify species incorrectly, and sampling effort often varies with weather, location, and participants' availability. As a result, researchers must apply statistical methods that account for uneven data collection before drawing conclusions about species populations.

stem: According to the text, why must researchers apply statistical methods to citizen science data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To increase the number of volunteers participating in ecological projects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To correct for inconsistencies in how and when data were collected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To ensure that species identifications are made by professional scientists.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To determine which locations have the most favorable weather for sampling.

explanation: The passage explicitly states that sampling effort varies with weather, location, and volunteer availability, so researchers must use statistical methods that account for uneven data collection. Choice B is the correct paraphrase.

passage.text: Early silent films were rarely shown without musical accompaniment. In small theaters, a single pianist might improvise from a printed cue sheet, while grand urban cinemas employed orchestras that performed original scores. Music served not merely as background noise; it shaped audiences' emotional responses and compensated for the absence of spoken dialogue. The choice of tempo, instrumentation, and melody could transform a scene's meaning entirely.

stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Silent films were usually shown with music because audiences disliked silence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Musical accompaniment in silent films ranged from a single pianist to a full orchestra.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The music in silent films was an essential tool for guiding audience response and meaning.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Improvised piano music was less effective than orchestral scores in shaping emotion.

explanation: The passage says music was not merely background noise but shaped emotional responses and could transform a scene's meaning. Choice C states this central idea, while the other choices are either unsupported or overly narrow details.

passage.text: The Bering Land Bridge, which connected Asia and North America during the last ice age, was not a permanent passage. Its exposure depended on global sea levels, which fell when glaciers locked up vast amounts of water. The bridge appeared and disappeared several times over thousands of years. The final submergence, around 10,000 years ago, cut off what had been a major route for human migration.

stem: According to the text, the Bering Land Bridge was exposed only when

choices.label: A
choices.text: glaciers had locked up enough water to lower global sea levels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: human migration between Asia and North America was occurring.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the global climate was warmer than it is today.

choices.label: D
choices.text: it had been permanently submerged for thousands of years.

explanation: The passage states that the bridge's exposure depended on global sea levels, which fell when glaciers locked up vast amounts of water. Therefore, lower sea levels caused by glacial water storage were necessary for the bridge to appear.

passage.text: Lunar lava tubes—caverns formed by ancient lava flows—are of great interest to space agencies. Because they are shielded by meters of rock, they offer stable temperatures and protection from radiation and micrometeorites. However, scientists caution that the tubes are not ready-made habitats: their floors are covered with loose rubble, entrances may be unstable, and no method yet exists to seal them airtight. They may serve as foundations for future bases, but considerable engineering is still required.

stem: The central idea of the text is that lunar lava tubes

choices.label: A
choices.text: are the best locations for future human settlements because of their stable temperatures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: have already been used as habitats during previous space missions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: are unlikely to be useful to space agencies because of loose rubble.

choices.label: D
choices.text: could support future bases but would need significant preparation and construction.

explanation: The passage presents both the appealing protective features of lunar lava tubes and the serious obstacles that make them not ready-made. The central claim is that they could serve as foundations for bases but would require considerable engineering, matching choice D.

passage.text: Urban heat islands arise partly because asphalt and dark roofs absorb sunlight and release heat at night. One widely promoted remedy is coating rooftops with reflective materials. In hot, sunny cities, such roofs lower indoor temperatures and reduce air-conditioning demand. Yet the same technology can raise winter heating costs, and its cooling benefit shrinks in cloudy or humid regions. Researchers caution that reflective roofs should be evaluated alongside local climate, building age, and energy costs before being adopted as a universal climate strategy.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cities can completely eliminate urban heat islands if all buildings use reflective roofs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The effectiveness of reflective roofs in reducing urban heat depends on local conditions and may not be uniformly beneficial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reflective roofs are a failed strategy because they increase heating costs more than they save on cooling.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urban heat islands are caused mainly by an absence of reflective materials on older buildings.

explanation: The passage presents reflective roofs as helpful in some climates but notes that their benefits depend on local factors, so B captures the central idea.

passage.text: For decades, researchers assumed that the brain consolidates new memories mainly during deep slow-wave sleep. Recent studies, however, have shown that memories can also be strengthened during bursts of wakeful rest following learning. When volunteers who learned word pairs spent ten quiet minutes undistracted, they recalled more than volunteers who performed an attention-demanding task. The researchers propose that some memory stabilization may depend less on sleep stage and more on the absence of competing sensory input.

stem: Which choice best expresses the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sleep is not involved at all in memory consolidation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Memory consolidation occurs only during deep slow-wave sleep.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Quiet wakefulness can strengthen memories if the brain is not distracted by competing input.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sensory input is necessary for memory consolidation after learning.

explanation: The passage's key claim is that quiet, undistracted wakeful rest can enhance memory, not that sleep is irrelevant or the only route.

passage.text: Although steel and aluminum scaffolding are available, bamboo scaffolding persists on many high-rise construction sites in Hong Kong. Builders cite several practical reasons: bamboo is lightweight but strong, and work crews can erect or remove a full facade scaffold within hours. The slender poles leave sightlines unobstructed, and the process produces almost no noise, a major advantage in crowded districts. Unlike metal, bamboo requires seasoned poles and skilled workers, but its low material cost and easy transport still make it attractive.

stem: According to the passage, one practical reason construction crews continue to use bamboo scaffolding is that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: can be erected or removed quickly and generates minimal noise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: is stronger and more durable than steel or aluminum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: does not require seasoned poles or specially trained workers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: is the only material accepted for high-rise construction in Hong Kong.

explanation: The passage explicitly states that crews can erect or remove bamboo scaffolding within hours and that the process produces almost no noise.

passage.text: Languages do not split into new languages merely because communities become politically separate. Linguists point to social networks as the more powerful engine. When speakers communicate frequently, their vernaculars stay mutually intelligible. But if trade, geography, or migration sharply reduces contact, small pronunciation and grammar changes accumulate. After several generations, what was one language becomes several. Thus the rate of linguistic divergence is better predicted by the strength of everyday connections than by the drawing of borders.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Political separation almost always results in the creation of a new language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grammar changes are caused chiefly by migration and trade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Frequent communication between speakers makes languages gradually diverge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The development of separate languages depends more on changes in social contact than on political borders.

explanation: The passage argues that contact between speakers, not political separation, best predicts language divergence.

passage.text: Forests are often described as the planet's lungs, but they are also the planet's cooling pumps. Trees release water vapor and organic compounds that promote low clouds. Those clouds shade the canopy and regulate regional rainfall. Deforestation disrupts this cycle: without trees, the land dries and clouds thin, allowing more sunlight to reach the soil. An expanding body of research suggests that protecting forests may matter as much for cloud formation and rainfall as for carbon storage.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deforestation increases cloud cover by exposing dry soil.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Forests are more valuable as sources of carbon storage than as regulators of rainfall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By contributing to low cloud formation, forests help regulate rainfall and shield the ground from sunlight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clouds form independently of vegetation and are influenced mainly by ocean temperatures.

explanation: The passage emphasizes that forests promote low clouds, which shade the land and maintain rainfall, making C the central idea.

passage.text: Some ecologists argue that standard mapping practices overlook desert water systems. Many maps draw waterways as permanent blue lines, ignoring ephemeral streams that flow only after rains. These dry channels nonetheless support rich plant and animal life: gravel beneath them stores water for years, sudden floods carry seeds, and desert wildlife relies on the vegetation that appears in wet seasons. Because these habitats are absent from permanent-water inventories, conservation plans in arid regions may be missing critical areas.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ephemeral streams flow only after rain and therefore contain water only occasionally.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because standard water maps focus on permanent waterways, the ecological value of ephemeral desert streams may be overlooked.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Desert wildlife depends more on ephemeral streams than on permanent rivers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conservation plans will fail unless they include every ephemeral stream on a map.

explanation: The passage develops the idea that standard mapping of permanent waterways leaves out ecologically important ephemeral desert streams, so conservation may overlook them. Choice B states this central idea. A is a detail rather than the main point, C overstates the comparison, and D makes an absolute claim the passage does not support.

passage.text: Psychologists have noticed a paradox in smartphone navigation. People who use turn-by-turn directions often remember almost nothing about the streets they traveled; their spatial memory is nearly blank. Yet people who had consulted a paper map earlier usually outperform GPS users when later asked to draw maps or give directions. Researchers propose that the problem is not inaccuracy but passivity: the device becomes the navigator, so the user's internal cognitive map never forms. The efficiency of the immediate journey comes at the cost of lasting spatial knowledge.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn-by-turn GPS directions are more accurate than paper maps.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who use paper maps to navigate are always better at drawing maps than GPS users.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The efficiency of turn-by-turn navigation may reduce long-term spatial learning.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Smartphone navigation creates no lasting memories because users are passive.

explanation: The passage contrasts the immediate efficiency of turn-by-turn GPS with the finding that it interferes with forming lasting spatial knowledge. Choice C captures this central paradox. A is unsupported, B is an overstatement of the research finding, and D misstates the passage by making an absolute claim about all smartphone navigation.
