passage.text: Trees can release chemical cues through underground fungal networks when insects attack, and nearby trees sometimes respond by boosting their defenses. Some researchers nevertheless dispute the popular image of a 'wood wide web.' The fungal partner exchanges nutrients and water, but transmitting chemical alarms seems to bring the fungus no measurable benefit. A signal that benefits only the receiver while imposing costs on the sender is not an evolved communication system, they argue; it may be an incidental side effect of nutrient sharing. Controlled experiments have not yet settled this debate.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether underground fungal networks are genuine communication systems remains unresolved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Trees deliberately warn neighboring trees about insect attacks through fungal networks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fungal networks primarily exist to exchange nutrients and water, not chemicals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Researchers have shown that chemical warning signals are only accidental side effects.

explanation: The text says that fungal networks exchange nutrients and can carry warning cues, but researchers disagree about whether this constitutes evolved communication. Choice A states the central unresolved debate. B is too confident, C treats a supporting observation as the main point, and D contradicts the passage's statement that the debate has not been settled.

passage.text: A 2024 study examined how traditional Polynesian farmers transformed dry lowland soils on Hawai'i Island. By fragmenting basalt into gravel, mixing in organic matter, and constructing mounds that trapped solar heat, they created microclimates suitable for crops such as sweet potato. Researchers measured soil temperatures in replicated mounds and found that stone mulching raised nighttime soil temperatures by as much as 4°C, preventing root damage during cool winter months. The same technique also slowed evaporation, which may have been more important for tuber yield than the warmth itself.

stem: According to the text, which factor may have been more important for sweet potato yield than the warmth provided by the stone mounds?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fragmentation of basalt into gravel

choices.label: B
choices.text: The construction of mounds that trap solar heat

choices.label: C
choices.text: The raising of nighttime soil temperatures by 4°C

choices.label: D
choices.text: The slowing of evaporation caused by the stone mulch

explanation: The text explicitly states that stone mulching slowed evaporation, 'which may have been more important for tuber yield than the warmth itself.' Therefore D is correct. A, B, and C describe techniques or effects mentioned in the passage, but the text identifies slowed evaporation as potentially more important than warmth.

passage.text: The decline of small languages is often blamed on globalization, but linguists point to a more immediate cause: the closure of rural schools. When school systems consolidate village classrooms into distant regional schools, children lose daily immersion in their home language. A language can survive with few speakers if children hear and use it continually; what destroys it is the interruption of intergenerational transmission. Economic pressures and media exposure matter, but largely because they intensify this interruption. Thus, maintaining local schools, not merely celebrating linguistic heritage, is the most practical way to protect endangered languages.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rural school consolidation is the only reason languages lose intergenerational transmission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The more direct cause of language decline is interruption of intergenerational transmission, often brought on by rural school closures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Economic pressures and media exposure have no effect on language use unless schools close.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Celebrating linguistic heritage is sufficient to keep endangered languages alive.

explanation: The passage argues that language loss is most directly caused by interrupted intergenerational transmission and that rural school closures are a major source of this interruption. Choice B states this central claim. A overstates the role of school consolidation, C incorrectly minimizes economic and media effects, and D contradicts the passage's claim that more than celebration is needed.

passage.text: Although urban trees are often celebrated for capturing carbon, their most immediate benefit to city residents may be reducing heat. By shading pavement and releasing water vapor, mature trees can lower neighborhood air temperatures by several degrees, a relief that becomes critical during heat waves. This cooling effect is especially pronounced in low-income districts, where paved surfaces and little greenery produce the highest temperatures. Cities therefore increasingly prioritize tree planting in these areas as a cost-effective climate-adaptation measure.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban trees offer a variety of environmental benefits, with carbon capture being the most valuable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low-income districts suffer from high temperatures because they lack trees.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Urban trees matter chiefly because they can cool particularly hot neighborhoods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cities are spending too much money on tree-planting programs.

explanation: The passage argues that although carbon capture is often mentioned, the most immediate benefit of urban trees is heat reduction, especially in hot low-income neighborhoods. Choice C matches this central idea.

passage.text: The single-celled slime mold Physarum polycephalum has no brain, yet it can solve mazes and optimize networks. When researchers scatter oat flakes in patterns mirroring Tokyo's rail system, the mold grows links that resemble the actual train lines, balancing efficiency and cost. Scientists do not claim the organism thinks; rather, its simple rule of expanding toward food while pruning costly branches produces apparently intelligent outcomes. Such behaviors suggest that complex problem-solving can emerge without centralized planning.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Slime molds are more intelligent than many animals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Simple rules can explain the apparently intelligent behavior of slime molds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Slime molds are capable of designing better rail networks than human planners.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Laboratory experiments show that Physarum polycephalum can solve mazes.

explanation: The passage says the slime mold's behavior arises from simple rules, not thought, and suggests complex problem-solving can emerge without centralized planning. Choice B captures that central idea.

passage.text: The 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia introduced many Americans to new technology. While Alexander Graham Bell's telephone made its public debut there, attendance records show that the Corliss steam engine, a giant machine that powered other exhibits, was the fair's biggest draw. Visitors also lined up to ride the compressed-air railroad brake demonstrated by George Westinghouse. The telephone, by contrast, attracted modest curiosity. Despite the fair's many international pavilions, the machinery hall remained the center of attention.

stem: According to the text, which exhibit drew the largest crowds at the Centennial Exhibition?
explanation: The text states that attendance records show the Corliss steam engine was "the fair's biggest draw," meaning it drew the largest crowds.

passage.text: Cooperation among unrelated animals often seems to defy natural selection. Biologists explain it through repeated interactions: when individuals meet many times, helping now can be repaid later, whereas cheating destroys future gains. Mathematical models based on the Prisoner's Dilemma show that this 'tit for tat' strategy—cooperate first, then punish defection—can thrive. Yet in large, anonymous populations, cooperation is harder to sustain because encounters are less likely to be repeated. Thus, the structure of social relationships, not just individual benevolence, determines whether cooperation evolves.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cooperation among animals is rare because cheating usually succeeds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In large populations, 'tit for tat' is always more effective than in small groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Prisoner's Dilemma proves that unrelated animals cannot cooperate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeated encounters and social structure can allow cooperation to evolve.

explanation: The passage explains that repeated interactions and the structure of social relationships determine whether cooperation evolves. Choice D states this central idea.

passage.text: Old maps often survive as treasured artifacts, but historians who study them warn against reading them as precise geographical records. A medieval map may show a mountain range that never existed, a city in the wrong place, or a sea monster filling an unexplored region. These features do not mean the mapmaker was careless; they reflect the map's purposes, such as asserting political power or telling a symbolic story. To understand an old map, one must ask what it was used for, not just compare it to modern geography.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medieval mapmakers were generally less skilled than modern ones.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sea monsters and misplaced cities prove that old maps are unreliable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Old maps should be understood in terms of their historical purposes rather than modern accuracy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Political power was the only reason medieval maps contained errors.

explanation: The passage maintains that features of old maps reflect their purposes and that understanding them requires asking what each map was used for. Choice C best states this central idea.

passage.text: In the early 2000s, several US cities relaxed bans on urban beekeeping, prompting a surge in rooftop and backyard hives. Proponents celebrated benefits: pollination of community gardens, local honey production, and educational opportunities. But researchers soon noticed a darker side. Domestic bees, when kept at high densities, compete aggressively with wild pollinators for nectar and pollen, and can transmit diseases to them. The very practice intended to support urban nature may, in some cities, be undermining native bee populations.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban beekeeping, despite being intended to help urban nature, can harm native wild pollinators.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cities should not allow rooftop and backyard beehives because domestic bees spread disease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beekeeping benefits cities by pollinating community gardens and producing local honey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Native bee populations are declining because domestic bees compete with them for nectar.

explanation: The passage presents the benefits of urban beekeeping, then introduces research showing that high-density domestic bees compete with and transmit diseases to wild pollinators. The central idea is that well-intentioned urban beekeeping may harm native bees.

passage.text: The 'digital detox' industry promises that disconnecting from smartphones will restore attention spans and reduce anxiety. Yet a growing number of media scholars argue that these programs misdiagnose the problem. The issue, they contend, is not screens themselves but the extractive design of social media platforms, which maximize engagement by exploiting psychological vulnerabilities. A week offline may provide temporary relief, but it does not teach users to recognize manipulative interfaces or advocate for healthier technology. Without structural changes, the detox becomes a bandage rather than a cure.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Digital detox programs are ineffective because they are too brief to change lasting habits.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Media scholars believe social media companies deliberately exploit users' psychology to keep them engaged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who want better attention spans should reduce their smartphone use rather than delete social media.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The anxiety associated with smartphones is less about screen time than about the manipulative design of social media platforms.

explanation: The passage argues that digital detoxes misdiagnose the problem: the source of anxiety and distraction is not screens but the manipulative design of social media platforms. The central idea is that the real problem is platform design, not screen time itself.

passage.text: Archaeologists once relied on excavation and ground surveys to locate ancient settlements. Today, satellite imagery and machine-learning algorithms can identify subtle surface features—buried walls, dried riverbeds, even traces of roads—across vast regions. This remote mapping is faster and cheaper than traditional methods and allows researchers to protect sites before they are destroyed by development. However, imagery cannot reveal datable artifacts or cultural layers; ground verification remains essential. The technology has expanded the scale of discovery, not replaced the need for fieldwork.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Satellite imagery has rendered traditional archaeological excavation unnecessary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Machine learning allows archaeologists to identify buried walls and roads from space.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Remote sensing enables archaeologists to survey more land but still requires on-the-ground checking.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Archaeologists need faster, cheaper ways to protect ancient sites from development.

explanation: The passage describes how remote sensing enlarges the scale of archaeological discovery, but then notes that imagery cannot replace ground verification. The central idea is expansion plus continued need for fieldwork.

passage.text: Healthy reefs are noisy: fish grunts, shrimp snaps, and the low hum of invertebrates. In a recent experiment, researchers played recordings of healthy reefs underwater near degraded reefs on the Great Barrier Reef. Fish larvae, which use sound to navigate, settled in the acoustically enriched areas at up to twice the rate of controls. The technique, called 'acoustic enrichment', is not a cure—it cannot restore coral or water quality—but it may help jump-start recovery by attracting fish that graze algae and create conditions for coral regrowth.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fish larvae navigate to suitable habitats by listening to the sounds of a healthy reef.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acoustic enrichment is the most effective technique for restoring deteriorated coral reefs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Playing recordings of healthy reefs can attract fish to damaged reefs and support recovery, but it does not fix the underlying problems.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coral regrowth depends on the presence of fish that graze on algae.

explanation: The passage explains that acoustic enrichment attracts fish to degraded reefs and may aid recovery, while also stating it is not a cure for underlying damage. This balanced description is the central idea.

passage.text: A sourdough starter is a community of yeast and bacteria. Enthusiasts often insist that a starter is unique to its kitchen, claiming local microbes give each loaf a distinct flavor. But experiments have shown that over time, the microbial mix in a starter is determined more by the type of flour and feeding schedule than by location. A San Francisco starter and a Tokyo starter made with the same flour and routine will become more alike than different. The romance of place in sourdough is largely a myth; the craft is in the maintenance, not the geography.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The microorganisms in a sourdough starter are primarily influenced by flour type and how it is fed, not by location.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A sourdough starter made in San Francisco cannot be distinguished from one made in Tokyo.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who believe local microbes affect sourdough flavor are ignoring basic science.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sourdough starters require careful maintenance to keep their yeast and bacteria alive.

explanation: The passage contrasts the myth of local uniqueness with experimental evidence that flour type and feeding schedule, not geography, determine the microbial mix. The central idea is that maintenance and ingredients matter more than location.

passage.text: Biologists studying Swainson’s thrushes have found that migrating birds can sleep while flying. Sensors attached to the birds during transoceanic flights recorded brief “micro-naps” lasting only seconds, during which the birds stayed on course. The naps occurred most often in the second half of the night, as if the thrushes waited until they were over open water before reducing alertness. This finding complicates the usual assumption that sleep requires sustained, uninterrupted blocks of time.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Migrating Swainson’s thrushes sleep less when flying over open water than over land.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sleep in animals may not require sustained blocks of time if brief in-flight naps can support it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The main danger of migrating at night is the risk of falling asleep while on course.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Biologists had long assumed that migrating birds never sleep while flying.

explanation: The text describes how Swainson’s thrushes take very brief micro-naps during flight, concluding that this “complicates the usual assumption that sleep requires sustained, uninterrupted blocks of time.” Thus, the central idea is that sleep may not require sustained blocks if brief naps can serve the purpose.

passage.text: Coastal desalination plants create fresh water by forcing seawater through membranes, leaving a salty brine that is often pumped back into the ocean. In the Red Sea, this brine can form plumes that sink and spread along the seafloor because it is denser than the surrounding water. A monitoring study of reefs near one plant found elevated salinity only within several hundred meters of the outfall; beyond that distance, readings matched normal seawater. The authors concluded that the site’s strong currents limit the area where brine could affect sensitive corals.

stem: According to the text, what did the monitoring study of the Red Sea reef find?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No elevated salinity was detected anywhere near the desalination plant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The impact of the brine plume on salinity was limited to a relatively small area.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Brine plumes affected coral reefs at greater distances than expected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Strong currents carried brine to reefs farther from the plant.

explanation: The text explicitly states that the monitoring study “found elevated salinity only within several hundred meters of the outfall; beyond that distance, readings matched normal seawater.” This means the brine plume’s effect on salinity was limited to a relatively small area.

passage.text: The mid-nineteenth-century spread of potatoes in colonial India is often told as a triumph of a useful crop, but the reality was more conditional. The British had introduced potatoes decades earlier, yet cultivation expanded unevenly and only after railroads connected inland markets to port cities. In regions with reliable irrigation and secure land tenure, farmers planted potatoes as a cash crop; in dry, insecure regions, they did not. Thus the potato did not conquer India on its own merits; it succeeded where infrastructure and institutions made it profitable.

stem: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Potatoes became widespread in colonial India only in areas where conditions made them commercially viable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The British introduced potatoes to India primarily to prevent famines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mid-nineteenth-century Indian farmers rejected potatoes because they were unfamiliar.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Railroads had little effect on the adoption of new crops in colonial India.

explanation: The passage argues that the potato’s spread was conditional and uneven, succeeding only where infrastructure such as railroads and institutions such as secure land tenure made it profitable. Choice A captures that central claim.

passage.text: Recent study of clay tablets from the ancient Mesopotamian city of Uruk challenges the view that writing was created solely for accounting. The earliest tablets do record barley, sheep, and laborers, and some bear cylinder-seal impressions from administrators. But a small number of tablets contain disputes over field boundaries and notes about deliveries of construction materials, suggesting that record keeping and official communication developed together. Even so, administrative archives far outnumber literary and legal texts for centuries after writing’s origin.

stem: According to the text, which of the following is true of the earliest Uruk tablets?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They were primarily administrative records rather than literary or legal texts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They contain no information about deliveries or construction materials.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They were written by farmers to document land ownership.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are entirely made of baked clay from cylinder seals.

explanation: The text says that the earliest tablets “do record barley, sheep, and laborers” and that “administrative archives far outnumber literary and legal texts.” Thus, they were primarily administrative records, not literary or legal works.

passage.text: Many gardeners believe that local wildflower species are blooming earlier in recent years because of warmer spring temperatures. A team of botanists studied this idea by comparing forty years of first-bloom dates with temperature records from the same region.

stem: Which finding from the study would most directly support the gardeners' belief?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In warm years, wildflowers produced more flowers per plant than in cool years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: First-bloom dates were nearly identical in warm springs and cool springs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In years with more rainfall, wildflowers bloomed earlier regardless of temperature.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In warmer springs, the average first-bloom date shifted earlier by about six days.

explanation: Choice D directly links warmer spring temperatures to earlier blooming. A concerns flower size, B contradicts the belief, and C supports rainfall rather than temperature as the cause.

passage.text: A transportation official argues that adding protected bicycle lanes to city streets decreases the number of serious traffic accidents involving all road users. The city compared accident records from streets with new bike lanes and similar streets without them.

stem: Which finding from the city's records would most directly support the official's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The number of cyclists riding on streets with protected lanes increased by about 10 percent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serious accidents on streets with protected lanes fell by 18 percent in the year after installation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Average traffic speed on streets with protected lanes increased slightly after installation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minor bicycle thefts in neighborhoods near protected lanes rose by 5 percent.

explanation: Choice B shows a decline in serious accidents after protected lanes were added, directly supporting the official's argument. A is about ridership, C is about speed, and D is about thefts rather than traffic accidents.

passage.text: Some historians claim that the road network of ancient Rome was designed mainly for military movement rather than for trade. To test this, a researcher read reports written by Roman army officers.

stem: Which finding from the army reports would most directly support the historians' claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Army commanders ordered legions to use the main roads when moving soldiers and equipment to threatened borders.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Merchants paid tolls to transport wine and olive oil along the main roads.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Roadside inns recorded the quantities of cloth and grain carried by traders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Engineers built the main roads with layered stone and gravel to support heavy carts.

explanation: Choice A directly shows military use of the roads, supporting the claim that the road network was mainly for military movement. B and C emphasize trade, while D describes construction technique, not purpose.

passage.text: A sleep researcher claims that people who use smartphones or tablets in the hour before bedtime have more difficulty falling asleep than people who do not. A clinic asked 500 adults to record their screen use and how long it took them to fall asleep each night for two weeks.

stem: Which finding from the clinic's data would most directly support the researcher's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Screen use before bed was more common on weekends than on weekdays.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who did not use screens before bed took longer to fall asleep than people who did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who used screens before bed took an average of 25 minutes longer to fall asleep than people who did not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: People who used screens before bed reported needing a brighter bedroom to fall asleep.

explanation: Choice C directly connects screen use before bed with taking longer to fall asleep. A is irrelevant, B contradicts the claim, and D does not address difficulty falling asleep.

passage.text: An astronomer proposes that a newly discovered exoplanet, K2-188c, may have liquid water on its surface. Liquid water requires surface temperatures roughly between 273 and 373 kelvin and sufficient atmospheric pressure.

stem: Which finding would most directly support the astronomer's proposal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The planet's surface temperature averages 500 kelvin, too hot for liquid water to exist.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The planet's estimated surface temperature is 280 kelvin, and its atmosphere is dense enough to support liquid water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The planet is made mostly of rock and iron, like the inner planets of our solar system.

choices.label: D
choices.text: K2-188c orbits very close to its star, so its surface is probably hotter than Mercury's.

explanation: Choice B provides the key conditions for liquid water: a suitable temperature and a dense enough atmosphere. A and D give temperatures too high, and C says nothing about water or temperature.

passage.text: Marina is a biologist studying urban heat islands. In one city, she notices that downtown districts have fewer trees and record higher summer temperatures than nearby residential districts. She hypothesizes that increasing the number of street trees in a district causes that district to have cooler summer temperatures.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Marina's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Districts that added street trees over a five-year period showed a measurable decrease in average summer afternoon temperatures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Districts with more paved parking lots have both fewer trees and higher summer temperatures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A neighborhood with tree-lined streets had lower temperatures than a neighborhood in a different city with no trees.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Street trees require watering during drought, and districts that watered their trees had cooler summers.

explanation: Choice A directly supports the causal claim by showing that when street trees are added, temperatures decrease. Choices B, C, and D involve additional factors or imperfect comparisons that do not provide direct causal support.

passage.text: Some psychologists claim that taking a short nap immediately after studying a list of foreign-language vocabulary words improves recall the next day. They argue that sleep soon after encoding helps consolidate the new words into long-term memory.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the psychologists' claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who stayed awake for 12 hours after studying remembered more words than those who napped.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants who napped for 20 minutes after studying recalled a greater percentage of vocabulary words after a night's sleep than those who did not nap.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants who napped before studying recalled fewer words than those who did not nap.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who napped for 2 hours recalled more words than those who napped for 20 minutes.

explanation: Choice B directly supports the claim by comparing participants who napped after studying with those who did not nap; the napping group had better recall. Choice A weakens the claim, Choice C is about napping before studying, and Choice D lacks a comparison with no nap.

passage.text: Some planetary geologists claim that Venus currently has active plate tectonics similar to Earth's, based on radar images showing rift zones and possible volcanic features.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the geologists' claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Radar images show large rift zones and volcanic features on Venus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Computer models suggest Venus had plate tectonics early in its history.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeated spacecraft radar measurements over eight years show no sideways shift or deformation along Venus's rift zones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The surface temperature of Venus is hot enough to melt lead.

explanation: Choice C weakens the claim by showing that Venus's crust is not currently moving, which is a key expectation of active plate tectonics. Choices A and B support or do not contradict the claim; Choice D is irrelevant to crustal motion.

passage.text: An environmental policy analyst argues that recycling lithium from old electric-vehicle batteries is currently more expensive than mining new lithium, and therefore manufacturers will not adopt it unless government incentives change.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Government subsidies for lithium mining have made battery production cheaper overall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A recycling plant can recover lithium for 20% less than the cost of mining new lithium.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several electric-vehicle makers announced they will use recycled lithium even if it costs the same as mined lithium.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Companies that purchase recycled lithium pay 25% more per ton than companies that purchase newly mined lithium.

explanation: Choice D directly supports the analyst's claim by showing that recycled lithium is more expensive than newly mined lithium. Choices B and C contradict or undermine the argument, and Choice A does not address the cost of recycling versus mining.

passage.text: A sports medicine researcher claims that for adults aged 20–35, high-intensity interval training is more effective than moderate continuous exercise at reducing self-reported anxiety after eight weeks.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adults aged 36–50 who did high-intensity interval training reported lower anxiety than adults aged 36–50 who did moderate continuous exercise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In a randomized trial of adults aged 20–35, high-intensity interval training participants scored significantly lower on an anxiety scale than moderate continuous exercise participants after eight weeks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In a randomized trial of adults aged 20–35, both exercise groups reported less anxiety than a control group that did not exercise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Moderate continuous exercise participants enjoyed exercising more than high-intensity interval training participants and were more likely to continue exercising.

explanation: Choice B directly supports the claim by comparing the exact age group and training types described, with high-intensity interval training leading to lower anxiety. Choice A involves a different age group, Choice C lacks a comparison between the two training types, and Choice D is about enjoyment rather than anxiety.

passage.text: Marine biologists have proposed that clownfish larvae use chemical cues to locate the sea anemones where they will live. According to this proposal, the ability to recognize anemone scent is innate and works from the moment the larvae hatch.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the proposal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Newly hatched clownfish larvae in a maze consistently chose water that had contained sea anemones over plain seawater.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adult clownfish raised in a tank without sea anemones showed no preference for anemone-scented water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clownfish larvae could not distinguish between the scents of two closely related species of sea anemones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When clownfish larvae were exposed to predator scents, they swam toward seagrass instead of toward sea anemones.

explanation: Choice A directly supports the proposal by showing that newly hatched larvae, with no prior experience, prefer anemone-scented water. The other choices either address learned preference, irrelevant discrimination, or predator avoidance.

passage.text: An educational psychologist argues that, when students listen to recorded lectures, taking notes by drawing sketches is more effective than typing notes because sketching forces students to organize visual information.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Students who typed notes spent more time reviewing their notes than students who sketched notes did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In a controlled experiment, students who sketched notes recalled more main ideas from a lecture than students who typed notes did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students who sketched notes said the lectures were more enjoyable than students who typed notes said they were.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Typed notes contained more abbreviations and incomplete phrases than sketched notes did.

explanation: Choice B most directly supports the claim by showing that sketch notes produce better recall, which is the outcome the argument predicts. The other choices address time spent, enjoyment, or note format rather than learning effectiveness.

passage.text: Some paleontologists have argued that the dinosaur Troodon was warm-blooded. They point to its rapid juvenile growth as evidence of a high metabolic rate.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Troodon fossils from polar regions have the same bone structure as fossils from tropical regions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Troodon growth rings show that the animal added new bone tissue continuously during every month of the year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Troodon nests have been found in large communal sites, suggesting adults cared for their young.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Troodon growth rings show that it stopped growing during cool months and resumed only when temperatures rose, a pattern seen in cold-blooded animals.

explanation: Choice D weakens the argument because it indicates that Troodon's growth depended on outside temperatures, contradicting the idea of a warm-blooded, internally regulated metabolism. Choices A and B support the warm-blooded interpretation, and C is irrelevant.

passage.text: A poetry critic argues that the line breaks in a new poem create a halting, interrupted rhythm, which mirrors the speaker's hesitation about entering a house.

stem: Which quotation from the poem best supports the critic's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "The sun / rose over the / hills and / the valley."

choices.label: B
choices.text: "She left / at dawn, / before the / streetlights went out."

choices.label: C
choices.text: "I meant / to knock, but / then something / inside me / turned away."

choices.label: D
choices.text: "Wind shook / the windows, / and the rain / began to fall."

explanation: Choice C best supports the critic's claim because its line breaks interrupt the sentence into hesitant fragments, especially at "I meant / to knock, but / then something," creating the halting rhythm described. The other quotations are neutral or descriptive.

passage.text: A historian argues that the Roman grain dole and public spectacles—sometimes called "bread and circuses"—decreased ordinary Romans' political involvement by keeping them entertained and distracted.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Public games were most crowded on days when no meetings of the popular assemblies were scheduled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After the Roman government lowered the price of grain, attendance at meetings of the popular assemblies stayed about the same.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Candidates for political office sometimes sponsored free games in order to build popularity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A fourth-century Roman wrote of spending all afternoon at the races, where "we cheer the charioteers but never discuss the city's affairs."

explanation: Choice D directly supports the historian's argument by showing a Roman choosing spectacles over political discussion. Choice B actually challenges the idea that cheap food reduced engagement, while A and C do not show decreased political involvement.

passage.text: In many cities, summer heat waves cause residents to rely heavily on air-conditioning, driving up electricity bills. Architects have proposed covering rooftops with vegetation, creating green roofs, which are thought to keep buildings cooler. A city planning department recruited owners of similar office buildings and arranged for green roofs to be installed on some of them. After a summer, the department compared electricity use for air-conditioning between buildings with green roofs and buildings with conventional dark roofs.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the claim that green roofs reduce air-conditioning energy use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Buildings with green roofs were home to more species of birds and insects than buildings with conventional roofs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Over the summer, buildings with green roofs used substantially less electricity for air-conditioning than similar buildings with conventional roofs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Workers in buildings with green roofs reported feeling cooler than workers in buildings with conventional roofs, even though indoor temperatures were the same.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The installation cost of a green roof is higher than that of a conventional roof, but green roofs require less frequent replacement.

explanation: Choice B directly links green roofs to lower electricity use for air-conditioning, which supports the claim. The other choices concern biodiversity, subjective comfort, or cost rather than energy use.

passage.text: Sleep researchers have long suspected that sleep helps consolidate newly learned information. To test this idea, a team asked college students to study a list of twenty unfamiliar vocabulary words. Half of the students then napped for twenty minutes; the other half stayed awake and watched a nature documentary. All students returned the next morning for a multiple-choice vocabulary test.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the claim that a short nap improves memory for newly learned material?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Students who stayed awake reported having studied the words more often than students who napped.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students who napped reported feeling more rested during the test than students who stayed awake.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students who napped answered more vocabulary questions correctly than students who stayed awake.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students who watched the documentary said they remembered more of it than the vocabulary words.

explanation: Choice C compares vocabulary performance, the outcome of interest, and shows an advantage for nappers over non-nappers. The other choices address study habits, alertness, or memory of a video rather than memory for the learned words.

passage.text: A popular environmental guideline is to eat local to reduce carbon emissions, since shipping food long distances consumes fuel. However, some food scientists argue that production methods, such as growing crops in heated greenhouses, can emit far more carbon than transportation. They therefore caution that local food is not always more climate-friendly than imported food.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the food scientists' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Locally grown tomatoes from heated greenhouses caused more carbon emissions per kilogram than tomatoes shipped from distant open fields.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Food imported by airplane caused more carbon emissions per kilogram than food grown locally and transported by truck.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Consumers at farmers markets said they choose local produce primarily because it is fresher, not because of environmental concerns.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Food shipped within the same country produced less carbon emissions than food shipped internationally by boat.

explanation: Choice A shows that growing method can outweigh transportation distance, exactly the food scientists' argument. Choices B and D emphasize the importance of transportation, and choice C concerns consumer motivation rather than emissions.

passage.text: Some psychologists study the effects of smartphone presence on focused thinking. In an experiment, participants performed a series of logic puzzles. Each participant's phone, silenced and set to not notify, was placed either on the desk in view, in the participant's pocket or bag, or in a separate room. The researchers recorded how many puzzles each participant solved correctly.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the claim that merely seeing one's phone reduces performance on cognitive tasks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants whose phones were in another room looked at the puzzles for more time than participants whose phones were on the desk.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants whose phones were on the desk solved fewer puzzles correctly than participants whose phones were in another room.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants whose phones were in their pockets solved about the same number of puzzles as participants whose phones were on the desk.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who saw a notification appear on a nearby screen solved fewer puzzles than participants who did not see a notification.

explanation: Choice B directly compares the visible phone condition with the phone-in-another-room condition and shows worse performance when the phone is visible. The other choices involve time spent, no difference, or active notifications rather than mere presence.

passage.text: Many people worry that social media increases loneliness, but researchers argue that the effect may depend on how it is used. Their hypothesis is that using social media actively, such as exchanging messages with close friends, strengthens social bonds, whereas passively scrolling through content without interacting makes people feel more isolated. To test this, they tracked adults' social media behavior and measured loneliness over one month.

stem: Which finding, if true, would best support the researchers' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who used social media passively for three or more hours a day showed no change in loneliness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants who sent direct messages to close friends were no less lonely at the end of the month than participants who only scrolled through feeds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most participants who reported low loneliness at the start of the month also reported high levels of active social media use at the end of the month.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who increased direct messaging with close friends showed lower loneliness, while those who increased passive scrolling showed higher loneliness.

explanation: Choice D directly matches the hypothesis: active use corresponds to lower loneliness and passive use to higher loneliness. Choice C is only an association that may reflect reverse causation, while A and B contradict or fail to support the proposed distinction.

passage.text: Some historians argue that the ancient city of Tazara collapsed primarily because a prolonged drought devastated its agriculture, not because it was conquered by outside forces. According to this view, the city's population dispersed when crops failed and water supplies shrank.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historians' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excavations reveal mass graves containing weapons and battle injuries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Soil samples from the period show a sharp drop in rainfall and in pollen from crop plants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A chronicle from a neighboring empire boasts of conquering Tazara.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trade goods from distant regions continued to appear in Tazara's ruins.

explanation: The hypothesis says drought caused collapse. Soil samples showing a sharp drop in rainfall and crop pollen directly indicate a severe drought that could devastate agriculture, supporting the hypothesis. The battle-related findings and the conquest chronicle suggest invasion, which weakens the hypothesis, and continued trade is irrelevant.

passage.text: Paleontologist Dr. Elena Voss argues that the dinosaur species Ferrosaurus was warm-blooded. She points to its large body size and active predatory habits, which in modern animals are associated with maintaining a constant internal body temperature. Voss's conclusion, however, remains controversial.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Dr. Voss's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ferrosaurus bones show a type of tissue associated with rapid, continuous growth, a feature common in warm-blooded animals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fossils of Ferrosaurus have been found in the same rock layers as fossils of crocodile-like reptiles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ferrosaurus had a large nasal cavity, which may have helped it shed excess heat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isotope ratios in Ferrosaurus teeth vary with seasonal temperature changes, as expected for an animal that cannot regulate its own body heat.

explanation: The isotope finding indicates that Ferrosaurus's body chemistry tracked external seasonal temperatures, which is evidence against warm-bloodedness. The growth-tissue and nasal-cavity findings are more consistent with warm-bloodedness, and the rock-layer association is irrelevant.

passage.text: Some linguists have argued that bilingual children develop stronger problem-solving skills than monolingual children, because managing two languages exercises executive-control functions.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support this argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In a series of sorting tasks, bilingual children outperformed monolingual children on tests requiring flexible switching between rules.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bilingual children scored lower than monolingual children on vocabulary tests in each language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monolingual children and bilingual children performed equally on a memory task involving lists of words.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bilingual children sometimes mixed words from two languages in a single sentence.

explanation: The argument claims that bilingualism improves executive-control functions. The sorting-task result directly shows bilingual children performing better on a test of flexible rule-switching, a core executive-control skill. The other choices either show a disadvantage, no difference, or behavior unrelated to problem-solving.

passage.text: Some marine biologists hypothesize that humpback whales use bubble nets primarily to corral small fish into dense groups, making them easier to eat.

stem: Which finding, if true, would best support this hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Humpback whales sometimes emit sounds while feeding but not while traveling.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When fish are scarce, humpback whales spend less time bubble-net feeding and more time migrating.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Underwater video shows that fish swim away from the center of the bubble net and become tightly clustered before the whale lunges upward.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bubble nets are used by humpback whales in all oceans but not by any other whale species.

explanation: The video directly shows the proposed mechanism: the bubble net causes fish to cluster tightly, which would make them easier for the whale to eat. The other choices describe behaviors or distributions that do not show bubble nets are used to corral fish.

passage.text: Some archaeologists propose that the stone statues on Rapa Nui were moved from the quarries to their platforms using a “walking” technique—rocking and rotating the statues upright—rather than by dragging them horizontally on sledges.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support this proposal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The statues' bases are carved flat, which would prevent rocking motion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Historical accounts from early European visitors describe statues being dragged on wooden sledges.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replicas with the statues' characteristic D-shaped bases can be “walked” forward by teams pulling on ropes while rocking the statue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Experiments with scale models show that horizontal dragging requires less force than rocking upright.

explanation: The replicas demonstrate that the proposed walking technique is physically feasible and uses features of the statues. The other choices describe obstacles or evidence that dragging was used, which would weaken rather than support the proposal.

passage.text: Marine biologists have hypothesized that the vivid orange stripes of the lionfish serve as a warning to potential predators, signaling that the fish is dangerous to eat.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the biologists' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lionfish are more active at night, when their orange stripes are difficult for other fish to see.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In aquariums, lionfish that are fed a diet lacking certain pigments lose their bright orange color.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Predators that have eaten a lionfish become sick and later avoid attacking fish with similar orange stripes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lionfish live among brightly colored coral, which may make them harder for predators to spot.

explanation: If predators become sick after eating a lionfish and then learn to avoid similarly striped fish, that directly supports the idea that the bright stripes function as a warning signal.

passage.text: Some historians argue that the collapse of the ancient city of Tira was caused primarily by a prolonged drought that drastically reduced crop yields.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historians' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Records show that Tira continued importing grain from neighboring regions after the alleged drought began.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lake sediments near Tira contain a layer of dust and reduced pollen that dates to the period just before the city's population declined.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Archaeologists have found evidence that Tira's outer walls were repaired several times before the collapse.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pottery from Tira appears in distant sites after the city was abandoned.

explanation: Sediment evidence of a drought beginning just before the population decline directly supports the claim that drought was a primary cause of the city's collapse.

passage.text: A psychologist proposes that people who write gratitude letters feel happier mainly because the activity strengthens social bonds, not merely because it forces them to focus on positive events.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the psychologist's proposal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: People who wrote gratitude letters showed greater increases in happiness than people who wrote neutral diary entries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who wrote gratitude letters were more likely to smile during the writing session than people who wrote neutral letters.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants who wrote about positive events without addressing them to another person experienced similar happiness gains.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When researchers statistically accounted for participants' increased feelings of connection to their letter recipients, the apparent benefit of writing gratitude letters was no longer significant.

explanation: If the benefit disappears once feelings of connection are taken into account, that indicates social connection is the key mechanism, supporting the psychologist's proposal.

passage.text: City planners have hypothesized that adding rows of trees along urban streets reduces traffic speeds by narrowing the driver's view of the roadway ahead.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support this hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Streets lined with trees had significantly lower average vehicle speeds than comparable streets without trees.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drivers on tree-lined streets were more likely to use their phones than drivers on open streets.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pedestrians on tree-lined streets reported feeling safer from crime.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tree species planted most often have deep roots that can uplift pavement.

explanation: Lower average speeds on tree-lined streets is the predicted outcome of the hypothesis, directly supporting the claim that trees reduce traffic speed.

passage.text: Some nutritionists hypothesize that eating fish rich in omega-3 fatty acids lowers the risk of age-related cognitive decline. To investigate, researchers surveyed older adults about their fish consumption and then tested their memory performance over five years.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Older adults who ate fish at least twice a week also tended to exercise more often than those who rarely ate fish.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fish eaten by most participants in the study was caught locally and contained low levels of mercury.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Among participants with similar exercise habits and education levels, those who ate fish at least twice a week showed slower memory decline than those who ate fish less than once a month.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who ate fish less than once a month were more likely to report a family history of memory problems.

explanation: This finding shows the predicted association between fish consumption and slower memory decline while controlling for other relevant factors, directly supporting the hypothesis.

passage.text: The director of the Oak Creek Public Library argues that its summer reading program helps students avoid summer learning loss. She claims that children who take part in the program return to school in the fall with stronger reading skills than they would have had without the program. Which finding, if true, would most directly support the director's claim?

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the director's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Students who completed the library's summer reading program scored significantly higher on September reading assessments than comparable students who did not participate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The library loaned out more books in July and August than in any other months of the year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Parents praised the summer reading program for offering flexible hours and a wide variety of books.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The summer reading program has been offered at the library for over twenty years.

explanation: Choice A directly supports the claim by showing that participating students had stronger reading performance than comparable nonparticipants. The other choices describe circulation, satisfaction, or program history, none of which establishes an effect on reading skills.

passage.text: An entomologist argues that the growing popularity of backyard beekeeping in cities could unintentionally hurt native bees. According to the entomologist, honeybees are abundant and efficient foragers, and when many hives are concentrated in one city, honeybees may outcompete native bees for limited nectar. Which finding, if true, would most directly support the entomologist's argument?

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the entomologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Honeybees can visit thousands of flowers in a single day.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In neighborhoods with many beehives, native bumblebees collected nectar from significantly fewer flowers and raised fewer new queens than in neighborhoods with few hives.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Native bees are generally solitary and do not produce honey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urban gardens provide a wide variety of flowering plants through the growing season.

explanation: Choice B directly supports the claim by showing that where honeybee hives are numerous, native bees collect less nectar and reproduce less successfully, consistent with competition for nectar. The other choices do not show harm to native bees.

passage.text: A historian is writing about the social effects of Johannes Gutenberg's printing press. The historian claims that the printing press transformed the production of books, but it did not immediately create a broadly literate public. Which quotation, if true, would most directly support the historian's claim?

stem: Which quotation, if true, would most directly support the historian's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gutenberg developed his printing press in Mainz, Germany, in the mid-fifteenth century.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The earliest printed books were designed to imitate handwritten manuscripts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By 1500, copies of printed books were common in European cities, but only a small elite could read them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Printing allowed identical copies of a text to be produced quickly and cheaply.

explanation: Choice C supports the claim by showing that although printed books were widespread, actual reading ability remained limited to a small elite. The other choices provide background details about the printing press but do not address the literacy of the public.

passage.text: A sleep researcher claims that sleep deprivation weakens the brain's ability to store new information. The researcher believes that getting too little sleep interferes with the consolidation of memories formed during the day. Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's claim?

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The brain cycles through several stages of sleep during the night.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some people report that they can function well on less than six hours of sleep.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bright light exposure can make people feel more alert after a short night's sleep.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adults who slept fewer than seven hours remembered significantly fewer items from a word list than adults who slept eight hours.

explanation: Choice D directly supports the claim by showing that less sleep is associated with worse memory performance. The other choices describe sleep architecture, subjective alertness, or light exposure, none of which directly addresses memory storage.

passage.text: After a city added protected bicycle lanes to a busy downtown avenue, the mayor said that the new bike lanes have slowed traffic and increased congestion for drivers. City planners now want to test this claim. Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the mayor's claim?

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the mayor's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The number of people riding bicycles on the avenue doubled after the lanes were installed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Average automobile travel time across the avenue decreased by 12 percent after the lanes were installed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surveyed drivers said they felt less safe when driving near cyclists.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bike lanes were installed as part of a broader street-resurfacing project.

explanation: Choice B weakens the mayor's claim by showing that automobile travel times actually decreased after the bike lanes were installed, which contradicts the claim of increased congestion. The other choices do not provide evidence about driving speed or congestion.

passage.text: Researchers have proposed that many desert plants cope with periods of little rain by increasing their production of flavonoids, compounds that help protect plant cells from damage caused by drought. To test this idea, they grew two groups of a common desert shrub under identical temperature and sunlight conditions. One group received normal watering; the other group received no water for three weeks, then was rewatered.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The shrubs that were kept dry produced significantly more flavonoids during the drought than the well-watered shrubs did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The well-watered shrubs grew taller than the drought-stressed shrubs over the study period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When the dry shrubs were rewatered, their flavonoid levels returned to the same level as the well-watered shrubs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drought-stressed shrubs showed wilting and yellowing leaves before the rewatering.

explanation: The hypothesis predicts that drought triggers increased flavonoid production. Choice A directly confirms this by showing that drought-stressed shrubs produced more flavonoids than well-watered shrubs did.

passage.text: A city council member claims that the bike-sharing system launched in the city last year has reduced traffic congestion in the downtown area. Supporting this claim requires evidence that congestion actually decreased after the system was introduced and that the decrease is connected to bike-sharing.

stem: Which finding would provide the strongest direct support for the council member's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bike-sharing system now has more than 1,000 registered users.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Since the bike-sharing launch, the number of downtown parking spaces has increased.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Average travel time during downtown rush hour decreased by 15% after bike-sharing stations opened.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several other cities have reported lower pollution levels after starting bike-share programs.

explanation: Choice C directly links the bike-sharing launch to reduced downtown congestion by showing that rush-hour travel time decreased after stations opened. The other choices either fail to measure congestion or refer to unrelated cities.

passage.text: Astronomers have hypothesized that an exoplanet orbiting a small star could contain liquid water on its surface. Liquid water can exist only within a narrow temperature range, so the planet's surface temperature is crucial to this hypothesis.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly undermine the hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The exoplanet has a thin atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The exoplanet's average surface temperature is -85 degrees Celsius.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The exoplanet is about 40 light-years from Earth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The exoplanet completes one orbit every 18 days.

explanation: Surface temperatures as low as -85 degrees Celsius are far below the range where liquid water can persist, directly weakening the hypothesis. The other choices do not address the possibility of liquid water.

passage.text: A school is considering a new vocabulary-learning policy. A teacher claims that students remember new words better if they practice for ten minutes each day rather than for an hour once a week, even when the total amount of study time is the same.

stem: Which evidence, if true, would most directly support the teacher's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Students in the daily-practice group reported that they enjoyed studying vocabulary more than students in the weekly group did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students in the weekly-practice group had to review more words in each session than the daily-practice group did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students in both groups spent a total of about one hour per week practicing vocabulary.

choices.label: D
choices.text: On a delayed vocabulary test, the daily-practice group correctly identified 25% more words than the weekly-practice group.

explanation: The teacher claims daily practice leads to better retention. Choice D directly measures retention and shows the daily group outperformed the weekly group on a delayed test.

passage.text: A conservation group has claimed that a proposed hiking trail would not harm the endangered bird population in a coastal reserve. Critics argue that new trails usually increase human disturbance and drive birds away.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the conservation group's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In a nearby coastal reserve where a similar trail was opened, the number of endangered bird nesting pairs dropped by 30% over the next five years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hikers who responded to a survey said they would remain on designated paths while using the trail.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The proposed trail would be built mainly in an area of the reserve where these birds are rarely observed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reserve currently has no hiking trails, but it has several unpaved roads used by park staff.

explanation: The group claims the trail will not harm birds. Choice A directly weakens that claim by showing that a similar trail elsewhere led to a significant decline in nesting pairs. The other choices either suggest limited disturbance or are irrelevant.

passage.text: Researchers investigated whether the timing of sleep affects how well students remember new vocabulary. In the study, one group of students learned a list of words and then went to sleep immediately. A second group learned the same words at the same time of day but stayed awake for several hours before sleeping. The next morning, both groups took a vocabulary test.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis that sleep soon after learning helps strengthen memory?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The two groups recalled nearly the same number of words on the test.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The students who slept immediately after learning recalled significantly more words than the students who stayed awake.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The students who stayed awake before sleeping recalled significantly more words than the students who slept immediately.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students who took a brief nap after learning performed about the same as students who did not nap.

explanation: The group that slept immediately after learning recalls more words, directly supporting the hypothesis that sleep soon after learning helps memory.

passage.text: Environmental scientists wanted to know whether tree cover can reduce high summer temperatures in cities. They selected twenty neighborhoods in the same city and measured the percentage of ground covered by tree canopies in each one. They also recorded the highest temperature in each neighborhood on five separate hot afternoons in July.

stem: Which finding, if true, would best support the claim that tree cover lowers urban air temperatures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The neighborhoods with the highest percentages of tree canopy had the lowest recorded afternoon temperatures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The neighborhoods with the highest percentages of tree canopy had the highest recorded afternoon temperatures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The neighborhoods with the highest percentages of tree canopy were also the most densely built.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No consistent relationship was found between tree canopy percentage and afternoon temperature.

explanation: The expected pattern—more tree canopy corresponding to lower temperatures—directly supports the claim that tree cover lowers urban heat.

passage.text: Health researchers investigated whether playing action video games can improve spatial abilities. They recruited high school students who had little experience with video games and measured their spatial ability with a standard mental rotation test. The students then played an action video game for forty-five minutes each day for eight weeks. At the end of the eight weeks, they took the same mental rotation test.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the claim that playing action video games improves spatial ability?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The students' average mental rotation score was significantly higher after eight weeks than before.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most students reported that they enjoyed playing the action video game.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students who played the action game also improved their reaction speed on a separate task.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The students' average mental rotation score was not significantly different after eight weeks from their score before.

explanation: If there was no significant improvement in the skills the game was expected to improve, the claim that playing the game improves spatial ability is weakened.

passage.text: A sociologist wanted to learn whether opening a community garden increases social connections among neighbors. The sociologist surveyed residents who lived within one block of a planned garden, asking them how many neighbors they knew by name. After the garden opened and had been in use for a year, the sociologist surveyed the same residents again with the same question.

stem: Which finding, if true, would best support the hypothesis that community gardens increase neighbors' social connections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Residents knew fewer neighbors by name after the garden opened than they had before.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Residents knew roughly the same number of neighbors before and after the garden opened.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residents knew more neighbors by name after the garden opened than they had before.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residents who reported visiting the garden most often knew the fewest neighbors by name.

explanation: An increase in the number of neighbors known by name after the garden opened directly supports the hypothesis that the garden increased social connections.

passage.text: An employment research group studied workers at a technology company who switched from working full time in the office to full time at home. The group sent the same job satisfaction survey to each worker six months before the switch and six months after the switch. All other major conditions, such as salary and job duties, stayed the same.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the conclusion that remote work increased job satisfaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The average job satisfaction score was significantly lower six months after the switch than before.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The average job satisfaction score was almost identical before and after the switch.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scores improved for some workers but decreased for others, so the overall average was unchanged.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The average job satisfaction score was significantly higher six months after the switch than before.

explanation: A significantly higher average score after the switch directly supports the conclusion that remote work increased job satisfaction.

passage.text: Biologists have hypothesized that the ornate tree lizard changes its skin color not primarily for camouflage but as a way to regulate body temperature. According to this hypothesis, a lizard that turns dark in the morning absorbs sunlight more quickly, while turning pale at midday helps it avoid overheating.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the biologists' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A closely related lizard species that does not change color is active at the same times of day as the ornate tree lizard.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lizards kept in warm rooms were more active than lizards kept in cool rooms, regardless of skin color.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When researchers prevented ornate tree lizards from changing color, the lizards' body temperatures rose and fell more dramatically during the day than when the lizards could change color.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ornate tree lizards change color in response to the presence of a predator, even if air temperature remains constant.

explanation: Choice C directly supports the hypothesis by showing that color change helps stabilize body temperature: without color change, temperature fluctuates more. The other choices either weaken the hypothesis or are irrelevant.

passage.text: Some historians argue that the collapse of the inland kingdom of Zerulia in the ninth century was caused less by foreign invasion than by a collapse in long-distance trade. They point to the kingdom's heavy reliance on exporting copper tools to distant markets.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historians' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excavations in Zerulia's capital have uncovered arrowheads and burned layers dating from the ninth century.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Trade records from a neighboring port show that shipments of Zerulian copper tools almost stopped several years before the kingdom's final collapse.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zerulian copper tools have been found in many distant regions, suggesting that the kingdom once had a wide trading network.

choices.label: D
choices.text: After the kingdom's collapse, other states began producing copper tools using methods that may have been learned from Zerulian artisans.

explanation: Choice B provides direct evidence that long-distance trade collapsed before the kingdom fell, which supports the historians' claim. Choice A supports an invasion explanation, while C and D do not address the cause of the collapse.

passage.text: A marketing researcher claims that consumers are more likely to remember a product's slogan when it rhymes than when the same information is presented in a plain, non-rhyming sentence, even if the two versions contain identical facts.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In a memory test, participants who read the rhyming slogan recalled the product's main feature more often than participants who read the plain sentence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants rated the rhyming slogan as more clever than the plain sentence but could not recall either version the next day.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants who read the plain sentence said they preferred plain language and recalled it slightly better than those who read the rhyming slogan.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who heard both versions later said they remembered the rhyme but could not state the product's main feature.

explanation: Choice A directly supports the claim by showing that the rhyming version produced better recall of the product's main feature. The other choices either show no recall advantage or contradict the claim.

passage.text: Some biologists hypothesize that the loud 'booming' call of the male Tapanuli frog is used mainly to attract female frogs. They argue that the call is too long and complex to serve simply as a warning to rival males.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Female Tapanuli frogs moved toward a speaker playing a male's call more often than toward a silent speaker.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Males called more frequently when females were placed nearby than when females were absent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Males that had their vocal sacs temporarily disabled were less successful at attracting females.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When a recording of a male's call was played, nearby males stopped calling and moved aggressively toward the speaker.
