A transportation analyst argues that the lanes will reduce traffic accidents involving all road users, not just cyclists, because slower vehicle speeds give drivers more time to react to unexpected situations.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Total collisions, including those involving pedestrians and motorists, decreased by 15 percent on streets after protected bike lanes were installed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Average vehicle speeds fell on streets where protected bike lanes were added.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In a review of cities with protected bike lanes, pedestrian injuries on streets with the new lanes rose even as cyclist injuries fell.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A survey of drivers found that most felt more alert and attentive when driving on streets with bike lanes.

explanation: The analyst claims the lanes reduce accidents involving all road users. The finding that pedestrian injuries increased on streets with bike lanes directly undermines that broad claim, even if cyclist injuries decreased.

passage.text: Some historians have claimed that the collapse of several ancient Maya cities around 900 CE was caused primarily by a prolonged drought that devastated agriculture. They argue that this environmental stress, rather than military conflict, led to the abandonment of major ceremonial centers.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historians' claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Skeletal remains from the period show a high rate of unhealed wounds, suggesting widespread violence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inscriptions at one Maya city record the defeat and capture of its ruler by a rival kingdom during the collapse period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Archaeological evidence shows that many Maya communities moved to higher elevations after 900 CE.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lake sediment cores from the region show a sharp decline in rainfall and a drop in water levels beginning at roughly the same time as the collapse.

explanation: A sharp decline in rainfall and water levels at the time of the collapse provides direct environmental evidence of drought, supporting the historians' claim that drought was the primary cause.

passage.text: Psychologist Dr. Marcus Reid proposed that quick decisions are often more accurate than decisions made after lengthy deliberation. He hypothesized that initial intuitive responses draw on subconscious pattern recognition, while delayed responses allow irrelevant information and doubt to interfere.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Dr. Reid's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who waited thirty seconds before deciding were more likely to change their initial answer to the correct choice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants asked to answer within five seconds identified the correct face in a matching task more often than participants asked to wait thirty seconds before answering.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants who answered immediately and those who answered after thirty seconds had nearly identical accuracy rates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When asked to explain their reasoning, quick responders gave less detailed justifications than slow responders.

explanation: The finding that quick responders were more accurate than delayed responders directly supports the hypothesis that quick decision-making can be more accurate than lengthy deliberation.

passage.text: A supplement company advertises that a daily dose of its vitamin blend improves memory in adults over 60. The company cites enthusiastic testimonials from customers who say they feel more mentally sharp after taking the supplement.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim that the supplement improves memory?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In a randomized controlled trial, adults who took the supplement for six months recalled significantly more words on a memory test than adults who took a placebo.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In a randomized controlled trial, adults who took the supplement for six months recalled no more words on a memory test than adults who took a placebo.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A survey found that customers who took the supplement for at least a year were more likely to recommend it to friends.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Researchers found that the vitamin blend is absorbed into the bloodstream quickly after it is consumed.

explanation: A randomized controlled trial showing no memory improvement over placebo is strong evidence against the claim that the supplement improves memory, especially compared with testimonials and surveys.

passage.text: Biologists have proposed the “urban diversity hypothesis”: honeybees in cities have more taxonomically diverse diets than honeybees in rural areas because urban green spaces contain many imported ornamental plant species that bloom at different times. The hypothesis predicts that pollen collected by urban hives should represent a wider range of plant families than pollen collected by rural hives.

stem: Which finding would most directly support the urban diversity hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban honeybees produce significantly more honey per hive than rural honeybees.

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA analysis of pollen from urban hives identified more plant families than DNA analysis of pollen from rural hives.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rural honeybees collected pollen from clover and dandelion more often than urban honeybees did.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urban hives had higher survival rates over winter than rural hives.

explanation: The hypothesis specifically predicts greater taxonomic diversity in urban bee diets. Directly measuring the number of plant families in urban versus rural pollen is the most direct test.

passage.text: Some educators have proposed that practice testing is an effective study method because it both identifies gaps in knowledge and strengthens memory. Researchers tested this “retrieval practice effect” by asking students to read a passage and then either restudy the passage or take a recall quiz.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the idea that the benefit of practice testing is due to retrieval strengthening, not simply to the extra time spent thinking about the content?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Students who took a recall quiz and received corrective feedback performed better than students who took a recall quiz without feedback.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students who restudied the passage performed better than students who took a recall quiz when both groups had the same amount of study time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students who took a recall quiz performed better than students who spent an equal amount of time restudying, even when the quiz was not graded.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students who took a recall quiz reported spending more time on the task than students who restudied.

explanation: If ungraded quizzes improve performance over restudying when time is equal, the advantage cannot be attributed to feedback or to extra time. This directly supports the retrieval-strengthening explanation.

passage.text: Art historians have suggested that the ancient Sun Disk pottery and Moon Vessel pottery found in the Gan Valley were produced by the same workshop, citing the repeated use of interlaced triangles in both styles. A counterargument holds that the two styles were created by separate communities that traded motifs over several generations.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the same-workshop hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both pottery styles contain a rare blue pigment that is known to come from a single clay source in the Gan Valley.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interlaced triangles also appear on bronze weapons made in the Gan Valley during the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vessels in both styles have been excavated together at a single ancient Gan Valley site.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thermoluminescence dating indicates that all known Moon Vessels were produced at least three centuries after all known Sun Disks were produced.

explanation: If the two styles were made centuries apart, they could not have been produced by the same workshop. This directly undermines the same-workshop hypothesis.

passage.text: A communication researcher hypothesizes that introverted university students contribute more in online seminar discussions than in face-to-face seminars. She argues that online platforms lower the social costs of speaking, so students who are normally reluctant to speak in a classroom feel more comfortable participating in text-based discussion.

stem: Which experimental finding would most directly strengthen this hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In a study of two seminar formats, introverted students made more written comments in online discussions than spoken comments in face-to-face discussions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extraverted students made more spoken comments in face-to-face seminars than introverted students made in online seminars.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students reported higher levels of social anxiety before online seminar discussions than before face-to-face discussions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Total participation by all students was lower in the online format than in the face-to-face format.

explanation: The hypothesis is specifically about introverted students participating more in online than in face-to-face settings. Directly comparing those two conditions for introverted students is the most relevant evidence.

passage.text: Planetary scientists have proposed a “Planet Nine” hypothesis to explain the unusual clustering of orbits among several distant objects beyond Neptune. The hypothesis claims that the gravity of an undiscovered large planet pulls these objects into similar elliptical orientations. If no such planet exists, the orbital clustering would be very unlikely by chance.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the Planet Nine hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Other telescopes had previously searched parts of the predicted region without success.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The known giant planets cause small perturbations in the orbits of the distant objects.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A comprehensive survey of the predicted region found no object larger than Earth within the stated distance range.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several of the clustered objects have diameters of less than 500 kilometers.

explanation: The Planet Nine hypothesis depends on an undiscovered large planet in the predicted region. A comprehensive survey that rules out such an object directly weakens the hypothesis.

passage.text: Urban planners studied the effect of street trees on air temperature in a midsized city. They observed that neighborhoods with dense tree canopies were as much as 4°C cooler in midafternoon than nearby neighborhoods with few trees. One planning advocate concluded that cities should plant more trees because trees lower daytime temperatures, and argued that the cooling comes mainly from shade blocking sunlight rather than from water vapor released by leaves.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the advocate's conclusion about the mechanism of cooling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neighborhoods with many trees also had higher daytime humidity, and the humidity itself had a small cooling effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The amount of water released by trees in the city was correlated with lower temperatures even in places where the trees' shadows did not reach.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Streets with trees cooled at night as well as during the day, whereas streets with artificial shade structures cooled only during the day.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In tree-lined areas, the air directly under tree canopies was cooler than air in open sunny areas, but the open areas within the same neighborhoods were just as hot as areas with no trees.

explanation: The advocate claims that canopy shade, not evapotranspiration, causes daytime cooling. Finding D shows that the cooling occurs only directly beneath tree canopies and does not extend to sunny open areas, directly supporting the shade mechanism. A and B support evapotranspiration as the cause, and C describes a nighttime difference that is not explained by shade alone.

passage.text: In a survey of 2,000 high school students, researchers measured how much time students spent on social media and how often they felt lonely. They found that total time spent on social media predicted loneliness. The lead author argued that the relationship is not simply a matter of screen time: rather, passively scrolling through others' posts is what makes students feel left out. By contrast, sending messages and commenting may reduce loneliness.

stem: Which finding would most directly support the author's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: After controlling for total screen time, passive scrolling still predicted higher loneliness, while direct messaging predicted lower loneliness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students who reported high loneliness tended to avoid social media altogether.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students who spent more time passively scrolling also spent more time on homework.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Social media companies reported that users spend more time on the apps than on any other activity.

explanation: The author distinguishes passive scrolling from active messaging. Finding A directly supports that distinction: passive scrolling uniquely predicts more loneliness even after total screen time is accounted for, while active direct messaging predicts less loneliness. B suggests a reverse relationship, while C and D say nothing about which social media behavior causes loneliness.

passage.text: A nutrition researcher claims that eating dark chocolate improves working memory because cocoa flavanols increase blood flow to the brain. To support this, she notes that dark chocolate contains flavanols and that flavanols have been shown to dilate blood vessels in the body.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the researcher's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dark chocolate contains more flavanols than milk chocolate, but milk chocolate also contains sugar.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the same experiment, people who ate dark chocolate showed increased blood flow in the brain immediately afterward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cocoa flavanols can cross the blood-brain barrier and are found in brain tissue after consumption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In an experiment, people who ate flavanol-free white chocolate with the same sugar and fat content improved on a working-memory test just as much as those who ate dark chocolate.

explanation: The researcher claims flavanols are the specific cause of memory improvement. D weakens this by showing that flavanol-free chocolate produces the same improvement, meaning some other ingredient or factor is responsible. B and C support the proposed mechanism, and A is irrelevant to whether flavanols improve memory.

passage.text: Environmentalists have debated the main source of plastic debris in the world's oceans. One team argues that the largest share of oceanic plastic comes from abandoned fishing equipment rather than from land-based consumer items such as bags, bottles, and packaging. If they are right, policies aimed at reducing consumer plastic waste will do little to solve the problem.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A survey of remote ocean gyres found that fishing nets and ropes accounted for more than four times as much plastic mass as all consumer packaging combined.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In surface trawls of the open ocean, the most common large items were plastic bottles, bags, and food packaging.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fishing vessels in coastal waters were found to discard plastic packaging and other household waste overboard.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microplastics from the breakdown of consumer plastic have been detected in seafood sold at markets.

explanation: A directly strengthens the claim that fishing equipment is the dominant source of ocean plastic: it shows nets and ropes contribute far more mass than consumer packaging. B and D point to consumer items as major contributors, and C does not distinguish fishing equipment from consumer waste as the dominant source.

passage.text: Archaeologists have debated who built the huge stone enclosures at the site of Karstaneh. Some scholars claim they were constructed by settled farming communities, because the monuments require organization, surplus food storage, and a permanent labor force. A different group argues that Karstaneh was built by hunter-gatherers who visited seasonally long before agriculture.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the hunter-gatherer interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excavations in the oldest layers of the enclosures uncovered grinding stones and domesticated wheat seeds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Radiocarbon dates show the first monuments were raised centuries before the earliest domesticated plants or permanent houses appeared at the site.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The largest stones weigh as much as ten tons and had to be hauled from a quarry several kilometers away.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pollen samples from the site's later occupation layers contain evidence of olive and grape cultivation.

explanation: The hunter-gatherer interpretation requires that the monuments predate farming and permanent settlements. B provides direct chronological evidence that the first monuments were built before domesticated plants or permanent houses appeared. A supports settled farmers, C suggests a complex labor organization typical of settled societies, and D describes a later agricultural phase, not the original builders.

passage.text: Neuroscience researchers are studying how light physical activity affects memory. They hypothesize that a short walk immediately after learning a new task improves recall because the mild rise in heart rate increases blood flow to the hippocampus, a brain region essential for memory consolidation. To test this, they plan to have college students either walk for ten minutes or sit quietly for ten minutes after studying a list of word pairs.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Students who walked after studying recalled significantly more word pairs than students who sat quietly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students who walked before studying recalled just as many word pairs as students who walked afterward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Functional brain scans taken during the walk showed increased blood flow to the hippocampus that was not present in students who sat quietly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students who walked for ten minutes reported feeling more alert and focused than students who sat quietly.

explanation: Choice C directly supports the proposed mechanism: the walk increases blood flow to the hippocampus. Choice A supports improved memory but does not show that increased hippocampal blood flow is the cause, so C is more direct.

passage.text: Archaeologists studying pottery fragments at a Bronze Age settlement in Iberia have proposed that the vessels were made from local clay. They argue that the distinctive mineral inclusions in the fragments match the streambed clay found less than a kilometer from the settlement, and that transporting heavy clay over long distances would have been impractical. To test this, they plan to compare the chemical composition of the pottery with samples from several possible clay sources.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken the archaeologists' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The streambed clay contains minerals that are also found in every other clay source within a hundred kilometers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pots' shapes resemble pottery made in a neighboring region rather than existing local wares.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Radiocarbon dating places the pottery at a time when the settlement was known to be an important trade hub.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The clay from the local streambed crumbles during firing at the temperatures used to make pottery at the site.

explanation: If local clay crumbles during firing, it could not successfully be used to make the pottery, directly undermining the hypothesis. The other choices suggest alternative influences but do not show that local clay was unusable.

passage.text: Marine biologists are investigating whether larval coral reef fish use underwater sounds to locate suitable habitats. The researchers hypothesize that the snapping and popping sounds produced by reef organisms attract young fish during their final approach to a reef after weeks drifting in the open ocean. They set up an aquarium experiment in which fish larvae are placed in a chamber with two water-filled arms; one arm plays recorded reef sounds and the other plays no sound.

stem: Which result, if true, would best support the hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Larvae exposed to reef sounds grew faster than larvae kept in silence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Larvae moved away from the arm that played reef sounds and toward the silent arm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Larvae spent significantly more time in the arm broadcasting reef sounds than in the silent arm.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Larvae responded to reef sounds by becoming less active and sinking to the bottom of the chamber.

explanation: The hypothesis predicts that larvae are attracted to reef sounds. Spending more time in the arm playing reef sounds is direct behavioral evidence of attraction, whereas the other results do not show that larvae are drawn to the sounds.

passage.text: City planners are evaluating green roofs—roofs covered with vegetation—as a way to reduce the massive amounts of energy used to cool buildings during summer. One engineering team hypothesizes that green roofs lower indoor cooling demand chiefly by reducing the temperature of the outer roof surface. They predict that rooftop surface temperature, not the amount of insulation in the building, is the main factor linking green roofs to lower air-conditioning use.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Buildings with green roofs showed lower rooftop surface temperatures and used significantly less air conditioning than buildings with conventional black rooftops.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When researchers added extra insulation to a building with a conventional black rooftop, cooling costs fell almost as much as they did after installing a green roof.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Green roofs absorbed most rainwater, reducing runoff into city sewers during storms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: On buildings with green roofs, the indoor temperature was most strongly correlated with the temperature of the inside ceiling, not the outdoor air.

explanation: Choice A directly links the proposed key factor—lower rooftop surface temperature—to the predicted outcome, reduced air-conditioning use. The other choices either address a different benefit, suggest an alternative explanation, or do not connect rooftop temperature to cooling demand.

passage.text: A developmental psychologist claims that children acquire verb meanings more easily when the verbs are introduced in a familiar sentence frame rather than in an unfamiliar one. She argues that a known frame, such as "The boy is ____-ing," reduces the amount of unknown syntactic information a child must process, allowing attention to focus on the action. She plans to teach four-year-olds novel action words using either a frame they hear daily or a rare, awkward frame.

stem: Which result, if true, would best support the psychologist's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Children learned novel verbs equally well regardless of which sentence frame was used.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Children who heard novel verbs in a familiar frame produced the verbs in new contexts more often than children who heard them in an unfamiliar frame.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Children who began the experiment with larger vocabularies learned more novel verbs than children with smaller vocabularies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Children paid more attention to videos of the actions when the unfamiliar frame was used.

explanation: Choice B shows that the familiar frame led to better learning and use of the novel verbs, which is exactly what the psychologist predicts. Choice A contradicts the claim, C offers an unrelated explanation, and D does not demonstrate better learning.

passage.text: Marine biologist Dr. Elena Torres has proposed that humpback whales use bubble-net feeding primarily as a way to concentrate prey rather than to communicate with other whales. She notes that bubble nets are often produced by solitary whales and that the pattern of bubbles forms a physical barrier that fish avoid. In a recent field study, researchers observed humpback whales in the Gulf of Maine and recorded the behavior of fish schools before and after bubble-net formation.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Torres's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the study, fish schools remained tightly clustered and did not alter their swimming direction when bubbles were released nearby.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the study, fish schools scattered in multiple directions as soon as bubble nets appeared, making it harder for whales to capture them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the study, fish schools were consistently observed to move away from the bubble wall, becoming more concentrated in the center of the net.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the study, whales that produced bubble nets were more likely to be joined by other whales within minutes than were whales that hunted without bubble nets.

explanation: Torres's hypothesis is that bubble nets concentrate prey. Choice C directly describes fish becoming more concentrated, which supports that claim. A and B describe no concentration or dispersal, and D supports a communication-based explanation.

passage.text: Some historians argue that the decline of the Roman road system in Britain after the fifth century was caused primarily by the collapse of central authority, not by a lack of engineering knowledge. Roads fell into disrepair because no single government had the resources or incentive to maintain them, even though local communities still possessed the skills to repair stone surfaces. A recent archaeological survey of abandoned Roman roads in Britain collected data on road conditions and local activity.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the historians' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Local communities in some parts of Britain kept roads passable for centuries by reusing old Roman stone and gravel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Roman road system was originally built by military engineers who were transferred back to Rome when the empire withdrew.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Roads in regions with strong local leadership survived longer than roads in regions without it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A sixth-century chronicle records that villagers tried to repair a collapsed road bridge but abandoned the effort because they could not reconstruct the Roman arch.

explanation: The historians claim decline was due to loss of central authority, not lack of skill. D weakens this by showing that a community lacked the technical knowledge to rebuild a Roman structure. A and C support the claim that local maintenance mattered, and B is irrelevant to whether communities lacked knowledge.

passage.text: Psychologist Dr. Amara Okafor claims that people's ability to detect sarcasm in written messages depends more on the presence of contextual cues than on the specific words used. In an experiment, she asked participants to read short text exchanges and judge whether a final remark was sarcastic. Some exchanges included a preceding statement that was clearly emotional; other exchanges began with the same final remark but with a neutral preceding statement.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Dr. Okafor's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants correctly identified sarcasm more often when the final remark contained exaggerated positive words than when it contained neutral words, regardless of context.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants correctly identified sarcasm more often in exchanges with an emotional preceding statement than in exchanges with a neutral preceding statement, even when the final remark was word-for-word identical.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants took significantly longer to judge the emotional-context exchanges than the neutral-context exchanges.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who were told to focus on the exact words used performed better than those who were told to focus on the emotional situation.

explanation: Okafor's claim is that contextual cues matter more than word choice. B shows that changing context changes accuracy while holding word choice identical, directly supporting the claim. A and D emphasize word choice, and C does not address accuracy.

passage.text: An urban planner argues that adding bike lanes on a city's main avenue would reduce traffic accidents involving cyclists, despite concerns that narrower car lanes would increase congestion. The planner reasons that bike lanes create a predictable space for cyclists and make them more visible to drivers. A city transportation department conducted a before-and-after study of the avenue after bike lanes were installed.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly challenge the urban planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: After the bike lanes were installed, the total number of accidents involving cars and cyclists on the avenue increased by 25 percent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cyclist traffic on the avenue increased by 40 percent after the bike lanes were installed, while the number of cyclist accidents stayed the same.

choices.label: C
choices.text: After the bike lanes were installed, drivers reduced their speed slightly and gave cyclists more space when passing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The number of car accidents not involving cyclists decreased slightly after the bike lanes were installed.

explanation: The planner claims bike lanes reduce cyclist accidents. A directly contradicts this by showing an increase in such accidents. B could even suggest improved safety per cyclist, C supports the planner's reasoning, and D is about car accidents not involving cyclists.

passage.text: An art historian has argued that the painting known as the Mona Lisa was not intended as a portrait of a real woman but as an allegorical representation of happiness. The historian notes that no contemporary record names a specific sitter and that the title can be read as 'my Lady Lisa,' a playful personification rather than a reference to a particular person. A recently discovered letter from Leonardo da Vinci's assistant may help resolve the question.

stem: Which quotation from the letter would best support the art historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He has taken the face of the wife of a silk merchant, who sat for him many times.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many believe the face belongs to a noblewoman, but he told me he was painting an idea, not a person.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The painting is unfinished, for he kept it with him always and never delivered it to anyone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The merchant paid Leonardo a large sum for the completed portrait of his wife.

explanation: B directly states Leonardo was painting an idea rather than a person, supporting the allegorical interpretation. A and D identify a real sitter, and C is about the painting's status, not its subject.

passage.text: Ecologists hypothesized that honeybees living in cities collect nectar from a greater variety of flowering plants than honeybees living in rural farmland do. The ecologists reasoned that city landscapes are fragmented into thousands of small private gardens, parks, and vacant lots, which together support many ornamental plant species, whereas rural landscapes are dominated by only a few crop species. To test the hypothesis, they collected honey samples from hives in six cities and six farms at the same time of year and identified the plant pollen embedded in each sample.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the ecologists' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: On average, honey from city hives contained pollen from 27 plant families, while honey from farm hives contained pollen from only 9 plant families.

choices.label: B
choices.text: City honey had a higher sugar content than farm honey, making it taste sweeter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Farm hives produced approximately twice as much honey per season as city hives did.

choices.label: D
choices.text: City honey contained more total pollen grains per gram of honey than farm honey did.

explanation: The hypothesis concerns the variety of nectar sources. The finding that urban honey contains pollen from more plant families than rural honey does directly supports the claim that city bees collect nectar from a greater diversity of plants. The other choices address sweetness, honey yield, or pollen abundance, not variety.

passage.text: An archaeologist proposed that the large paved plazas at the ancient city of Teotihuacan were used primarily for large civic ceremonies, not for everyday buying and selling. According to this proposal, workshops and small neighborhood centers handled trade, while plazas were reserved for ritual gatherings. A later excavation of the plazas recovered numerous small bronze scales, cacao beans, and fragments of ceramic figurines from many different regions. In Mesoamerican societies, bronze scales and cacao beans were commonly used in marketplace transactions, whereas ceramic figurines were typical ceremonial offerings.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the archaeologist's proposal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The plazas were large enough to hold, at one time, far more people than the city's estimated total population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sixteenth-century Indigenous accounts describe ceremonies being performed in these plazas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The workshops in the city produced many more goods than the city's own residents could consume.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The recovered cacao beans and metal scales were concentrated in small pits that also contained remains of temporary wooden stalls.

explanation: Cacao beans and metal scales are associated with marketplace transactions, and the remains of temporary stalls strongly suggest that buying and selling occurred in the plazas. This directly contradicts the proposal that plazas were primarily ceremonial and not used for everyday trade. The other choices either support the ceremonial interpretation or do not show that trade occurred in the plazas themselves.

passage.text: Some species of poisonous sea slugs called nudibranchs display brilliant colors, and biologists have disagreed about why. One research team hypothesized that their colors function as warning signals that deter predators, rather than as ornaments for attracting mates. To distinguish between these explanations, the team compared how predators responded to bright and dull nudibranchs and how color affected nudibranch mating success.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Male nudibranchs with brighter markings mated more often than males with duller markings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fish predators that were offered toxic nudibranchs attacked the dull-colored individuals more often than the bright-colored individuals, even when the two types were equally toxic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bright-colored nudibranchs produced no more chemical toxin than dull-colored nudibranchs did.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Under natural light, the nudibranchs' bright patterns are difficult for fish to see against the coral.

explanation: The warning-signal hypothesis predicts that bright colors reduce attacks from predators. The finding that predators attack dull toxic nudibranchs more often than bright toxic nudibranchs directly supports that prediction. Choice A supports mate attraction instead, while choices C and D either fail to address predator deterrence or undermine it.

passage.text: A school district delayed its high school start time from 7:30 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. Researchers hypothesized that if students' grades improved, the main cause would be an increase in total sleep time. They predicted that sleep, not reduced morning stress, changed homework habits, or extra time for breakfast, would account for most of the grade gains.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Students at the later-start school reported no significant change in total sleep because they went to bed later, but their attendance improved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students who ate a school breakfast were more likely to pass their first-period classes than students who skipped breakfast.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A separate district that delayed its start time but added mandatory morning study hall saw grades rise, even though sleeping times stayed the same.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When the researchers analyzed all four factors together, only increased sleep time significantly predicted grade improvement; changes in stress, homework time, and breakfast frequency did not.

explanation: The researchers' hypothesis identifies increased sleep as the key mechanism for grade improvement. The finding that increased sleep was the only significant predictor directly supports that claim. The other choices point to attendance, breakfast, or study hall as alternative causes, which would weaken rather than support the sleep-focused hypothesis.

passage.text: Medieval Iceland's laws were famously memorized and recited aloud for centuries before they were written down in the thirteenth-century manuscript Grágás. Historians hypothesized that because the laws were composed in short, highly rhythmic phrases, they could be transmitted orally with remarkable accuracy from generation to generation. If the hypothesis is true, then passages in Grágás with strong rhythmic patterns should show closer agreement with earlier independent references to the same laws than passages without such rhythms do.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historians' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A seventeenth-century copy of Grágás contains legal expressions that do not appear in any manuscript from earlier centuries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rhythmic passages in Grágás closely match legal statements quoted in sagas written one hundred years earlier, while non-rhythmic passages show substantial differences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scribes in different monasteries produced versions of Grágás with almost identical wording in the non-rhythmic passages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modern readers can memorize rhythmic legal passages more easily than prose versions of the same laws.

explanation: The hypothesis predicts that rhythm helped oral transmission remain accurate, so rhythmic passages should match earlier sources better than non-rhythmic passages do. Choice B directly tests that prediction. The other choices are irrelevant to the rhythm hypothesis or even suggest that accuracy was unrelated to rhythm.

passage.text: Researchers have proposed that sleep spindles—brief bursts of brain activity during non-REM sleep—play a causal role in memory consolidation. According to this proposal, increased spindle activity shortly after learning should correlate with stronger memory for newly learned information.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' proposal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who napped after learning a word list had fewer sleep spindles than participants who stayed awake.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among participants who napped, the amount of sleep spindle activity was positively correlated with their recall of the word list the next day.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants who napped remembered fewer words than participants who stayed awake, even though the nappers had more spindles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sleep spindle activity was unrelated to memory recall for participants who did not nap.

explanation: Choice B establishes the predicted positive relationship between sleep spindle activity and memory recall, directly supporting the claim that spindles aid consolidation.

passage.text: Some urban planners argue that small 'pocket parks' near residences are more beneficial to mental health than large regional parks, because their close location makes casual, frequent use more likely. The argument depends on the assumption that frequent visits, not park size alone, drive psychological benefits.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the urban planners' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Residents living near large regional parks visited them less frequently than residents living near pocket parks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Residents living near pocket parks reported lower stress than residents near large regional parks, but there was no difference in visit frequency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residents living near pocket parks visited them more often than residents near large regional parks and showed lower self-reported stress.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residents living near large regional parks reported higher stress than residents living near pocket parks, despite having more park space.

explanation: Choice C links both more frequent visits and better psychological outcomes to proximity to pocket parks, matching the planners' proposed mechanism.

passage.text: In a study of consumer behavior, researcher Marta Velez hypothesized that the sunk cost effect would lead people to finish a paid-for ebook more often than an identical free ebook. She predicted that, even among readers who reported the same level of interest in the book, those who paid for the ebook would be more likely to read it to the end.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Velez's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Among readers with similar interest ratings, those who received the ebook for free finished it at the same rate as those who paid for it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Readers who paid for the ebook finished it at a significantly higher rate than readers who received it for free.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Readers who paid for the ebook were more likely than free readers to report that the price made them expect a good story.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Readers who received the ebook for free rated the book as no more interesting than readers who paid for it.

explanation: Velez predicted a difference due to payment even when interest is held constant. Choice A shows no such difference, directly weakening the hypothesis.

passage.text: Archaeologists discovered a Bronze Age settlement along a river corridor. Some researchers claim it was a major trading center, rather than a self-sufficient farming village. To evaluate this claim, excavators looked for evidence of long-distance exchange, centralized storage, and craft specialization.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the claim that the settlement was a major trading center?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nearly all pottery fragments at the site were made from locally available clay.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The settlement was surrounded by defensive walls and contained few storage facilities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The settlement's population was smaller than that of nearby villages, and its fields produced only enough food for its own residents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A large central building contained standardized weights, seals, and imported copper and lapis lazuli.

explanation: Choice D provides direct evidence of long-distance exchange and centralized commercial activity, supporting the trading center claim.

passage.text: A language learning company claims that its app's spaced repetition algorithm—which schedules vocabulary reviews at gradually increasing intervals—helps users remember words longer term than massed practice, in which words are reviewed repeatedly in a single session. The company bases its claim on the reasoning that spacing encounters with to-be-learned information strengthens memory retrieval.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the company's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In a head-to-head trial, users who used massed practice recalled more vocabulary words after one day than users who used spaced repetition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When tested two weeks after learning, users who used spaced repetition recalled significantly more words than users who used massed practice, despite the two groups having studied for the same total amount of time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Users who used spaced repetition spent more total time studying than users who used massed practice and showed no difference in recall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Users who used massed practice rated the app as more enjoyable, but neither group could recall many words after two weeks.

explanation: Choice B directly links spaced repetition to better long-term retention while controlling for total study time, matching the company's claim.

passage.text: Remote work has become a permanent fixture for many companies, but its long-term effects are still being measured. Flexibility and fewer commutes are obvious benefits. A junior employee who never overhears a senior colleague troubleshooting a problem misses lessons that are not written in manuals. Some firms have responded by assigning every new hire a formal mentor, and office attendance is unlikely to return to pre-2020 levels.

stem: Which quotation from the passage best supports the claim that remote work poses hidden risks to early-career employees?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "Flexibility and fewer commutes are obvious benefits."

choices.label: B
choices.text: "A junior employee who never overhears a senior colleague troubleshooting a problem misses lessons that are not written in manuals."

choices.label: C
choices.text: "Some firms have responded by assigning every new hire a formal mentor."

choices.label: D
choices.text: "Office attendance is unlikely to return to pre-2020 levels."

explanation: Choice B directly identifies a lost learning opportunity for junior employees, which is a hidden risk of remote work. The other choices either describe benefits, a response to the problem, or general trends.

passage.text: Astronomers using the Webb telescope produced a new spectrum of the hot exoplanet WASP-96b. They detected the signature of water molecules filtering starlight at a specific infrared wavelength. However, clouds at high altitude might absorb part of the signal, and some researchers argue that the data could be explained by a hazy atmosphere with no water. The planet's overall composition therefore remains under debate.

stem: Which quotation from the passage best supports the claim that scientists have evidence of water vapor in the exoplanet's atmosphere?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "Astronomers using the Webb telescope produced a new spectrum of the hot exoplanet WASP-96b."

choices.label: B
choices.text: "However, clouds at high altitude might absorb part of the signal."

choices.label: C
choices.text: "They detected the signature of water molecules filtering starlight at a specific infrared wavelength."

choices.label: D
choices.text: "The planet's overall composition therefore remains under debate."

explanation: Choice C is the only quotation that directly states a water-vapor detection. Choices A and B describe methods and uncertainties, while D says the composition is uncertain.

passage.text: Town officials initially praised the mall proposal as a way to draw outside investment, but locals resisted. The farmers' market that anchored the transformation was organized by residents, not developers. A state grant did fund the rewiring of Main Street, yet the market's success came from volunteers who built stalls and recruited vendors. By the following summer, the town had become a regional destination.

stem: Which quotation from the passage best supports the claim that the town's revival was driven by residents rather than outside groups?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "The farmers' market that anchored the transformation was organized by residents, not developers."

choices.label: B
choices.text: "Town officials initially praised the mall proposal as a way to draw outside investment."

choices.label: C
choices.text: "A state grant did fund the rewiring of Main Street."

choices.label: D
choices.text: "By the following summer, the town had become a regional destination."

explanation: Choice A directly identifies residents, not developers or other outside groups, as the organizers of the key change. The other choices focus on outside investment, a grant, or the result rather than the cause.

passage.text: Ornithologists monitoring a declining songbird identified two likely causes: loss of nesting habitat to logging and warmer, shorter winters. Although logging removed many woodlots, the team found that nest availability remained high in protected fragments. The strongest predictor of year-to-year population drops was an unusually warm January, which shifted insect hatches before chicks needed them. Habitat restoration efforts alone would therefore not be sufficient.

stem: Which quotation from the passage best supports the claim that climate change, not habitat loss, is the primary driver of the songbird's decline?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "Ornithologists monitoring a declining songbird identified two likely causes: loss of nesting habitat to logging and warmer, shorter winters."

choices.label: B
choices.text: "Although logging removed many woodlots, the team found that nest availability remained high in protected fragments."

choices.label: C
choices.text: "Habitat restoration efforts alone would therefore not be sufficient."

choices.label: D
choices.text: "The strongest predictor of year-to-year population drops was an unusually warm January, which shifted insect hatches before chicks needed them."

explanation: Choice D directly ties the strongest population declines to a climate-related phenomenon. Choice B weakens the habitat-loss explanation, but D actively supports climate change as the primary driver.

passage.text: Many students believe that typing lecture notes is more efficient than writing them by hand. In a classroom study, however, those who wrote by hand were better able to answer conceptual questions a week later. Typing captured more words but encouraged verbatim transcription, while handwriting forced students to paraphrase ideas. Laptops may therefore be useful for review, not as a replacement for handwritten notes.

stem: Which quotation from the passage best supports the claim that handwritten notes are more effective for learning than typed notes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "Many students believe that typing lecture notes is more efficient than writing them by hand."

choices.label: B
choices.text: "Typing captured more words but encouraged verbatim transcription."

choices.label: C
choices.text: "In a classroom study, however, those who wrote by hand were better able to answer conceptual questions a week later."

choices.label: D
choices.text: "Laptops may therefore be useful for review, not as a replacement for handwritten notes."

explanation: Choice C provides direct empirical evidence that handwritten notes led to better performance on conceptual questions. The other choices state a belief, describe a disadvantage of typing, or offer a practical implication.

passage.text: Researchers conducted a study on memory consolidation. Participants learned a finger-tapping sequence, a motor skill, and a paired list of words, a factual task. After training, half of the participants were allowed to sleep for eight hours, while the other half stayed awake. On retesting, the participants who slept improved their tapping speed by 21%, whereas those who stayed awake improved by only 2%. On the word-pair task, however, the sleep group remembered 48% of the pairs and the wake group remembered 45%.

stem: Which choice best supports the claim that sleep is more critical for consolidating motor skills than for strengthening factual recall?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who slept recalled 48% of word pairs, while those who stayed awake recalled 45%.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants who slept improved tapping speed by 21%, while those who stayed awake improved by only 2%.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants who stayed awake after finger-tapping improved by 2%, and those who stayed awake after learning word pairs recalled 45%.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who slept showed larger gains on the motor task than on the word-pair task.

explanation: Choice B directly shows a large sleep advantage for the motor task but, combined with the passage's nearly equal word-pair results, supports the claim that sleep especially benefits motor skill consolidation. Choice D compares different measurement scales and is less direct.

passage.text: Researchers compared the microclimate of three city blocks: one lined with mature oak trees, one with tall fabric shade sails, and one with no shade. All three blocks had similar paved surfaces and traffic levels. At midday, the block with trees was 3.2°C cooler than the unshaded block, and the block with shade sails was 3.0°C cooler. The tree-lined block had higher relative humidity than the shade-sail block, but the temperature difference between the two shaded blocks was negligible.

stem: Which choice best supports the claim that the cooling effect of street trees is caused primarily by shading rather than by moisture released from leaves?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Although shade sails release no moisture, the block with shade sails was nearly as cool as the block with trees.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The block with trees was cooler and more humid than the block with shade sails.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Temperatures in the unshaded block were more variable than temperatures in either shaded block.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tree-lined block had significantly higher humidity, indicating that trees release water vapor.

explanation: Choice A supports the claim because artificial shade, which produces no moisture, achieved almost the same cooling as trees. This indicates shade, not water vapor, is the main cooling mechanism.

passage.text: To test whether infants can learn words from screen media, researchers showed 18-month-olds a new object and named it with a made-up word. One group saw a live experimenter sitting across the room; a second group watched the same woman on a pre-recorded video; a third group interacted with the woman through a live video chat. When tested with two objects, infants in the live and video-chat groups looked significantly longer at the named object, while infants in the pre-recorded-video group looked equally at both objects.

stem: Which choice best supports the claim that merely watching a video is insufficient for infants to learn new words?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Infants who interacted via video chat learned the word, just as those who saw a live person did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In live and video-chat conditions, infants heard the same number of object labels.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infants who watched the pre-recorded video did not look longer at the named object.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infants who watched the pre-recorded video were less attentive than those in the live condition.

explanation: Choice C directly supports the claim: the pre-recorded-video group showed no evidence of learning the word, while the live and video-chat groups did. This indicates passive video exposure alone was insufficient.

passage.text: After the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines, researchers noticed that global temperatures dropped by about 0.5°C over the following year. Pinatubo released roughly 20 million tons of sulfur dioxide high into the stratosphere. In contrast, the 2010 eruption of Eyjafjallajökull in Iceland released far less sulfur dioxide but vast clouds of ash; it caused no measurable change in global temperature. Satellite data confirmed that Pinatubo's sulfur dioxide formed sulfate aerosols that spread worldwide, while Eyjafjallajökull's ash settled out of the atmosphere within days.

stem: Which choice best supports the claim that global cooling after volcanic eruptions is driven by sulfur dioxide, not ash?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eyjafjallajökull's ash cloud disrupted air travel for several weeks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pinatubo's sulfate aerosols spread throughout the stratosphere.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eyjafjallajökull released large amounts of ash but very little sulfur dioxide.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pinatubo released far more sulfur dioxide than Eyjafjallajökull and cooled the planet, while Eyjafjallajökull released mainly ash and did not cool the planet.

explanation: Choice D provides the strongest support because it links a sulfur-rich eruption to cooling and an ash-rich, sulfur-poor eruption to no cooling. The other choices present relevant details, but D directly connects both eruptions to the proposed mechanism.

passage.text: To examine how exercise intensity affects attention, researchers had 40 adults perform 20 minutes of cycling at either high intensity, moderate intensity, or no exercise as a control. Immediately afterward, participants completed a flanker task requiring rapid responses to target arrows surrounded by either congruent arrows pointing the same way or incongruent arrows pointing the opposite way. The high-intensity group made significantly fewer errors on incongruent trials than the moderate-intensity group, while the moderate-intensity group performed better than the control group. On congruent trials, all groups performed at about the same high level.

stem: Which choice best supports the claim that high-intensity exercise improves the ability to ignore distracting information, but it does not affect easy, low-conflict attention tasks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The high-intensity group made fewer errors than the moderate-intensity group on incongruent trials, and all groups scored the same on congruent trials.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The moderate-intensity group outperformed the control group on both congruent and incongruent trials.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The high-intensity group responded faster than the moderate-intensity group on congruent trials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There was no significant difference between the moderate-intensity and control groups on incongruent trials.

explanation: Choice A directly supports both parts of the claim: high-intensity exercise reduced errors only when distracting incongruent arrows were present, while performance on easy congruent trials stayed the same across all groups.

passage.text: Researchers have hypothesized that birds in urban environments sing at higher frequencies than their rural counterparts because low-frequency traffic noise masks lower-pitched songs. If this hypothesis is correct, urban birds should have evolved songs with a higher minimum frequency than rural birds of the same species.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In a comparison of recorded songs from the same species, urban birds consistently produced songs with a higher minimum frequency than rural birds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Urban birds produced songs with a longer average duration than rural birds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rural birds produced songs with a higher maximum frequency than urban birds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No consistent difference was found in the frequency range of urban and rural birds.

explanation: The hypothesis predicts that urban birds sing at higher frequencies, specifically with a higher minimum frequency. Choice A directly confirms this prediction. The other choices are irrelevant or contradict the hypothesis.

passage.text: Some sleep researchers have proposed that a short daytime nap improves performance on tasks that require procedural memory, such as learning to play a melody. They argue that sleep strengthens the neural connections formed during practice. To test this, participants practiced a keyboard sequence and then either napped for 45 minutes or stayed awake.

stem: Which result, if true, would most directly challenge the researchers' proposal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who napped made more errors on the keyboard sequence after waking than participants who stayed awake.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants who napped performed better on the keyboard sequence after waking than participants who stayed awake.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants who stayed awake reported feeling more alert before practicing than those who napped.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who napped performed slightly worse on a vocabulary test but better on the keyboard sequence.

explanation: The proposal says naps improve procedural memory. Finding A shows napping actually worsened performance on the keyboard sequence, directly contradicting that proposal. Choice B would support it, C is irrelevant, and D still supports the proposal for the keyboard task.

passage.text: Archaeologists have hypothesized that early inhabitants of an arid region depended primarily on permanent springs rather than seasonal rivers for their water supply. If that is true, settlement and artifact sites should cluster near reliable springs, not along waterways that flowed only part of the year.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The oldest artifacts are found almost exclusively near dry streambeds that would have been seasonal rivers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Radiocarbon dating shows that sites near springs were occupied earlier and for longer periods than sites near seasonal rivers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Artifacts are evenly distributed across the region with no clear relation to water sources.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seasonal rivers were located far from any known springs.

explanation: The hypothesis predicts settlement near permanent springs. Choice B directly supports this by showing that sites near springs were occupied earlier and longer than sites near seasonal rivers. A and C contradict the prediction, and D does not address settlement patterns.

passage.text: Researchers have claimed that the more time people spend on social media, the more politically polarized they become. They argue that algorithms feed users content that is increasingly extreme to keep them engaged. A research team conducted a randomized experiment to test this claim.

stem: Which result, if true, would most directly weaken the researchers' claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who deactivated their social media accounts for a month became more polarized in their views.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants who deactivated their social media accounts for a month became less polarized in their views.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants who spent the most time on social media showed the largest increases in polarization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who used social media only to share personal photos showed no change in polarization.

explanation: If reducing social media use made people more polarized, then social media is not producing the increase in polarization claimed. Choice A directly undermines the claim, whereas B and C support it and D is irrelevant to the overall time-and-polarization relationship.

passage.text: Historians have debated why a certain ancient civilization collapsed. One hypothesis holds that a severe multiyear drought destroyed the food supply and caused the collapse; another argues that warfare among rival city-states was the main cause. A team analyzed sediment cores from the civilization's lake bed to test these hypotheses.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the drought hypothesis over the warfare hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sediment layers show a rapid increase in charcoal from burned buildings immediately before the collapse.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sediment layers contain evidence of an abrupt drop in rainfall that corresponds to the period immediately before the collapse.

choices.label: C
choices.text: City walls and defensive structures were built a century before the collapse.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sediment cores show no significant change in rainfall during the final years of the civilization.

explanation: The drought hypothesis predicts evidence of a severe rainfall reduction at the time of collapse. Choice B provides exactly that evidence. A points to warfare, C is not directly relevant, and D contradicts the drought hypothesis.

passage.text: Marine biologists hypothesized that newly hatched clownfish locate their host anemone primarily by smell. To test this, researchers raised clownfish in a tank with no contact with anemones, then released individual fish into a choice chamber. One side of the chamber contained seawater that had previously held anemones; the other side contained identically filtered seawater from an anemone-free tank. The fish were observed for 10 minutes.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the biologists' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clownfish in the choice chamber moved immediately toward the side with visual images of anemones projected on the wall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clownfish spent significantly more time on the side containing seawater that had held anemones than on the side containing plain seawater.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clownfish whose nasal passages were blocked still spent significantly more time near a visible anemone than in open water.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clownfish moved equally between the two sides when the water in both arms was taken from the anemone tank.

explanation: If clownfish primarily use smell, they should prefer water carrying anemone odor. Choice B directly demonstrates that preference. The other choices either point to visual cues, fail to distinguish odor, or describe behavior that does not support the smell hypothesis.

passage.text: An organizational psychologist claims that allowing employees to work remotely undermines their loyalty to the company because they miss the spontaneous mentoring and social reinforcement that occur in offices. According to this claim, the loss of informal office interaction is the main reason remote employees are more likely to leave their jobs.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the psychologist's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Remote employees were less likely than office employees to report having a close friend at work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Companies that allowed remote work reported lower overhead costs than companies that did not allow remote work.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Companies with mostly remote workforces had lower turnover than comparable in-office companies, despite remote workers reporting fewer informal office interactions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Remote employees said that flexible hours, not company loyalty, was the main reason they stayed in their jobs.

explanation: The claim says remote work reduces loyalty mainly because it removes informal office interaction and thus makes employees more likely to leave. Choice C directly challenges this by showing that remote companies had lower turnover even though remote workers had fewer informal interactions. The other choices either support the claim, are irrelevant to loyalty, or do not address the proposed cause.

passage.text: An archaeologist argues that the large Roman water-powered grain mills at Barbegal in southern France were built mainly to supply the Roman army with flour. She points out that the site is near a major military road and that the mills' output would have been far more than the local civilian population could consume.

stem: Which additional finding, if true, would most directly support the archaeologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Charred wheat found at the site was the same high-grade variety issued to Roman military units elsewhere.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The millstones were made from a type of volcanic rock not found locally.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A large civilian settlement near the mills was probably large enough to consume all the flour produced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tablets found at the site record flour shipments to civilian bakeries in several distant towns.

explanation: Evidence linking the wheat at Barbegal to Roman military supply directly supports the claim that the mills served the army. The other choices either are irrelevant, suggest the flour went to civilians, or indicate it was consumed locally rather than used by the military.

passage.text: A cognitive scientist hypothesizes that people make less emotionally driven decisions when they use a foreign language than when they use their native language. To test this, she asks bilingual volunteers to respond to moral dilemmas in either their native language or a foreign language. In the dilemmas, participants must decide whether to sacrifice one person to save several others.

stem: Which result, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who read the dilemma in their native language made the same choices as those who read it in a foreign language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants who read the dilemma in a foreign language took significantly longer to make their decisions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants who read the dilemma in a foreign language were less likely to choose to sacrifice one person to save several others.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who read the dilemma in a foreign language were more likely to choose to sacrifice one person to save several others.

explanation: Choosing to sacrifice one person to save several is generally seen as the less emotionally driven, more utilitarian response. The hypothesis predicts that using a foreign language reduces emotional interference, so participants reading in a foreign language should be more likely to make that choice. Choice D states exactly this result. Choice C is the opposite and would weaken the hypothesis.

passage.text: A city transportation official claims that replacing on-street parking spaces with protected bike lanes will hurt local shops because drivers who would otherwise stop to shop will go elsewhere. The city is considering removing parking on a commercial street to install a bike lane.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly challenge the official's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: After a similar city replaced parking with a bike lane, retail sales on the street remained about the same over the following year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In surveys, drivers said they would be less likely to shop on streets with protected bike lanes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Shoppers who arrived by bicycle spent about half as much per visit as shoppers who arrived by car.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most merchants on the street opposed the bike-lane proposal because they feared losing parking.

explanation: The official claims the bike-lane plan will hurt local shops. Choice A directly contradicts this by showing that retail sales were unchanged after a similar change. The other choices either support the claim that fewer drivers will hurt sales or reflect opinions rather than evidence about the plan's effect.

passage.text: Dr. Elena Vance has spent two decades documenting insect species in the Amazon. Her papers are widely cited and have brought invitations to prestigious universities. Yet when asked about her greatest reward, she lists the names of children in river villages who now identify medicinal plants, and she speaks of workshops where farmers test sustainable harvesting methods. "A monograph is read by a few dozen specialists," she says, "but when a community decides to protect a forest because their children helped collect the data, that is a change that lasts."

stem: Which quotation from the passage most directly supports the claim that Dr. Vance values community impact more than academic recognition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her papers are widely cited and have brought invitations to prestigious universities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A monograph is read by a few dozen specialists.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Workshops where farmers test sustainable harvesting methods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When a community decides to protect a forest because their children helped collect the data, that is a change that lasts.

explanation: The correct quotation explicitly ties Dr. Vance's sense of achievement to a lasting community outcome. The other choices focus on academic recognition, limited readership, or isolated program details rather than on community impact.

passage.text: The ancient city of Tavis collapsed abruptly around 800 CE. Most archaeologists long assumed the cause was a severe drought that reduced harvests and emptied the city over several decades. Dr. Nia Osei has challenged this view. Her excavations uncovered a thick layer of ash and broken pottery at a collapsed city gate, along with arrowheads in the main street. The remains of valuables left behind in homes suggested that residents fled suddenly, rather than gradually abandoning homes as drought would have caused.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Dr. Osei's claim that Tavis was destroyed by an invasion rather than by drought?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A sediment core from a nearby lake shows a 50-year drought that began just before the city's collapse.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An inscription found on the city gate describes a successful raid by a neighboring kingdom in the year of the destruction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pottery found in the city includes styles from several distant trading partners.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city's canals were expanded several decades before the collapse.

explanation: An inscription recording a raid in the year of destruction provides direct textual evidence of invasion. The drought-core finding supports the alternative explanation, while trade and canal expansion are unrelated to the immediate cause of collapse.

passage.text: Environmental educator Maya Lin believes virtual reality can help students experience inaccessible places. In an essay, she notes that a virtual dive can demonstrate the colors and shapes of a coral reef. But she warns that such experiences are not equivalent to being there: "No screen, however vivid, can substitute for the weight of the water, the pull of the current, or the smell of the salt air." She concludes that digital tools should open a door to nature, not close it.

stem: Which quotation from the passage most directly supports the claim that Lin considers virtual experiences of nature inferior to direct encounters?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Virtual reality can help students experience inaccessible places.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A virtual dive can demonstrate the colors and shapes of a coral reef.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No screen, however vivid, can substitute for the weight of the water, the pull of the current, or the smell of the salt air.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Digital tools should open a door to nature, not close it.

explanation: The correct quotation directly says that no screen can substitute for the physical sensations of being in nature, which expresses inferiority to direct experience. The other options describe benefits of virtual tools but do not directly claim that they are inferior.

passage.text: Sea otters disappeared from the Aleutian Islands in the fur trade, and kelp forests shrank because sea urchins overgrazed them. After otters returned, kelp recovered in some areas. Scientists wondered whether the recovery was due to otter predation on urchins or to a regional rise in ocean temperature. Dr. T. Nguyen surveyed islands where otters had returned and islands where they had not. If temperature explained kelp recovery, she reasoned, then kelp should have come back even where otters remained absent.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the claim that the return of sea otters, rather than higher water temperature, caused kelp recovery?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At islands with otters, kelp recovered only in years when water temperatures were above normal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At islands without otters, kelp remained sparse even during years when water temperatures were above normal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At islands without otters, sea urchin numbers declined when temperatures rose.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At islands with otters, water temperatures were significantly higher than at islands without otters.

explanation: If kelp remained sparse at otter-free islands despite warm temperatures, then warmer water alone cannot explain kelp recovery; otter presence is necessary. The other choices either support temperature as a cause, offer only a correlation, or directly weaken the conclusion.

passage.text: Researchers investigated whether explaining why an answer is wrong improves learning more than simply labeling it wrong. In the study, participants solved a series of analogies. Whenever they chose an incorrect option, the program either displayed only "Incorrect" or displayed a sentence explaining which assumption made the selected option flawed. Both groups received the same total number of questions. Later, participants were shown their original incorrect answers and were allowed to revise them.
