stem: Which result from the study, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis that explanatory feedback is more effective than simple negative feedback?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who received explanatory feedback correctly revised a significantly higher percentage of their original incorrect answers than did participants who received only "Incorrect."

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants who received only "Incorrect" spent more time reviewing each question than did those in the explanation group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There was no significant difference between the two groups in the percentage of original incorrect answers they correctly revised.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who received explanatory feedback correctly revised a lower percentage of their original incorrect answers than did participants who received only "Incorrect."

explanation: A higher percentage of correct revisions in the explanatory-feedback group directly shows that explanatory feedback led to better learning. The other choices either show no advantage, favor the simple feedback group, or address time spent rather than accuracy.

passage.text: Marine biologist Dr. Ito hypothesizes that juvenile clownfish locate their home anemone by following chemical cues released by that anemone, and that they ignore chemical cues from non-host anemone species. In a laboratory Y-maze, a single juvenile clownfish is released at the base and can swim toward either a water stream containing odors from its host anemone or a water stream containing odors from a non-host anemone.

stem: Which experimental result would most directly support Dr. Ito's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Test fish spent significantly more time near the stream carrying host-anemone odor than near the stream carrying non-host-anemone odor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Test fish avoided the host-anemone stream and spent most of the trial near the non-host-anemone stream.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Test fish spent about equal time in the two streams and showed no clear preference.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Test fish approached the non-host stream first but then remained in a neutral central area for the rest of the trial.

explanation: The hypothesis says juvenile clownfish are attracted to host-anemone cues and ignore non-host cues. Spending more time near the host-anemone stream is the direct behavioral prediction of that hypothesis.

passage.text: Rural historian Miguel Alvarez argues that the expansion of rural free mail delivery in the early twentieth century reduced farm families' isolation. According to Alvarez, receiving daily mail gave farm families a reliable connection to national news, commercial advertisements, and personal correspondence that they had previously lacked.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Alvarez's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many rural families continued to depend on traveling peddlers and word of mouth for news even after delivery began.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cost of mailing a letter doubled during the first decade of rural free delivery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: After rural free delivery began, daily newspaper subscriptions in small farming communities increased far more rapidly than in urban areas.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rural free delivery routes were discontinued in several states within ten years.

explanation: If rural families greatly increased their daily newspaper subscriptions after receiving regular mail delivery, that directly supports the claim that rural free delivery connected them to national news and reduced isolation.

passage.text: Psychologist Dr. Anne Whitfield hypothesizes that a brief session of playing a violent video game immediately after experiencing frustration increases aggressive behavior. To test this, participants first complete an impossible puzzle to induce frustration, then play either a violent or nonviolent game for ten minutes, and finally choose how much harsh noise to blast at an opponent in a reaction-time task. Dr. Whitfield predicts the violent-game group will select louder and longer noise blasts.

stem: Which result, if true, would most weaken Dr. Whitfield's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who played the violent game chose significantly louder and longer noise blasts than participants who played the nonviolent game.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants who played the violent game chose significantly quieter and shorter noise blasts than participants who played the nonviolent game.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants who played the violent game rated the game as more enjoyable and more exciting than did the nonviolent group.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who played the nonviolent game chose significantly louder noise blasts than participants who played no game at all.

explanation: The hypothesis predicts that the violent-game group will be more aggressive. If that group instead chose quieter and shorter noise blasts than the nonviolent group, the predicted aggressive effect is directly contradicted.

passage.text: Urban planner Chen argues that installing protected bike lanes reduces injury crashes on nearby streets. Chen explains that the lanes physically separate cars from bicycles, calm traffic, and make cyclists more visible to drivers. Chen's office compares crash statistics before and after protected lanes are installed on a set of downtown streets.

stem: Which finding would most directly support Chen's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: After installation, the number of cyclists using the protected lanes declined sharply.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After installation, car-bicycle collisions on those streets increased slightly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At the same time, the city installed protective bollards at several downtown intersections.

choices.label: D
choices.text: After installation, injury crashes on those streets decreased by 30 percent.

explanation: Chen claims that protected bike lanes reduce injury crashes. A 30 percent decrease in injury crashes on streets after lanes were installed is exactly the kind of evidence that would support that claim.

passage.text: An archaeologist hypothesizes that the distinctive painted pottery excavated at a riverside settlement was produced locally rather than imported from a distant trading center. She thinks local production is likely because the pots' clay resembles local riverbed clay and the painted designs resemble motifs on other local artifacts.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the archaeologist's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chemical analysis shows that the pottery's clay composition is identical to clay found in local riverbed deposits.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Written records from the distant trading center list pottery as a major export.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The painted motifs on the pottery are unlike any designs found on other local artifacts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fragments of imported pottery are common at other settlements along the same river.

explanation: If the pottery's clay composition exactly matches local riverbed clay, that directly supports the idea that the pottery was made locally rather than imported.

passage.text: Some sleep researchers have hypothesized that a short daytime nap—about 20 minutes—mainly strengthens procedural memory, the kind of memory used for skills and habits, rather than declarative memory, which involves facts and events. To investigate, a team recruited healthy adults and randomly assigned them either to take a 20-minute nap or to remain awake during the same rest period. Afterward, all participants completed two tasks: a finger-tapping sequence task and a vocabulary recall task.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nappers outperformed non-nappers on the finger-tapping task but did no better on the vocabulary task.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nappers outperformed non-nappers on both the finger-tapping task and the vocabulary task.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Non-nappers outperformed nappers on the vocabulary task, while the two groups performed equally on the finger-tapping task.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nappers who slept for 45 minutes outperformed 20-minute nappers on a geography quiz.

explanation: The hypothesis predicts a selective benefit to procedural memory, not declarative memory. Choice A matches that prediction exactly: nappers improved on finger-tapping (a procedural skill) but not on vocabulary (a declarative task).

passage.text: In her book on the history of farming, historian Elena Voss challenges the tendency of earlier writers to depict preindustrial agriculture as a serene, pastoral world. She argues that this romanticized view ignores the constant threat of crop failure, the physical strain of manual labor, and the economic insecurity of rural families. According to Voss, a more accurate account must acknowledge both the skills that farmers developed and the severe hardships they endured.

stem: Which quotation from Voss’s book would most directly support the claim that Voss avoids romanticizing preindustrial agriculture?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is a quiet beauty in the yearly cycle of sowing, tending, and reaping that modern people have lost.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many traditional farming tools were remarkably well suited to the soil and climate of the regions where they were used.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A poor harvest could push an otherwise stable farm family into debt and hunger within a single season.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Farmers passed down practical knowledge through apprenticeships, ensuring that specialized techniques survived for generations.

explanation: Choice C emphasizes economic insecurity and hunger, which are exactly the harsh realities that romanticized depictions overlook. The other choices either celebrate pastoral beauty or highlight positive aspects of farm life.

passage.text: Researchers have proposed that passive use of social media—scrolling through posts without commenting or interacting—increases loneliness because it fosters upward social comparisons, or judgments that one’s own life is worse than others’. According to this hypothesis, the negative effect of passive use should be strongest when users compare themselves with others they perceive as happier or more successful, and it should diminish when such comparisons are removed.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the researchers’ hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In a survey, passive users who reported frequent upward comparisons also reported more loneliness than passive users who reported few such comparisons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In a diary study, active social media users reported no more loneliness than non-users.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In a longitudinal study, participants who reduced passive scrolling reported less loneliness after two months than those who continued as usual.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In an experiment, passive users instructed to avoid any social comparison while scrolling reported approximately the same high level of loneliness as passive users who scrolled normally.

explanation: If the hypothesis were correct, removing upward comparisons should reduce loneliness. Choice D shows that loneliness remained high even when comparisons were suppressed, which undercuts the claim that comparisons are the key mechanism.

passage.text: Labor organizer Marta Reyes is often described as an advocate for union members’ economic interests. Yet a careful reading of her speeches suggests a broader political vision. Reyes repeatedly links the fate of unions to the health of democratic institutions, arguing that organized labor gives working people a way to participate in decisions that affect their lives. According to one historian, Reyes’s rhetoric is best understood as a defense of unions as pillars of democracy rather than as interest groups seeking special advantages.

stem: Which quotation from Reyes’s speeches would most directly support the historian’s characterization?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first duty of a union is to secure a fair paycheck and safe working conditions for its members.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A union that bargains only for wages is forgetting its larger duty to protect the voice of working people in public life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Strikes and boycotts are tools that should be used only when negotiations have failed and no other remedy remains.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Union membership is voluntary, and every worker must decide for himself or herself whether dues are worth the benefits.

explanation: Choice B contrasts a purely economic goal with a democratic one and explicitly says unions should protect working people’s voice in public life. This directly supports the historian’s view that Reyes framed unions as pillars of democracy.

passage.text: By the early 1990s, Mercer Park had become a landscape of cracked asphalt and neglected flower beds, a symbol of civic retreat. Residents avoided it; city officials considered it a liability. Then a coalition of neighborhood associations began planting native gardens and organizing weekend cleanups. Within a decade, the park was hosting farmers' markets and outdoor concerts. Its transformation was less a tribute to government planning than to the persistence of ordinary citizens.

stem: Which choice best describes the structural trajectory of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From a case study of municipal decline to an endorsement of centralized urban policy

choices.label: B
choices.text: From a portrait of local disinvestment to an account of grassroots renewal

choices.label: C
choices.text: From a chronological history of a park to a proposal for future park maintenance

choices.label: D
choices.text: From a neutral observation about a park to a skeptical assessment of volunteer efforts

explanation: The passage first depicts Mercer Park as neglected and avoided, then describes a neighborhood coalition that transformed it. Thus the structure moves from local disinvestment to grassroots renewal. The other choices misread the conclusion: the passage does not endorse centralized policy, propose maintenance, or express skepticism about volunteers.

passage.text: It is easy to understand why artificial sweeteners make people uneasy. The names are chemical, the history includes regulatory scandals, and every few years a new study revives old fears. Yet the weight of current evidence offers a more reassuring picture: at approved doses, these compounds show no consistent link to cancer in humans. The unease, in other words, may have more to do with how risks are communicated than with the compounds themselves.

stem: The author's overall structure can best be described as doing which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Presenting a public concern, then dismissing it as entirely baseless

choices.label: B
choices.text: Evaluating competing studies, then calling for stricter safety standards

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acknowledging a plausible source of concern, then reframing it in light of evidence

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tracing a historical controversy, then predicting its future resolution

explanation: The first sentence concedes that concern about artificial sweeteners is understandable, but the rest of the passage introduces evidence and suggests the concern is more about risk communication than about the compounds themselves. This is best described as acknowledging a plausible concern and then reframing it in light of evidence.

passage.text: Limestone caves begin with rain. Carbon dioxide in the air dissolves into droplets, forming weak carbonic acid. When this acidic water seeps through cracks in limestone, it slowly dissolves calcium carbonate, widening fissures over millennia. Eventually the trickles enlarge into passages, and lowering water tables leave chambers behind. What starts as ordinary weather becomes, on a geological timescale, an astonishing architecture.

stem: In the passage, the first sentence most likely serves to establish which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rain as the primary obstacle to cave formation

choices.label: B
choices.text: The causative agent that initiates the process described

choices.label: C
choices.text: A comparison between cave formation and atmospheric weather patterns

choices.label: D
choices.text: The final stage in a sequence of geological events

explanation: The passage explains how caves form, beginning with rain as the initial cause: rain absorbs carbon dioxide, becomes acidic, and dissolves limestone. The first sentence therefore introduces the causative agent that starts the process. Rain is not an obstacle, a comparison, or the final stage.

passage.text: Streaming services promise effortless access to a vast library, and for many viewers they deliver exactly that. But the same system that erases late fees also erodes ownership: titles vanish when licenses lapse, and catalogs shuffle without warning. A film watched one month may be gone the next. Thus the convenience of streaming is real, yet it rests on a foundation of impermanence that viewers seldom notice.

stem: Which choice best describes the relationship between the first sentence and the argument that follows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first sentence states a promise; the rest uses anecdotal examples to show that the promise has been fulfilled

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first sentence provides background; the rest proposes a new business model for streaming platforms

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first sentence establishes a contrast; the rest resolves that contrast by recommending a specific service

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first sentence acknowledges a benefit; the rest complicates that benefit by emphasizing its hidden cost

passage.text: At first glance, the object seems unremarkable: a small clay pot with a chipped rim. Stand closer, though, and the maker's fingerprints appear inside the neck. passage.text: Many city residents assume that installing beehives on rooftops is an unambiguous environmental good. passage.text: I used to rush through every assigned chapter, skimming for plot points and ignoring the texture of the language. Then a summer of reading one long novel taught me to slow down. passage.text: Teams often assume that a shared digital whiteboard will make meetings more collaborative. But the tool can be used to reinforce the very hierarchy it promises to flatten. passage.text: Old maps are often treated as objective snapshots of past landscapes. Yet every map was also an argument, shaped by the cartographer's patron, trade routes, and even religious beliefs. To read such maps only as documents of geography is therefore to miss much of their story.

passage.text: Consumers buy DNA ancestry kits expecting a definitive answer to the question 'Who am I?' The marketing promises precision: percentages reveal migrations traced back thousands of years. passage.text: Many residents initially dismissed the town library's proposed maker space as a costly gimmick. passage.text: Supporters of urban beekeeping often emphasize honey production and pollination, but the practice also fosters a more subtle connection between city dwellers and the natural world. These habits of attention, beekeepers argue, can change how residents notice the plants, weather, and seasons around them.

passage.text: Ada Lovelace's mathematical notes are filled not only with formulas but with questions to herself: 'Why does this follow?' 'What if we reverse the operation?' passage.text: Public discussions of electric vehicles often treat driving range as the single most important number. The real question, some transportation researchers argue, is not how far a car can go but how well it fits a driver's ordinary routines.

passage.text: Nineteenth-century maps of African inland regions are notoriously incomplete, and modern readers may mistake their blank spaces for ignorance. passage.text: Many people assume that keeping honeybees is an unqualified environmental good. In truth, the surge of urban hives can do little to reverse broader pollinator losses. passage.text: Many readers assume that a memoir's value lies in its factual accuracy. A memoir that openly acknowledges its shaping hand is not therefore defective; it merely makes visible what all memory does. passage.text: Home assistants are usually discussed in terms of convenience: they set timers, play music, and answer trivial questions. The more consequential effect, though, is spatial. passage.text: Buying produce from nearby farms shortens supply chains and supports regional economies. It does not, by itself, guarantee environmental sustainability. passage.text: Supporters of public murals often praise them for beautifying neglected neighborhoods. But the murals' deeper value lies in what they do to civic perception. A wall that was once blank or defaced becomes a site of collective storytelling, signalling that the community is watched and valued. This is why murals can reduce vandalism: not by covering surfaces, but by transforming how residents read their surroundings.

passage.text: Many people assume that honeybee colonies in cities are healthier than those in rural areas because agricultural pesticides are less common there. City beekeeping is not, therefore, an automatic refuge from the threats facing pollinators; it simply exchanges one set of pressures for another.

passage.text: Many readers assume that shorter stories are simply less developed versions of longer ones. passage.text: Citizen science programs enlist volunteers to collect data, and their contributions have expanded the scope of ecological research. passage.text: On Main Street, the morning light catches the red brick of the old dry-goods store, and the smell of fresh bread drifts from the bakery. passage.text: Some educators argue that requiring students to memorize historical dates is obsolete in an age of instant search. passage.text: Night markets may seem chaotic: vendors shout, crowds press between stalls, and the smell of oil and spice hangs in the air. passage.text: The professor begins each lecture by writing a single question on the board, then asks the class to answer before opening the textbook. passage.text: Though many residents had long regarded the town's old train station as an eyesore, its recent renovation has changed that perception. passage.text: Research on white noise machines often focuses only on whether people fall asleep more quickly, yet the more telling measure may be sleep quality. passage.text: Most accounts of the Great Chicago Fire treat the disaster as a single catastrophic event, but this framing obscures the distinct challenges the city faced afterward. passage.text: Wetlands have long been praised for flood control, but their capacity to store carbon is less widely understood. If carbon storage is counted among their benefits, the economic calculus changes substantially.

explanation: The second sentence reports the researchers' empirical finding; the third sentence interprets that finding as having significance beyond a single measurement, challenging a larger practice. It does not describe methodology or question the data's reliability.

passage.text: At the beginning of her career, the novelist was praised for quick wit and comic timing, but reviewers usually stopped there, labeling her an entertainer. In her final novels, the same jokes had a darker edge, exposing rather than softening social cruelty. Most critics attributed this shift to personal experience. Yet a careful reading suggests something else: what changed was not her voice, but the world her voice was trained on.

stem: The final sentence primarily serves to do which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Challenge an earlier critical explanation by offering a different interpretation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dismiss the relevance of the novelist's early comic works.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Summarize the stylistic elements common to all of her novels.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Confirm that personal experience caused the shift in her work.

explanation: The passage notes that most critics attributed the novelist's change to personal experience; the final sentence disputes that view by proposing an alternative explanation involving the world her voice responded to.

passage.text: Many homeowners see dandelions as weeds to be eradicated, but the humble dandelion provides an early-season nectar source for pollinators emerging from winter. Its deep taproot also aerates compacted soil and draws nutrients to the surface. Rather than spend money on herbicides that can harm beneficial insects, a gardener might simply tolerate a few yellow blooms until spring growth begins.

stem: Which best describes the overall movement of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From a common assumption to a practical alternative

choices.label: B
choices.text: From a scientific claim to a personal anecdote

choices.label: C
choices.text: From a policy proposal to a historical account

choices.label: D
choices.text: From a statistical finding to a philosophical reflection

explanation: The passage begins with the common view that dandelions are weeds and ends by recommending a practical alternative: tolerating them for their ecological benefits.

passage.text: The town council's weekly meetings are rarely dramatic. Citizens raise complaints about potholes and barking dogs; council members defer issues to committees; votes on routine expenditures pass by wide margins. Yet last Tuesday, order dissolved. A dispute over the proposed bike lane grew heated, interrupted by shouting from the audience, and the mayor had to call a recess twice. By adjournment, the council had abandoned its usual measured rhythm entirely.

stem: Which choice best describes how the passage shifts from beginning to end?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From formal debate to informal conversation

choices.label: B
choices.text: From civic duty to private interest

choices.label: C
choices.text: From measured deliberation to unanimous agreement

choices.label: D
choices.text: From ordinary routine to turbulent conflict

explanation: The opening describes routine council business, while the ending describes a heated dispute with shouting and recesses, so the shift is from ordinary routine to turbulent conflict.

passage.text: To greet an unfamiliar dog, avoid staring directly and allow it to approach you at its own pace. Extend a closed hand slowly; a sniff is the dog's way of deciding whether you are trustworthy. Suddenly reaching toward its head can be perceived as threatening. Once the dog relaxes, you may gently scratch its chest or the side of its neck, areas that dogs typically enjoy, rather than its face.

stem: The primary purpose of the paragraph is to

choices.label: A
choices.text: caution readers against adopting an aggressive stance

choices.label: B
choices.text: instruct readers in a safe sequence of actions

choices.label: C
choices.text: compare dogs' preferences with those of humans

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why dogs may be fearful of strangers

explanation: The paragraph gives ordered directions for safely approaching a dog, so its main purpose is to instruct readers in a safe sequence of actions.

passage.text: A successful city park does not begin with landscaping. It begins with observation. Designers must study how people actually move through open spaces, where they pause to chat, and which sunny benches are empty by noon. Only after mapping these patterns can they choose plants, paving, and seating. A plan that ignores existing habits is not a design; it is a decoration.

stem: The author's main purpose in the paragraph is to

choices.label: A
choices.text: advocate a specific set of plants for city parks

choices.label: B
choices.text: summarize the history of urban park design

choices.label: C
choices.text: challenge a common misconception about park design

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why sunny benches are often unused

explanation: The author rejects the idea that park design starts with landscaping, arguing instead that it must begin with observing people's behavior, thereby challenging a common misconception.

passage.text: Reusable shopping bags are often praised for saving plastic, but their environmental impact is less straightforward than it appears. Producing a cotton tote can require more than a thousand gallons of water, and a bag must be used many times before it matches the carbon footprint of a lightweight plastic bag. This does not mean reusable bags are useless; it means shoppers should choose durable bags and actually keep using them.

stem: Which choice best describes how the author develops the argument in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It states a popular assumption, presents countervailing evidence, and offers a nuanced conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It attacks a familiar practice, dismisses all evidence against its position, then reaffirms an earlier claim.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It summarizes a scientific debate, rejects both major positions, and calls for more research.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces a simple solution, illustrates its drawbacks, and then endorses a different solution.

explanation: The passage begins with the common praise for reusable bags, complicates it with evidence about water and carbon footprints, and ends with a balanced recommendation rather than wholesale rejection.

passage.text: At first glance, the lava tubes of Craters of the Moon appear barren: walls of basalt, floors of loose rubble, no trace of water. Yet a researcher measuring temperature drops near the tube entrances notices something unexpected. Those cooler zones mimic the conditions under which ice has been found on Mars, and for planetary geologists, that resemblance transforms an ordinary cave into a laboratory.

stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It moves from a discouraging initial impression to a reason for scientific interest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It compares two kinds of geological formation found on Mars.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It argues that lava tubes are more common than most researchers believe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It proposes a new method for measuring temperatures in caves.

explanation: The paragraph opens with the seemingly barren appearance of the lava tubes, then shifts to the unexpected temperature measurements and their significance for planetary geologists. This structure moves from a discouraging impression to a reason the site is scientifically valuable.

passage.text: Many workers assume that meaningful time off requires at least a week. A growing body of research, however, suggests that even a single long weekend, approached with intention, can lower stress indicators measurably. The term 'micro-holiday' may sound whimsical, but it names a deliberate strategy: choose a nearby destination, leave work communications behind, and treat the break as a genuine vacation.

stem: Which choice best describes the primary function of the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To trace the history of the term "micro-holiday" from its humorous origins to its current use.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To weigh the advantages of long weekends against the advantages of longer vacations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To challenge a common assumption and offer a more deliberate alternative.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To argue that workplace stress can be eliminated with a single long weekend.

explanation: The paragraph begins by identifying a popular assumption about needing at least a week off, then undercuts it with research and presents the micro-holiday as a deliberate, evidence-informed alternative.

passage.text: Public records requests are often characterized as burdens on government staff, and indeed the volume of requests can be crushing. But the administrative difficulty of locating a document does not determine whether the public has a right to see it. The purpose of disclosure law is accountability, not convenience.

stem: Which choice best describes the relationship between the first sentence and the rest of the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It provides an example of the accountability that disclosure law is supposed to guarantee.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It summarizes the central argument that the paragraph goes on to support with statistics.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It identifies a problem that the following sentences solve by proposing a procedural reform.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It describes a common objection that the following sentences treat as less important than a public right.

explanation: The first sentence acknowledges the common complaint that records requests burden government staff. The rest of the paragraph argues that such difficulty does not override the public's right to access and that accountability, not convenience, is the law's purpose.

passage.text: When the Northbridge Public Library opened its makerspace in 2019, some residents dismissed it as a gimmick. Within eighteen months, however, weekly attendance tripled, and local small-business owners identified the facility as a primary source of prototyping help. The library board is now proposing to expand the makerspace and add evening hours.

stem: The paragraph is primarily structured to accomplish which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Present a problem and evaluate competing solutions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Document a change in public perception and suggest a resulting action.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Contrast a library's stated goals with its actual achievements.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Criticize residents who dismissed the makerspace as a gimmick.

explanation: The paragraph begins with skepticism about the makerspace, then provides evidence of its success and concludes with a proposal to expand it. This structure tracks a shift in perception and an action that follows from that shift.

passage.text: City officials often cite tree canopy as a luxury amenity, something to improve once more urgent needs are met. This ordering of priorities rests on a narrow view of stormwater management. In a single high-intensity rainfall, mature trees can absorb hundreds of gallons that would otherwise rush into overwhelmed sewers. The costs of replacing damaged infrastructure, by this measure, far exceed the costs of planting and maintaining trees.

stem: The paragraph's structure can best be described as...

choices.label: A
choices.text: Presenting a common view, then undermining it with evidence and reasoning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endorsing a city policy and then illustrating its benefits.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Summarizing a debate between environmentalists and engineers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tracing the history of tree-planting initiatives in cities.

explanation: The paragraph opens by describing officials' view of tree canopy as a luxury, then labels that view narrow and counters it with concrete evidence about stormwater absorption and infrastructure costs. This is a structure of presenting and then undermining a position.

passage.text: Proponents of the new transit terminal celebrate its gleaming concourses and seamless connections. Yet those who have lived in the neighborhood for decades tell a different story: the station's concrete pillars now stand where a produce market, a barbershop, and a community garden once thrived. In displacing these everyday gathering places, the terminal has not simply moved people more efficiently; it has erased the informal networks that made the area resilient. The architecture may be inclusive in design, but its social consequences have been exclusive in practice.

stem: Which choice best describes the structure of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It moves from an account of a project's apparent benefits to a criticism of its hidden costs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts from a neutral description of a structure to a technical analysis of its engineering.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It progresses from a celebration of a neighborhood's character to a lament for its lost traditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It begins with a policy debate and ends with a specific recommendation for reform.

explanation: The opening describes what supporters celebrate about the terminal, while the rest of the passage emphasizes the displacement and loss the project caused. This is a shift from apparent benefits to hidden costs.

passage.text: Some critics argue that requiring public libraries to filter internet content protects children. But filters are blunt instruments: they often block health information, political speech, and artistic works that adults have a right to read. More troubling, these systems typically decide what is objectionable without public oversight, effectively outsourcing a core civic judgment about access to knowledge to private software vendors. What begins as a protective measure can thus become an unaccountable form of censorship.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It concedes that filters may have some merit, weakening the author's overall argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It summarizes the broader implication of the points made in the preceding sentences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces a new example of the problem discussed earlier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It shifts from a discussion of policy consequences to a personal anecdote.

explanation: The final sentence draws a general conclusion from the earlier claims about blocked content, lack of oversight, and privatization of judgment: protective measures can become censorship. It does not concede, introduce an example, or become anecdotal.

passage.text: Researchers have long known that sleep consolidates memory, but the mechanisms have been uncertain. In a recent experiment, participants who heard a soft tone while learning a set of facts heard the same tone again during deep sleep; on a test the next morning, they recalled those facts more accurately than facts paired with no tone. The targeted cue seemed to reactivate the memory during sleep, strengthening it. The finding is striking, but the study used only one type of material and a small sample; cautious interpretation remains necessary.

stem: Which choice best describes the structure of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It presents a hypothesis, describes an experiment that supports it, and concludes that the hypothesis is confirmed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It outlines a scientific controversy, compares competing models, and recommends further research.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It identifies a scientific question, describes a study that addresses it, and then qualifies the study's findings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reports an unexpected experimental result and then proposes a new theory to explain it.

explanation: The passage begins with an open question about how sleep consolidates memory, describes an experiment that addresses that question, and ends with cautions about the study's limitations. Choice C accurately captures that structure.

passage.text: At first glance, the mayoral candidates' housing plans appear irreconcilable: one promises to eliminate rent regulation, the other to expand it. Yet both proposals share a deeper assumption—that changing tenant-landlord law will quickly fix a housing shortage rooted in decades of underbuilding. By treating rental policy as a lever that can transform supply overnight, they direct attention away from zoning restrictions, construction costs, and slow permitting. Seen this way, the supposed battle over rent regulation is less a genuine disagreement than a shared evasion of more difficult choices.

stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to

choices.label: A
choices.text: defend one candidate's housing plan over the other.

choices.label: B
choices.text: explain a legal dispute between tenants and landlords.

choices.label: C
choices.text: summarize evidence about housing construction costs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: argue that opposing policies obscure a common underlying failure.

explanation: The author says the two candidates' plans seem opposed but actually share an assumption and together distract from deeper problems. The purpose is therefore to argue that apparent opposition hides a common failure.

passage.text: In the arid highlands, farmers once relied on scattered granite outcrops that collected dew and funneled it to seeds below. These dew rocks were neither engineered nor accidental; they emerged from generations of observation, as farmers cleared soil around favorable stones and stacked smaller rocks to enlarge the collecting surface. The practice was itself an experiment, repeated and refined over centuries, keeping marginal land productive without wells or dams. Modern irrigation projects later replaced it, but the stones remain a quiet record of how people adapt to scarcity without transforming the land beyond repair.

stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It describes a traditional practice, explains how it developed, and reflects on its significance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It contrasts two irrigation methods and argues that one should replace the other.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It recounts a personal discovery and then recommends a return to an old technology.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It traces the history of a region and criticizes the effects of modern agriculture.

explanation: The passage first describes how dew rocks worked, then explains that they developed through long observation and experimentation, and finally says they are a record of adaptation to scarcity. This matches choice A.

passage.text: Many people assume that sidewalk cracks are purely an eyesore, evidence of neglected infrastructure. Yet these narrow fissures host a surprising variety of plants, from dandelions to native grasses, that provide nectar for urban bees. Recognizing this hidden flora does not require a degree in botany; it requires only a shift in attention. What looks like decay, in other words, can be reframed as a microhabitat worth preserving.

stem: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that neglected sidewalks should be repaired

choices.label: B
choices.text: explain why dandelions are valuable to city bees

choices.label: C
choices.text: challenge a common assumption by offering an alternative perspective

choices.label: D
choices.text: present experimental evidence about urban plant diversity

explanation: The passage begins with a common assumption that sidewalk cracks are eyesores but then reframes them as microhabitats worth preserving, so the purpose is to challenge that assumption with an alternative perspective.

passage.text: The first commercially successful electric car appeared in the 1880s, decades before the Model T. Yet by the 1920s, gasoline engines had largely prevailed, thanks to cheap oil and the lack of a power grid outside cities. A century later, the calculus has changed: battery costs have fallen, charging networks have expanded, and climate concerns have made emissions politically untenable. The history of electric vehicles thus reads less like a linear triumph than a series of reversals.

stem: The final sentence serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: introduce a new topic about contemporary climate policy

choices.label: B
choices.text: reinterpret the historical information presented earlier in the passage

choices.label: C
choices.text: contradict the claim that electric cars existed in the 1880s

choices.label: D
choices.text: call for immediate government investment in charging networks

explanation: After presenting details about the early success, decline, and later revival of electric vehicles, the final sentence synthesizes that information by calling the history a series of reversals rather than a linear triumph.

passage.text: At first, the committee's proposal to shorten the school day seems fiscally prudent: fewer hours mean lower utility and staffing costs. But the plan ignores a crucial variable. Students who leave early often spend those hours in unsupervised settings, and research links such gaps to increased juvenile crime. The proposal would therefore save money in the short term only to impose larger costs on the community later.

stem: Which choice best describes how the passage shifts from beginning to end?

choices.label: A
choices.text: from endorsing a proposal to celebrating its passage

choices.label: B
choices.text: from questioning a policy to recommending a compromise

choices.label: C
choices.text: from detailing a problem to dismissing all proposed solutions

choices.label: D
choices.text: from presenting an apparent benefit to exposing an overlooked consequence

explanation: The passage opens with the seemingly positive financial benefit of the proposal but then reveals a hidden negative consequence, so the shift is from an apparent benefit to an overlooked consequence.

passage.text: An editorial proclaimed that the new library is a waste of public funds, noting that foot traffic is lower than at the old building. That comparison is misleading. The old library was on a busy commercial street, while the new one sits beside a transit hub, where residents commute rather than browse. A more meaningful measure would consider digital borrowing, meeting-room reservations, and youth programs, all of which have increased since the move.

stem: The author's primary purpose is to

choices.label: A
choices.text: question the validity of an argument against the new library

choices.label: B
choices.text: compare the old and new library buildings in detail

choices.label: C
choices.text: endorse the editorial's conclusion about public funds

choices.label: D
choices.text: propose that the library adopt more digital services

explanation: The author identifies the editorial's claim, calls its comparison misleading, and offers other measures that undermine the editorial, so the purpose is to question the validity of that argument.

passage.text: People often describe memory as a filing cabinet: stored, labeled, and retrieved intact. Cognitive scientists, however, offer a different metaphor. Remembering is more like piecing together a quilt from available scraps; each retrieval subtly alters the pattern. Far from being a flaw, this reconstructive quality makes memory flexible, allowing people to update outdated beliefs and imagine novel futures.

stem: The shift from the first sentence to the rest of the passage primarily serves to

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that memory is completely unreliable

choices.label: B
choices.text: trace the historical development of memory research

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast a common metaphor with a more nuanced scientific description

explanation: The first sentence states the popular filing-cabinet view of memory, and the rest of the passage contrasts it with a reconstructive, flexible account offered by cognitive scientists.

passage.text: Many historians portray the Industrial Revolution as a sudden rupture, a dramatic break from agrarian life. Yet close analysis of parish records reveals a slower transformation. Occupational labels shifted gradually; families combined farming with textile work for generations. The language of invention itself borrowed older craft terms. Perhaps the more accurate image is not a switch being thrown but a tide slowly rising.

stem: Which choice best describes the structure of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It presents a common interpretation, offers evidence that complicates it, and suggests a revised image.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It summarizes a long-standing debate, then dismisses both sides for lacking evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lists evidence for a familiar view, then concludes that the view is wholly incorrect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It traces a sequence of inventions, then compares them to natural phenomena.

explanation: The passage starts with a common historical view, complicates it with evidence from parish records and craft language, and ends by offering a revised image: not a switch being thrown but a tide slowly rising.

passage.text: The detective did not need the photograph. The witness's description had been precise—the scar, the watch, the way he stood. But the photograph, placed on the table, made the suspect real in a way words could not. It was not evidence of guilt; it was evidence of attention. Someone had cared enough to keep it.

stem: The main purpose of the final sentence ("Someone had cared enough to keep it.") is to...

choices.label: A
choices.text: imply that the witness's recollection may be unreliable

choices.label: B
choices.text: explain why the detective asked to see the photograph

choices.label: C
choices.text: shift the photograph's significance from the person pictured to the act of keeping it

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that the suspect had once cared about the detective

explanation: The sentence follows the claim that the photograph is "not evidence of guilt; it was evidence of attention," so it makes the point that the photograph's meaning lies in the act of preserving it.

passage.text: Cities often celebrate their skylines as symbols of progress. Murals, by contrast, are easy to overlook: they occupy alley walls and underpasses, appearing without ceremony. Over time, however, these neglected images accumulate into a public record—of shifting populations, lost stores, forgotten slang. A city's unofficial biography may be written not in its towers but in its overlooked corners.

stem: Which choice best describes how the passage moves from beginning to end?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It defines a term, gives two examples, and then recommends a course of action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It states a popular belief, then argues that belief is contradicted by statistical evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It compares two forms of public art and argues that both deserve equal recognition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It sets up a contrast between prominent and overlooked urban symbols, then asserts that the overlooked ones may be more revealing.

explanation: The passage contrasts celebrated skylines with overlooked murals and ends by asserting that these overlooked corners may contain the city's unofficial biography.

passage.text: Some see the decline of handwritten letters as a cultural loss. The private voice, they argue, is flattened into email's quick efficiency. But efficiency has its own eloquence. The brief note—'got the job—will call tonight'—carries a different intimacy, one shaped by speed and trust. What appears at first to be a thinning of expression may in fact be a change of key.

stem: The final sentence ("What appears at first to be a thinning of expression may in fact be a change of key.") serves mainly to...

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismiss the view that email is efficient as overly simplistic

choices.label: B
choices.text: reframe the preceding contrast between loss and gain as a difference in form rather than quality

choices.label: C
choices.text: concede that handwritten letters may indeed be superior in intimacy

choices.label: D
choices.text: propose an explanation for why people prefer email's quick efficiency

explanation: The final sentence reinterprets the "thinning of expression" as a "change of key," so it reframes earlier claims about loss and gain as a shift in form, not in value.

passage.text: The proposed policy would lower the speed limit near schools. Supporters cite reduced accidents, and their data are persuasive. But the policy also treats all hours alike. At 2 a.m., with empty streets, the same limit slows emergency vehicles responding to calls. A measure aimed at protecting children may inadvertently endanger them. Safety is not a single number; it is a balance.

stem: Which choice best describes the structure of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acknowledges the strength of an argument, raises an objection, and draws a broader principle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It weighs evidence on both sides of a policy, then calls for additional study.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It traces the history of similar policies, then predicts their likely consequences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It ridicules a proposal, then suggests an alternative that is more equitable.

explanation: The passage concedes that supporters' data are persuasive, notes the policy's failure to account for different times of day, and concludes with the general principle that safety is a balance.

passage.text: Once dismissed as a faded relic of midcentury popular culture, the Meadowbrook Playhouse has lately become the object of something like reverence. Audiences who initially came to mock its peeling proscenium and creaky seats have found themselves charmed by its stubborn authenticity. Renovation plans once limited to demolition are now being redrawn to preserve the building’s quirky details. What began as an ironic pilgrimage has quietly turned into genuine tribute.

stem: Which choice best describes how the passage shifts from beginning to end?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From questioning the theater’s historical value to insisting on its artistic excellence

choices.label: B
choices.text: From treating the theater as an object of contempt to regarding it with genuine affection

choices.label: C
choices.text: From describing the theater’s physical decay to analyzing its financial difficulties

choices.label: D
choices.text: From criticizing the theater’s management to celebrating its devoted patrons

explanation: The passage begins with words like “dismissed” and “mock,” showing contempt, and ends with “genuine tribute,” showing affection and respect.

passage.text: Municipal zoning boards often treat beehives as a nuisance, lumping them with livestock and requiring large setbacks from property lines. Yet urban beekeeping has flourished in cities that revised such rules. When New York legalized hives in 2010, registered keepers increased from dozens to hundreds within a few years; similar changes in Chicago and Minneapolis produced comparable jumps. These figures suggest that outdated regulations, not urban conditions, were the main obstacle to urban beekeeping.

stem: The sentence “These figures suggest...” serves which function in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It introduces a counterexample to the claim that zoning boards are too restrictive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It summarizes the sequence of legal changes described in the preceding sentences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It qualifies the argument by conceding that some cities still restrict beekeeping.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It states the conclusion that the preceding examples were presented to support.

explanation: The examples of New York, Chicago, and Minneapolis support the final claim that outdated regulations, not urban conditions, were the main obstacle. The final sentence draws that conclusion.

passage.text: Educators have long assumed that typing notes is merely faster, not better. In classrooms where students type, however, researchers have noticed a curious pattern: typed notes tend to be verbatim transcriptions, while handwritten notes require students to summarize and rephrase. The mental work of that rephrasing seems to aid retention. What appears to be an efficiency gain may therefore be a learning loss.

stem: Which choice best describes how the passage shifts from start to end?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From reporting a common assumption to undercutting it with evidence and a reinterpretation

choices.label: B
choices.text: From presenting research findings to questioning the validity of those findings

choices.label: C
choices.text: From comparing two note-taking methods to recommending one for classroom use

choices.label: D
choices.text: From explaining the benefits of typing to acknowledging its disadvantages

explanation: The passage opens with the assumption that typing is “merely faster,” then uses research to suggest the opposite: that typing may actually cause a learning loss.

passage.text: Lucille Clifton’s poems are often described as quiet, a word that undersells their force. In compact lines, she addresses grief, injustice, and bodily joy without ever raising her voice. The apparent modesty of her style is part of her argument: that the most intimate experiences carry political weight. To read her work only as gentle is to miss its blade.

stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to...

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide a brief overview of the major themes in Clifton’s poetry

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that Clifton’s poetry can be appreciated only by readers familiar with political history

choices.label: C
choices.text: correct a common misreading of Clifton’s work as merely mild or delicate

choices.label: D
choices.text: encourage contemporary poets to imitate Clifton’s compact style

explanation: The passage challenges the view that Clifton’s poems are merely “quiet” or “gentle,” asserting that their force and political weight are often missed.

passage.text: Why do some public warnings go unheeded even when the danger is real? Emergency managers have often assumed that more alarming language will move people to act. Yet studies of evacuation behavior show that excessive urgency can make residents doubt the source. A warning that is too restrained, of course, can be equally ignored. The challenge, then, is not to shout louder but to calibrate trust.

stem: The opening question chiefly serves to...

choices.label: A
choices.text: acknowledge that the author is uncertain about the cause of the phenomenon

choices.label: B
choices.text: identify a problem that the following sentences examine and refine

choices.label: C
choices.text: reject a common assumption before offering a solution

choices.label: D
choices.text: ask readers to recall a personal experience of ignoring a warning

explanation: The question introduces the problem of unheeded warnings, and the rest of the passage explores possible explanations before arriving at a more refined conclusion.

passage.text: Although the Oakridge Public Library has historically closed at 6 p.m., the board recently voted to extend weekday hours until 9 p.m. Supporters noted that evening patrons make up a growing share of visitors, many of whom are shift workers or students. By accommodating these residents, the library hopes to increase circulation without significant added cost, since the building is already heated and staffed for evening programs.

stem: What is the primary purpose of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To raise concerns about the cost of extending library hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: To argue for the value of extending the library's weekday hours

choices.label: C
choices.text: To describe the history of the library's closing time

choices.label: D
choices.text: To encourage residents to attend evening library programs

explanation: The text presents the board's decision, notes the growing evening patronage, and argues that added costs are minimal, so it is best read as a justification for extending hours.

passage.text: Naomi's early canvases were filled with precise, sunlit landscapes, each tree and shadow mapped with nearly photographic accuracy. After a trip to the desert, however, her work grew spare and abstract. She began leaving large swaths of raw canvas and reducing forms to simple bands of pigment. Viewers who admired her early precision often found the later paintings disorienting, yet Naomi insisted that this reduction was a way of seeing more clearly.

stem: Which statement best describes the structure of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contrasts an early style with a later one and includes the artist's rationale for the change.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It presents a problem faced by the artist and then describes how she solved it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It describes audience criticism before defending the artist's early work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It narrates a trip chronologically and explains its influence on the artist's technique.

explanation: The first half describes Naomi's precise early landscapes; the second describes her spare abstract style and her justification that reduction is clearer, so the passage contrasts her creative phases and gives her rationale.

passage.text: City planners have announced a proposal to convert a vacant rail corridor into a pedestrian bike path. Opponents argue that the project would attract crime and reduce parking. Yet the corridor has sat unused for decades, and nearby residents have consistently requested more green spaces. Moreover, similar conversions in other cities have increased nearby property values rather than diminished safety. The proposal deserves approval.

stem: What is the function of the third sentence ("Yet the corridor has sat unused...") in the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It makes a concession to opponents while proposing a compromise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It establishes when the rail corridor was originally built.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces evidence that weakens the opponents' argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It summarizes the expected financial benefits of the project.

explanation: The sentence counters opponents by noting the corridor's decades of disuse and residents' requests for green space, thus undermining the claim that the project is unnecessary.

passage.text: Many assume that the Civil War ended when Lee surrendered at Appomattox in 1865. But scattered Confederate forces continued fighting for months, and by the summer the federal government was struggling to reunite a country still deeply divided. Reconstruction, therefore, did not begin with a single triumphant moment but rather as a lengthy, contested process.

stem: How does the text shift from its beginning to its end?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From acknowledging a fact to denying it

choices.label: B
choices.text: From praising a general to criticizing his strategy

choices.label: C
choices.text: From describing a cause to explaining its effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: From presenting a common assumption to offering a more complex account

explanation: The text starts with the popular assumption that the war ended at Appomattox, then complicates it by noting continued fighting and the long, contested nature of Reconstruction.

passage.text: To understand why ancient Maya cities collapsed, researchers have long examined climate records. Some argue that prolonged droughts caused food shortages and political unrest. Yet drought alone cannot explain why some cities endured while others vanished. A more complete explanation may involve deforestation and trade networks. The clues are still incomplete, but each new sediment core brings us closer to answering one of archaeology's greatest questions.

stem: What is the main purpose of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To prove that climate records from the ancient Maya region are unreliable

choices.label: B
choices.text: To argue that a single-cause explanation for the Maya collapse is too simplistic

choices.label: C
choices.text: To illustrate how archaeologists choose excavation sites

choices.label: D
choices.text: To celebrate a recent breakthrough in the study of Maya civilization

explanation: The text acknowledges the drought theory but then states that drought alone cannot explain the pattern and points to additional factors, so its purpose is to argue against a one-factor explanation.

passage.text: Although many residents regard urban beekeeping as a nuisance and worry about stings, the practice has expanded rapidly in major cities. Rooftop hives not only pollinate community gardens but also provide researchers with valuable data on environmental health. Indeed, the very conditions that once made city beekeeping seem improbable—dense buildings, varied microclimates, and abundant ornamental plants—now make cities among the most informative laboratories for studying pollinator decline.

stem: Which choice best describes the structure of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It presents a problem facing urban beekeepers and then proposes a solution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It summarizes public opposition to urban beekeeping before recommending stricter regulations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It opens with a common concern, then offers benefits that undercut that concern, and ends with a further supportive point.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It contrasts urban and rural beekeeping practices to explain why cities are unsuitable.

explanation: The passage first mentions a common negative view of urban beekeeping, then counters it with benefits such as pollination and research data, and strengthens that counter with the final sentence about cities as informative laboratories.

passage.text: For decades, museum audio guides were dismissed as bulky, isolating gadgets that distracted visitors from actual artworks. Yet the latest generation of audio guides is challenging that stereotype. Curators now design them to prompt slow looking, encouraging visitors to notice a painting's brushwork or a sculpture's texture. What was once a crutch has become a catalyst for sustained attention.

stem: The shift in the passage is best described as a movement from

choices.label: A
choices.text: a history of museum technology to a prediction about its future.

choices.label: B
choices.text: an acknowledged criticism of audio guides to a redefinition of them as tools for engagement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: a defense of traditional museum visits to a rejection of curatorial authority.

choices.label: D
choices.text: a comparison of audio guides with guided tours to an endorsement of guided tours.

explanation: The opening phrase 'dismissed as bulky, isolating gadgets' establishes a negative view, while 'Yet' marks the turn toward a positive view, and the final sentence redefines audio guides from a crutch to a catalyst.

passage.text: When policymakers talk about cutting carbon emissions, they often turn first to solar and wind farms. These familiar technologies, however, cannot supply steady power when the sun sets or the air is still. That limitation has led a growing number of engineers to reconsider nuclear energy, especially small modular reactors. Unlike their massive predecessors, these reactors can be built in factories and installed on sites that once seemed too small for nuclear power.

stem: The mention of solar and wind farms primarily serves to

choices.label: A
choices.text: contrast their high cost with the lower cost of small modular reactors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: explain why solar and wind farms continue to dominate new energy construction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: criticize policymakers for supporting renewable energy sources.

choices.label: D
choices.text: identify a limitation that motivates the discussion of an alternative energy source.

explanation: The first two sentences establish a shortcoming of solar and wind power, and the phrase 'That limitation has led' shows that this shortcoming motivates the turn to small modular reactors.

passage.text: Cities are often imagined as the opposite of wilderness, places where pavement has erased every trace of the natural world. Ecologists now argue, however, that cities contain a distinctive ecology of their own. Vacant lots become meadows of pioneer species; street trees host insects found nowhere else; even drainage ditches function as wetlands. By treating these habitats as genuine ecosystems, researchers are less likely to misjudge the few wild spaces that remain.

stem: Which choice best describes how the passage develops?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It introduces a widely held assumption, then presents a professional perspective that contradicts it, and concludes by noting a practical benefit of that perspective.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It summarizes a debate between ecologists and city planners, then recommends a compromise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It traces the history of urban development, then criticizes current land-use policies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It offers examples of urban wildlife, then argues that cities should be converted into protected wilderness.

explanation: The passage begins with a common assumption about cities, contrasts it with ecologists' view, and ends by noting that treating urban habitats as ecosystems helps researchers avoid misjudging wild spaces.

passage.text: Digital calendars are remarkably efficient, but they may fail to give time a memorable shape. A handwritten journal, by contrast, turns the record of a year into something physically present: date-planned pages, hurried scribbles, blank stretches. The very inefficiency of slowing down to write makes the past harder to delete and easier to revisit. This is why the journal has survived every prediction of its obsolescence.

stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that digital calendars are unreliable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: contrast two methods of scheduling and conclude that handwritten journals are more accurate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: explain why a seemingly outdated practice continues to be valuable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: propose a design for digital calendars that approximates the experience of journaling.

explanation: The passage contrasts digital calendars' efficiency with the distinctive value of handwritten journals and concludes that this value explains why journals have endured.

passage.text: In a memory experiment, participants who reviewed a lecture within one hour after hearing it recalled 90 percent of the material a week later. Participants who delayed their first review by a full day recalled only 30 percent, and those who delayed it by a week recalled almost nothing. The researchers concluded that even a relatively brief delay in initial review can have a ________ effect on long-term retention.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
explanation: The results show a clear, large drop in recall when the first review is delayed, so the effect of even a short delay is substantial. 'Negligible' contradicts the data, 'permanent' is too strong, and 'unpredictable' is unsupported by the consistent pattern.

passage.text: An alpine wildflower blooms weeks earlier in years when winter snowpack melts early. In a greenhouse, scientists simulated the soil moisture and air temperature of an early snowmelt, but the plants did not flower early. This result made the scientists suspect that some other snowmelt-related change, rather than moisture or temperature alone, triggers flowering. The most likely candidate was ________.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: B
choices.text: a burst of nutrients released into the soil as snow melts

choices.label: C
choices.text: a reduction in the number of pollinators

explanation: The text eliminates moisture and temperature as sufficient cues, so the correct completion must be another change associated with snowmelt. Increased day length is not caused by snowmelt, pollinator reduction is not mentioned, and declining nighttime temperature is a temperature cue.

passage.text: A city coated the roofs of some buildings with a white reflective material. Measurements showed that the roof surfaces on those buildings became about 4°C cooler than before, while roofs on nearby untreated buildings stayed the same. Yet residents of the coated buildings said the indoor temperature was no more comfortable than before. The most likely reason is that lowering the roof surface temperature did not ________.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: lower the indoor air temperature enough to be noticeable

choices.label: B
choices.text: change how much sunlight the roof absorbed

choices.label: C
choices.text: increase the amount of heat entering the building

explanation: The residents' unchanged comfort implies the cooler roof surface did not lead to a noticeable change inside. The coating would have changed sunlight absorption, and the other options are either contradicted or outside the scope of the passage.

passage.text: Hatchling sea turtles swim toward the open ocean shortly after emerging from their nests. In an experiment, scientists exposed hatchlings to an artificial magnetic field matching a location hundreds of kilometers away from their actual beach and then observed their swimming direction. The turtles oriented as though they were at the simulated location rather than at their home beach. This result indicates that hatchlings rely on ________ to guide their initial swim.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: B
choices.text: the smell of their home beach

explanation: Because the artificial magnetic field changed the turtles' orientation, the turtles must use magnetic information. The other options are not supported by the experiment.

passage.text: A school district changed from 45-minute classes to 60-minute classes but reduced the number of class periods per day so that total instructional time remained unchanged. Teachers reported that the longer periods allowed for deeper discussions, and students reported lower stress. Standardized test scores, however, were no different from the previous year. The superintendent concluded that the schedule change improved the school climate but did not, by itself, ________.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: B
choices.text: require teachers to alter their lesson plans

choices.label: C
choices.text: increase the time available for each subject

explanation: Since test scores did not improve, the schedule change did not raise student achievement. The other choices are either contradicted or not supported by the evidence given.

passage.text: In the mountains, spring flooding occurs when deep snowpack melts quickly. This year, weather forecasters measured the snowpack at nearly twice its usual depth for this time of year. Therefore, ___

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the risk of spring flooding is greater than usual.

choices.label: B
choices.text: spring will arrive earlier than usual.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the river will be lower than usual this spring.

explanation: Nearly double the usual snowpack supplies more meltwater, making spring flooding more likely; the other options draw unsupported conclusions.

passage.text: In a controlled experiment, tomato plants watered with diluted coffee produced more tomatoes than tomato plants given plain water, while soil, light, and temperature were the same. This suggests that ___

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: coffee is necessary for tomato plants to produce tomatoes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: tomato plants require caffeine in order to grow.

choices.label: C
choices.text: diluted coffee can improve tomato production.

explanation: Because the only difference was diluted coffee versus plain water, the increased yield suggests that diluted coffee can improve production; the other choices are too absolute or unsupported.

passage.text: A theater owner noticed that attendance nearly doubled on evenings when she offered a student discount. To improve attendance, she decides to ___

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: B
choices.text: offer the student discount more often.

choices.label: D
choices.text: reduce the number of evening performances.

explanation: The observed pattern links student discounts to higher attendance, so the most logical action is to offer that discount more often.

passage.text: Archaeologists found pottery with the same distinctive pattern at two ancient sites 500 miles apart, and radiocarbon dating indicates the two sites were occupied at the same time. This finding most strongly suggests that ___

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the two groups never had contact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the pottery was made at only one of the sites.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the two sites were actually one city.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the groups may have traded or shared cultural traditions.

explanation: Shared distinctive pottery at contemporaneous sites suggests cultural contact or trade; the other options are either unsupported or contradict the finding.

passage.text: A tutoring program gave students a practice test before and after eight weeks of weekly tutoring sessions. On average, scores rose by 15 points. Therefore, ___

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the tutoring sessions are the only way to improve test scores.

choices.label: B
choices.text: all students will improve by at least 15 points.

choices.label: C
choices.text: students who attended the tutoring sessions are likely to show improved scores.

choices.label: D
choices.text: students who did not attend tutoring probably scored worse.

explanation: The average score rise supports the conclusion that students in the program are likely to improve; the other choices make unsupported absolute claims.

passage.text: At Oak Ridge Community Pool, children under 10 must wear a swim vest while in the deep end. Children under 10 may be in the shallow end without a vest only if an adult is in the water with them. Tessa is seven years old, and her mother is sitting on a poolside chair in the shade, not in the water. Tessa would like to go swimming.

stem: Which conclusion most logically follows from the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tessa cannot use the shallow end without a swim vest right now.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tessa can use the deep end without a swim vest if her mother watches her.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tessa may use the shallow end without a swim vest because her mother is at the pool.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tessa cannot enter the pool at all unless her mother gets into the water.

explanation: Since Tessa is under 10 and no adult is in the water, the condition that would allow her to be in the shallow end without a vest is not met. The other choices contradict the stated rules or overstate what is required.
