explanation: The phrase "with its narrow cobblestone streets" is a nonessential modifier that gives extra information about Brightwater. It must be enclosed by commas.

passage.text: Even though the conductor had prepared extensively, neither the conductor nor the orchestra members ___ satisfied with the opening-night performance.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: When a compound subject is connected by "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer part of the subject; "members" is plural, so the plural past-tense verb "were" is correct.

passage.text: At the emergency board meeting, neither the CEO nor the shareholders were willing to disclose ___ projected losses before the regulatory deadline.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The pronoun refers to the compound antecedent "the CEO nor the shareholders"; because the nearer noun "shareholders" is plural, the plural possessive pronoun "their" is correct.

passage.text: By the time the fire department arrives, the blaze ___ through the warehouse roof, and thick black smoke is pouring into the night sky.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The present-tense verbs "arrives" and "is pouring" establish a present time frame; the present perfect "has already eaten" is used for an action completed before that present time.

passage.text: Marcus is the only one of those candidates who ___ convinced that the ability to connect emotionally outweighs policy detail, yet he performs brilliantly on the stump.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: With "the only one of those candidates who," the relative pronoun "who" refers to "one," not "candidates"; therefore the singular verb "is" is correct, and the present tense agrees with "performs."

passage.text: The city council members, as well as the mayor, ___ opposed to the new zoning proposal, and they plan to voice their concerns at tomorrow's public hearing.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The grammatical subject is "members," which is plural; the intervening phrase "as well as the mayor" does not change the number, so the plural present-tense verb "are" is required.

passage.text: Some companies have found that allowing employees to work from home leads to higher output per worker. Without commuting and office interruptions, employees can focus for longer stretches. These gains suggest that remote work is not merely a convenience but a genuine boost to productivity.
passage.text_b: Remote work may increase individual output in the short run, but it weakens the informal interactions that drive long-term innovation. Employees who never meet in person exchange fewer ideas, and teams lose the creativity that emerges from spontaneous conversation. A temporary rise in productivity is a poor trade for a lasting loss of collaboration.

stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that remote work boosts productivity by arguing that...

choices.label: A
choices.text: individual productivity is less important than the collaborative benefits lost with remote work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: remote work actually decreases productivity once commuting time is factored in.

choices.label: C
choices.text: productivity should be measured by number of hours worked rather than output.

choices.label: D
choices.text: companies should adopt remote work only if they can measure collaboration.

explanation: Text 2 argues that remote work's short-term productivity gains are a poor trade for the loss of collaboration and innovation. The author would therefore respond that the collaborative benefits lost are more important than individual productivity.

passage.text: City officials often promote bike-sharing programs as a way to reduce traffic congestion. Because bikes take up far less road space than cars, every person who chooses a shared bike over a car is thought to free up street capacity and shorten commute times for everyone.
passage.text_b: Surveys of bike-sharing users show that most replace short walking trips or bus rides, not car trips. People who are willing to pedal are usually already traveling without a car. As a result, bike-sharing does little to remove vehicles from the road, and congestion remains essentially unchanged.

stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that bike-sharing reduces congestion by asserting that...

choices.label: A
choices.text: bike-sharing fleets add to congestion because bikes are parked on streets.

choices.label: B
choices.text: bike-sharing mainly substitutes for other non-car transportation, so it has little effect on traffic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: bike-sharing will reduce congestion if enough stations are built.

choices.label: D
choices.text: officials should promote bike-sharing for its health benefits, not congestion relief.

explanation: Text 2 explicitly states that bike-sharing users mostly replace walking or bus trips, not car trips, so the program does little to reduce congestion. This directly counters Text 1's claim.

passage.text: Standardized tests are often criticized as biased because students from well-resourced schools tend to score higher. The tests use language and content that assume certain cultural experiences, placing some students at a disadvantage before they even enter the exam room.
passage.text_b: Standardized tests are designed to evaluate the same academic skills for all students. The fact that scores differ across groups does not prove bias; it may reflect real differences in educational preparation. A test that measures what students have learned is not biased simply because learning opportunities are unequal.

stem: How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument in Text 1 that standardized tests are culturally biased?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The tests should be redesigned to eliminate cultural references.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher scores by some groups show that the tests are too easy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Score differences are better explained by unequal schooling than by test design.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Standardized tests should measure effort rather than cultural knowledge.

explanation: Text 2 argues that score gaps may reflect unequal educational preparation, not test bias. The author would thus attribute the differences to schooling rather than to the test itself.

passage.text: Research on adolescent sleep cycles shows that teenagers naturally fall asleep later and need more sleep in the morning. Starting school at 8:30 or later aligns the school day with these biological rhythms, improving attendance, mood, and academic performance.
passage.text_b: Moving school start times later may seem beneficial, but it creates serious problems for working parents and after-school activities. Buses must be rescheduled, sports practices run later, and many students miss out on afterschool jobs. The practical costs for families are too high to justify the change.

stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely respond to the proposal in Text 1 by arguing that...

choices.label: A
choices.text: later start times would not actually improve students' academic performance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: teenage sleep cycles are not as fixed as researchers claim.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the proposal ignores the needs of students who work after school.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the logistical problems created for families outweigh the potential benefits.

explanation: Text 2 acknowledges that later start times may seem beneficial but emphasizes the serious family and scheduling problems, concluding that practical costs are too high to justify the change.

passage.text: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence are already automating tasks once done by humans, from customer service to data analysis. If this trend continues, many millions of workers could be displaced, and new jobs may not appear quickly enough to prevent widespread unemployment.
passage.text_b: History suggests that technological change eliminates some jobs but creates others in unexpected fields. When agriculture mechanized, farmworkers moved to factories; when factories automated, service jobs expanded. There is no strong evidence that AI will break this pattern, so fears of permanent mass unemployment are likely exaggerated.

stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that AI will cause widespread unemployment by pointing out that...

choices.label: A
choices.text: the disruption caused by AI will be worse than in the past.

choices.label: B
choices.text: past technological shifts eventually created new types of jobs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: AI should be regulated to protect workers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: automation has never eliminated any jobs.

explanation: Text 2 directly counters Text 1's fear of mass unemployment by citing historical patterns in which technology eliminated some jobs but created others. The author would respond with those historical examples.

passage.text: The marine biologist is one of those researchers who [blank] the complex migration patterns of sea turtles with painstaking care.

stem: Which choice completes the passage so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: In “one of those researchers who [blank],” the relative pronoun “who” refers to the plural noun “researchers,” so the verb must be the plural form “trace.” “Traces” and “has traced” are singular, and “tracing” is not a finite verb.

passage.text: Every one of the volunteers in the coastal cleanup crew carefully logged [blank] hours before leaving the beach.

stem: Which choice completes the passage so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The possessive pronoun “their” correctly refers back to the singular indefinite antecedent “Every one . . . of the volunteers” without specifying gender. “They” is a subject pronoun, “there” is an adverb, and “it” is not a possessive pronoun.

passage.text: By the time the conference ended, the keynote speaker [blank] delivered the same lecture at three other venues.

stem: Which choice completes the passage so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The phrase “By the time the conference ended” establishes a past time frame, and the action of delivering the lecture was completed before that past time. This requires the past perfect form “had delivered.” “Has” is present perfect, “have” does not agree with the singular subject “speaker,” and “having” is nonfinite.

passage.text: Neither the head of the audit committee nor the junior accountants [blank] able to identify the source of the discrepancy in the ledger.

stem: Which choice completes the passage so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: With a correlative “neither . . . nor” construction, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Since “junior accountants” is plural, the plural past form “were” is correct. “Was” and “is” are singular, and “be” is not a finite verb in this context.

passage.text: Many a composer [blank] struggled to balance artistic ambition with the practical demands of commercial performance.

stem: Which choice completes the passage so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The phrase “Many a” is a singular construction that requires a singular verb: “Many a composer has struggled.” “Have” and “are” are plural, and “having” is not a finite verb.

stem: The graph of a parabola in the xy-plane is shown above. Which of the following equations represents the parabola?
explanation: The graph has vertex \((1,-3)\), so in vertex form \(y=a(x-h)^2+k\) with \(h=1\) and \(k=-3\). Thus the equation is \(y=(x-1)^2-3\).

stem: The graph of \(f(x)=x^2\) is translated \(2\) units to the right and \(5\) units up. Which equation represents the resulting function \(g\)?
explanation: A translation \(2\) units to the right replaces \(x\) with \(x-2\), and a translation \(5\) units up adds \(5\). So \(g(x)=(x-2)^2+5\).

stem: Which of the following equations represents a parabola with vertex at \((3,-1)\) and opening upward?
explanation: For vertex \((h,k)=(3,-1)\), the vertex form is \(y=(x-3)^2-1\). The positive leading coefficient makes the parabola open upward.

stem: The graph of a parabola is shown above. If the vertex is at \((2,1)\), which of the following equations could represent the graph?
explanation: The vertex is \((2,1)\), so the vertex form must be \(y=(x-2)^2+1\). The graph also passes through \((0,5)\), which confirms the equation.

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=x^2\). The function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x)=f(x+3)-4\). Which of the following describes the transformation from the graph of \(f\) to the graph of \(g\)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shift left \(3\) units and down \(4\) units.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shift right \(3\) units and down \(4\) units.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Shift left \(3\) units and up \(4\) units.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shift right \(3\) units and up \(4\) units.

explanation: In \(f(x+3)\), replacing \(x\) with \(x+3\) shifts the graph \(3\) units left. The \(-4\) shifts the graph \(4\) units down.

stem: The parabola shown in the xy-plane has its vertex at \((-2,3)\). Which equation defines this parabola?
explanation: The vertex is \((-2,3)\), so the equation has form \(y=a(x+2)^2+3\). Because the parabola opens upward, \(a>0\), and the simplest equation is \(y=(x+2)^2+3\).

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=x^2\). The function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x)=f(x-4)+1\). What are the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of \(g\)?
explanation: The graph of \(f(x-4)\) is the graph of \(f(x)\) shifted 4 units right, and adding 1 shifts it 1 unit up. Thus the vertex moves from \((0,0)\) to \((4,1)\).

stem: The graph of \(y=f(x)\) is shown in the xy-plane. The graph of \(g\) is obtained by translating the graph of \(f\) 2 units left and 3 units up. What are the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of \(g\)?
explanation: The original vertex is \((1,-2)\). Moving 2 units left changes the x-coordinate to \(1-2=-1\). Moving 3 units up changes the y-coordinate to \(-2+3=1\). So the new vertex is \((-1,1)\).

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=-3(x+2)^2+5\). Which statement about the graph of \(f\) is true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The vertex is \((-2,5)\), and the parabola opens downward.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The vertex is \((2,5)\), and the parabola opens upward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The vertex is \((-2,-5)\), and the parabola opens downward.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The vertex is \((2,-5)\), and the parabola opens upward.

explanation: In vertex form \(f(x)=a(x-h)^2+k\), the vertex is \((h,k)\). Here \(h=-2\) and \(k=5\), so the vertex is \((-2,5)\). Since \(a=-3<0\), the parabola opens downward.

stem: The parabola shown in the xy-plane has vertex \((-1,2)\) and passes through \((1,-2)\). Which equation defines this parabola?
explanation: With vertex \((-1,2)\), the equation has form \(y=a(x+1)^2+2\). Substituting \((1,-2)\) gives \(-2=a(2)^2+2\), so \(-4=4a\), and \(a=-1\). Thus \(y=-(x+1)^2+2\).

passage.text: A study of shallow-water fish in the Gulf of Mexico found that when water temperatures exceeded 30°C, fish moved to deeper, cooler waters. However, in a protected marine reserve where fishing is prohibited, fish remained in shallow water even at 31°C, but they consumed less food and grew more slowly. The researchers propose that the reserve’s abundant large predators discourage fish from leaving their home reefs. This suggests that ____.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: fish in the marine reserve have adapted to tolerate warmer water than fish outside the reserve.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the presence of predators can override a fish’s preference for optimal temperatures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: marine reserves are ineffective at protecting fish from the effects of climate change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: fish in the protected reserve moved to deeper water only when temperatures exceeded 31°C.

explanation: The passage states that fish remained in shallow water despite high temperatures because abundant predators discourage them from leaving, so the presence of predators can override a preference for optimal temperatures. The other choices are unsupported or contradicted by the passage.

passage.text: A newly deciphered clay tablet from the ancient city of Ebla lists shipments of tin and copper to a workshop that produced bronze objects. The tablet is dated to the twenty-fourth century BCE. Previously, scholars believed that long-distance metal trade in this region began around the twentieth century BCE. Because tin is not found locally in Ebla, the tablet makes it likely that ____.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the workshop in Ebla produced bronze objects primarily for export.

choices.label: B
choices.text: tin was imported to Ebla from distant sources centuries earlier than previously thought.

choices.label: C
choices.text: copper was more valuable than tin in twenty-fourth-century BCE Ebla.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the tablet was actually created in the twentieth century BCE and misdated.

explanation: Since tin is not local to Ebla, the tablet's 24th-century-BCE date implies that tin was being imported from distant sources much earlier than scholars had believed. The other choices are unsupported or contradict the evidence in the passage.

passage.text: In an experiment, participants were shown pairs of products and asked to choose one. Half the participants were asked to decide "which product would you buy?" and half were asked "which product would others buy?" Later, when asked to rate how satisfied they were with their own choices, the first group expressed significantly lower satisfaction than the second. The researchers interpreted this as evidence that focusing on one's own preferences can highlight the trade-off between options, making the chosen product seem less ideal. This finding implies that ____.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: asking people to predict others' choices can make them more satisfied with their own subsequent choices.

choices.label: B
choices.text: consumers are generally unable to predict which products others would buy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: satisfaction with a choice is unrelated to the way the decision is framed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: people who choose for themselves always experience less satisfaction than those who choose for others.

explanation: The second group, which focused on others' choices, later reported higher satisfaction with their own choices, so directing attention away from one's own preferences can increase satisfaction. The other choices are unsupported, contradicted, or overgeneralized.

passage.text: A study of plastic waste in the North Pacific found that fragments smaller than 5 millimeters contained higher concentrations of chemical additives used as plasticizers than did larger fragments. Since plasticizers are mixed into plastic resins during production, the presence of high concentrations in tiny fragments indicates that ____.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: microplastics are more toxic to marine life than larger plastic debris.

choices.label: B
choices.text: plasticizers are gradually lost as larger plastic items break down.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the chemical additives in microplastics were originally present in larger items before those items fragmented.

choices.label: D
choices.text: larger plastic fragments in the North Pacific contain no chemical additives.

explanation: Because plasticizers are added during production and are found in small fragments, they must have been present in the larger items that broke down, showing that these additives persist through fragmentation. The other choices are unsupported or contradicted.

passage.text: At a highland settlement in South America dating to 1200 BCE, archaeologists found potsherds with traces of cinnabar. The nearest known natural cinnabar deposits are in the coastal lowlands, where the earliest evidence of mining dates to around 1000 BCE. Because cinnabar does not occur naturally in the highlands, the potsherds imply that ____.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: some contact existed between the highland settlement and the coastal lowlands before 1000 BCE.

choices.label: B
choices.text: cinnabar was first used in the highlands before it was used in the lowlands.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the potsherds were brought to the highlands from the coast after 1000 BCE.

choices.label: D
choices.text: cinnabar can be reliably dated, and the potsherds are older than the cinnabar.

explanation: Since cinnabar comes from the coastal lowlands but the highland settlement predates the earliest mining evidence, there must have been some earlier contact, perhaps through collection of surface deposits. The other choices are unsupported or contradict the dating in the passage.

passage.text: The city's new art museum designed by a renowned architect opened to the public last week.

stem: Which choice correctly punctuates the sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city's new art museum, designed by a renowned architect, opened to the public last week.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city's new art museum, designed by a renowned architect opened to the public last week.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The city's new art museum designed by a renowned architect, opened to the public last week.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city's new art museum—designed by a renowned architect opened to the public last week.

explanation: The phrase 'designed by a renowned architect' is a nonessential modifier and must be set off by paired commas: one before the phrase and one after it. Choice A is the only version that does this correctly.

passage.text: The cabin a quiet retreat from the noisy city sits at the edge of a pine forest.

stem: Which choice correctly punctuates the sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cabin—a quiet retreat from the noisy city sits at the edge of a pine forest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cabin, a quiet retreat from the noisy city, sits at the edge of a pine forest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cabin, a quiet retreat from the noisy city sits at the edge of a pine forest.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cabin a quiet retreat from the noisy city, sits at the edge of a pine forest.

explanation: The phrase 'a quiet retreat from the noisy city' is a nonessential appositive. It must be enclosed by paired commas: one after 'cabin' and one after 'city'.

passage.text: The old lighthouse a familiar landmark to sailors still guides ships into the harbor.

stem: Which choice correctly punctuates the sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The old lighthouse, a familiar landmark to sailors still guides ships into the harbor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The old lighthouse—a familiar landmark to sailors still guides ships into the harbor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The old lighthouse; a familiar landmark to sailors, still guides ships into the harbor.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The old lighthouse—a familiar landmark to sailors—still guides ships into the harbor.

explanation: The phrase 'a familiar landmark to sailors' is a nonessential appositive. Paired dashes correctly isolate it from the rest of the sentence.

passage.text: The novel written during the author's year abroad explores themes of exile.

stem: Which choice correctly punctuates the sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The novel, written during the author's year abroad explores themes of exile.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The novel written during the author's year abroad, explores themes of exile.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The novel, written during the author's year abroad, explores themes of exile.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The novel—written during the author's year abroad, explores themes of exile.

explanation: The participial phrase 'written during the author's year abroad' is nonessential and must be set off with paired commas. Choice C places the commas correctly.

passage.text: The winning team exhausted from the long match celebrated with their fans.

stem: Which choice correctly punctuates the sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The winning team, exhausted from the long match, celebrated with their fans.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The winning team—exhausted from the long match, celebrated with their fans.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The winning team, exhausted from the long match celebrated with their fans.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The winning team exhausted from the long match, celebrated with their fans.

explanation: The phrase 'exhausted from the long match' is a nonessential modifier. It must be enclosed by paired commas, so Choice A is correct.

stem: The graph of a parabola in the xy-plane is shown. Which of the following equations could represent the graph?
explanation: The parabola has vertex \((-2,3)\) and opens upward, so in vertex form \(y=a(x-h)^2+k\) with \(h=-2\), \(k=3\), and \(a=1\). Thus \(y=(x+2)^2+3\).

stem: The graph of \(g\) is shown in the xy-plane. If \(g\) is a vertical translation of the graph of \(f(x)=x^2\), which of the following defines \(g\)?
explanation: The graph shows the parabola \(y=x^2\) shifted upward by 3 units, so \(g(x)=f(x)+3=x^2+3\).

stem: The graph of a quadratic function is shown. Which equation represents the graph?
explanation: The parabola has vertex \((1,-2)\) and opens downward, so \(a\) is negative and the equation is \(y=-(x-1)^2-2\).

stem: The graph of a quadratic function is shown. It is a translation of the graph of \(f(x)=x^2\). Which equation represents the graph?
explanation: The parabola has vertex \((-4,-2)\), so the graph of \(f(x)=x^2\) is shifted 4 units left and 2 units down: \(y=(x+4)^2-2\).

stem: The graph of \(g\) in the xy-plane is a translation of the graph of \(f(x)=x^2\), as shown. Which of the following describes the transformation from \(f\) to \(g\)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A shift 3 units to the right

choices.label: B
choices.text: A shift 3 units to the left

explanation: The parabola has vertex \((3,0)\), so the graph of \(f(x)=x^2\) has been shifted 3 units to the right: \(g(x)=(x-3)^2\).

passage.text: Neither the project manager nor the software engineers _______ comfortable with the revised launch date, although the client believed the schedule was reasonable.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: With a neither...nor construction, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: "software engineers" is plural, so "were" is correct. "Was" wrongly treats the compound subject as singular.

passage.text: The board of directors finally announced _______ decision after months of deliberating over the merger.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "Board" is a singular collective noun acting as a unit, so the singular possessive pronoun "its" is correct. "Their" wrongly treats the board as plural, "our" is the wrong person, and "it's" is a contraction meaning "it is."

passage.text: By the time the evening news crew reached the intersection, the traffic jam _______ into the surrounding suburbs.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The action of the traffic jam spreading was completed before another past action (the news crew reaching the intersection), so the past perfect "had spread" is needed.

passage.text: The introduction of the new safety protocols, along with several updated equipment manuals, _______ expected to reduce workplace accidents.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is the singular noun "introduction"; the phrase "along with several updated equipment manuals" does not make the subject plural, so the singular verb "is" is correct.

passage.text: Each of the environmental reports, including the water-quality analyses, _______ to be reviewed before the public hearing.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is the singular indefinite pronoun "Each," so the singular verb "has" is required. The intervening plural nouns "reports" and "analyses" do not change the agreement.

passage.text: Paleontologists have proposed that the newly discovered dinosaur Thalassovenator was primarily aquatic, spending much of its life catching fish in coastal waters rather than hunting on land. The hypothesis is based on the animal's long, flattened tail and small forelimbs, but some researchers argue that these features could also be adaptations for life on muddy shorelines. Which of the following findings, if true, would most directly support the proposal that Thalassovenator was primarily aquatic?

stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most directly support the proposal that Thalassovenator was primarily aquatic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chemical analysis of Thalassovenator bones shows ratios of oxygen isotopes that match those of seawater, not freshwater or local land plants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thalassovenator skeletons are found in mudstone layers that also contain fossilized tree roots and land-dwelling insects.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fossil eggs attributed to Thalassovenator are found in clusters that would have been buried on sandy beaches.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The closest known relatives of Thalassovenator are small, fast-running dinosaurs from desert environments.

explanation: Oxygen isotope ratios matching seawater are direct chemical evidence that Thalassovenator lived and fed in a marine environment, supporting the claim that it was primarily aquatic. The other choices suggest land, shore, or desert associations and do not support the aquatic hypothesis.

passage.text: The city's 'play streets' program closed residential blocks to cars for a few hours each afternoon. City officials claim that this program reduced child pedestrian injuries. However, critics argue that the reduction was actually caused by a separate citywide campaign to lower speed limits, not by the play streets. Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the critics' argument?

stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the critics' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In neighborhoods with play streets, child pedestrian injuries fell by 20% compared with similar neighborhoods without play streets.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Child pedestrian injuries declined at the same rate in residential areas with and without play streets during the period of the speed limit campaign.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surveys showed that drivers became more alert when children were playing in the street during play street hours.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pedestrian injuries among adults also declined slightly during the same period that the play streets program was in effect.

explanation: If child pedestrian injuries declined equally in areas with and without play streets, the play streets themselves cannot explain the decline. This supports the critics' claim that the separate speed limit campaign, which affected all areas, was the more likely cause.

passage.text: A biologist hypothesizes that the bright orange skin of a tropical frog has evolved as a warning signal to deter predators, not as camouflage to hide the frog from predators. Which of the following findings, if true, would most directly support the biologist's hypothesis?

stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most directly support the biologist's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Frogs with bright orange skin are more likely than frogs with dull brown skin to be captured by birds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When placed on orange leaves, the frogs are harder for human observers to see than when placed on green leaves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Predators that eat the frog become ill and subsequently avoid attacking frogs with the same orange coloration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The orange color fades in captive frogs that are kept in dim light.

explanation: The finding that predators become ill after eating the frog and then avoid similarly colored frogs directly supports the warning-signal explanation: the bright color deters predators because it is associated with toxicity or distastefulness.

passage.text: In the late medieval period, the inland city of Aldeburg lost much of its population and economic importance. A historian argues that this decline was caused mainly by the growing use of Atlantic sea routes, which bypassed the overland caravan routes through Aldeburg. Which of the following pieces of evidence, if true, would most weaken this argument?

stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence, if true, would most weaken the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aldeburg's population declined sharply immediately after a severe outbreak of plague, decades before the Atlantic sea routes became commercially important.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aldeburg was a major producer of wool cloth, a commodity traded widely along overland routes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Written records show that Aldeburg's merchants began using Atlantic sea routes in large numbers during the period of decline.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A neighboring city located on the Atlantic coast grew rapidly during the same period that Aldeburg declined.

explanation: If Aldeburg's decline began with a plague outbreak well before Atlantic sea routes grew in importance, then the shift to sea routes cannot be the main cause of the decline. This directly weakens the historian's causal claim.

passage.text: A psychologist claims that students who take handwritten notes remember lecture material better than students who use laptops to take notes. Which of the following experimental results, if true, would most directly support the claim?

stem: Which of the following experimental results, if true, would most directly support the psychologist's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Students who used laptops typed more words per minute than students who wrote by hand.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students who wrote by hand and students who used laptops scored the same on a delayed recall test.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students who were allowed to choose their note-taking method overwhelmingly preferred laptops.

choices.label: D
choices.text: On an unannounced test given one week after a lecture, handwritten note-takers answered 80% of factual questions correctly, while laptop users answered 55%.

explanation: The handwritten note-takers outperforming laptop users on a delayed test directly supports the claim that handwritten notes lead to better memory of lecture material. The other choices address typing speed, preference, or equal performance, none of which support the claim.

passage.text: Until recently, archaeologists assumed that the ancient city's water system was primarily for irrigation ___ new excavations have revealed a complex network of pipes beneath residential buildings, suggesting domestic use.

stem: Which choice completes the text with correct punctuation and grammar?
explanation: The blank separates two independent clauses. A comma plus the coordinating conjunction "but" correctly joins them. The other options are incorrect because they either omit the required comma before "but," use a semicolon before a coordinating conjunction, or use a colon before a conjunction.

passage.text: The committee reviewed the proposal for nearly two hours ___ the chair called for a vote before all members had finished speaking.

stem: Which choice completes the text with correct punctuation and grammar?
explanation: The blank separates two independent clauses, and "however" is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction. A semicolon before "however" and a comma after it correctly connect the clauses. A comma alone creates a splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and a colon does not appropriately introduce a contrasting clause here.

passage.text: The museum's new wing has doubled its exhibition space ___ the number of visitors has not increased accordingly.

stem: Which choice completes the text with correct punctuation and grammar?
explanation: The blank separates two independent clauses that are closely related but not joined by a conjunction. A semicolon alone is correct. A comma creates a splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and a colon would incorrectly imply that the second clause explains or expands on the first.

passage.text: Applicants must submit their portfolios by Friday ___ their submissions will not be considered for the summer residency.

stem: Which choice completes the text with correct punctuation and grammar?
explanation: The blank separates two independent clauses. "Otherwise" is a conjunctive adverb, so it requires a semicolon before it and a comma after it. A comma alone creates a splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and a colon does not correctly introduce this consequence.

passage.text: Solar panels generate electricity without producing greenhouse gases ___ they remain a minor source of energy in many regions due to upfront costs.

stem: Which choice completes the text with correct punctuation and grammar?
explanation: The blank separates two independent clauses. The coordinating conjunction "yet" must be preceded by a comma. Omitting the comma creates a run-on, while placing a semicolon or colon before "yet" is incorrect because "yet" is a coordinating conjunction, not a conjunctive adverb or an introducer of a colon phrase.

passage.text: Community gardens contribute to public health by encouraging residents to exercise outdoors, eat fresh vegetables, and form social connections with neighbors. These benefits are especially valuable in cities where green space and affordable produce are scarce.
passage.text_b: Supporters celebrate community gardens, but their presence can also raise nearby property values. As rents climb, the low-income residents who originally built and used the gardens may be forced to move away.

stem: The author of Text 1 would most likely respond to the concern raised in Text 2 by making which point?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The health and social advantages of community gardens are still worth pursuing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Community gardens should be removed from areas where property values are high.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rising property values are irrelevant to the success of community gardens.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fresh vegetables are less important than affordable housing.

explanation: Text 1 emphasizes health and social benefits, so its author would likely say those benefits justify pursuing community gardens despite the possible side effect noted in Text 2.

passage.text: Switching from printed textbooks to digital tablets would lighten students' backpacks and make it easier for teachers to distribute updated materials. Schools that make this switch can save printing costs over time and prepare students for technology-heavy careers.
passage.text_b: A tablet-only classroom depends on reliable wireless networks, durable devices, and technical support. Many rural districts cannot afford these resources, so replacing printed books with tablets could leave some students without any way to complete their homework.

stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely characterize the proposal in Text 1 as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unhelpful because digital tablets are no better than printed textbooks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: impractical for many districts because it overlooks costs and unequal access.

choices.label: C
choices.text: too expensive only because tablets weigh more than textbooks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: wise only if schools first distribute the same information on paper.

explanation: Text 2 focuses on financial and infrastructure obstacles to replacing printed textbooks with tablets, so it would say Text 1 overlooks these practical concerns.

passage.text: Even with the internet, public libraries remain indispensable. They provide free computer access, job-search assistance, and quiet workspaces for people who lack reliable internet at home.
passage.text_b: Some books may no longer circulate, but libraries have reinvented themselves as centers for digital inclusion and community gathering. Their physical spaces are more valuable than ever.

stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between Text 1 and Text 2?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Text 1 argues that libraries are outdated, while Text 2 says they are necessary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Text 2 strengthens Text 1's argument by pointing to a similar, current library service.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Text 2 contradicts Text 1 by suggesting that libraries no longer lend books.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Text 1 focuses on books, while Text 2 focuses on buildings.

explanation: Text 1 argues that libraries are essential because of digital-access services; Text 2 reinforces that view by describing libraries as centers for digital inclusion.

passage.text: Later high school start times would respect teenagers' biological sleep patterns. Studies show that when the first bell shifts from 7:30 to 8:30 or later, attendance rises and car crashes among young drivers decline.
passage.text_b: Later start times are difficult for many families because bus schedules must be reorganized and parents who leave for work early cannot supervise their children in the morning.

stem: The author of Text 1 would most likely answer the practical concerns in Text 2 by arguing that

choices.label: A
choices.text: school start times should be moved earlier to accommodate parents' work schedules.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the difficulties raised in Text 2 are unimportant and should be ignored.

choices.label: C
choices.text: bus schedule reorganization would prove that later starts are a bad idea.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the health and safety benefits are great enough that districts should address the scheduling challenges.

explanation: Text 1 emphasizes health and safety benefits, so its author would likely argue that those benefits justify working through the scheduling problems raised in Text 2.

passage.text: The best way to preserve an old building is to adapt it for a new use. For example, a vacant factory can be turned into apartments, keeping the structure alive while providing needed housing.
passage.text_b: Adaptive reuse has risks. When a warehouse is renovated into apartments, industrial details such as exposed pipes and worn floors are often replaced with modern finishes, leaving nothing of the history that made the building distinctive.

stem: Which statement best represents how the author of Text 2 would respond to the proposal in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The factory may lose the historic character that made it worth preserving.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factories should never be used for housing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Old buildings are best preserved by leaving them empty.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modern apartments are more important than historic details.

explanation: Text 2 warns that renovation can remove the historic details that made a building distinctive, so it would respond to Text 1's factory example with that concern.

passage.text: The honeyguide [_______] has evolved an unusual partnership with humans, guiding people to bee colonies and waiting while they open the hives.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: , a small African bird known for guiding people to bee colonies,

choices.label: B
choices.text: , a small African bird known for guiding people to bee colonies

choices.label: C
choices.text: ; a small African bird known for guiding people to bee colonies,

choices.label: D
choices.text: , a small African bird known for guiding people to bee colonies;

explanation: The phrase "a small African bird known for guiding people to bee colonies" is a nonessential appositive modifying "the honeyguide," so it must be set off by paired commas. The other choices omit one comma or use a semicolon incorrectly.

passage.text: The Orionid meteor shower [_______] is most visible from locations far from city lights.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: which occurs every autumn when Earth passes through debris left by Halley's Comet,

choices.label: B
choices.text: —which occurs every autumn when Earth passes through debris left by Halley's Comet,

choices.label: C
choices.text: , which occurs every autumn when Earth passes through debris left by Halley's Comet,

choices.label: D
choices.text: , which occurs every autumn when Earth passes through debris left by Halley's Comet

explanation: The clause "which occurs every autumn when Earth passes through debris left by Halley's Comet" is nonessential and must be enclosed by matching commas. Omitting the comma before or after the clause, or mixing a dash with a comma, violates standard punctuation.

passage.text: Ada Lovelace [_______] recognized that Charles Babbage's analytical engine could do far more than simple arithmetic.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: , widely considered the first computer programmer

choices.label: B
choices.text: , widely considered the first computer programmer,

choices.label: C
choices.text: , widely considered the first computer programmer;

choices.label: D
choices.text: ; widely considered the first computer programmer,

explanation: The phrase "widely considered the first computer programmer" is a nonessential modifier identifying Ada Lovelace. It must be set off by a comma before and a comma after; a semicolon or an absent closing comma creates a boundary error.

passage.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault [_______] is designed to preserve crop diversity in the event of a large-scale catastrophe.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ; carved into a mountainside on a Norwegian island,

choices.label: B
choices.text: , carved into a mountainside on a Norwegian island

choices.label: C
choices.text: —carved into a mountainside on a Norwegian island,

choices.label: D
choices.text: , carved into a mountainside on a Norwegian island,

explanation: The participial phrase "carved into a mountainside on a Norwegian island" is nonessential and must be isolated by paired commas. Semicolons, an opening dash with a closing comma, or a missing closing comma are all incorrect.

passage.text: The Sahara Desert [_______] contains surprising seasonal blooms of flowers in the weeks after rare rainfall.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.label: A
choices.text: , far from being a lifeless expanse

choices.label: B
choices.text: ; far from being a lifeless expanse,

choices.label: C
choices.text: , far from being a lifeless expanse,

choices.label: D
choices.text: far from being a lifeless expanse,

explanation: The phrase "far from being a lifeless expanse" is an interrupting modifier that must be enclosed by matched commas. Omitting the opening comma, using a semicolon, or omitting the closing comma creates a punctuation error.

passage.text: Some scientists argue that a research finding should be regarded as established only after independent labs replicate it. Replication is valuable, but it is not a simple sieve: if an effect is real but small, the chance of obtaining a statistically significant result in any one replication may be well under 100 percent. Consequently, if a discipline insisted that a finding be confirmed in every replication attempt before accepting it, ______.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: many legitimate findings with small effects would be rejected.

choices.label: B
choices.text: replication rates in the discipline would improve dramatically.

choices.label: C
choices.text: researchers would be forced to abandon statistical hypothesis tests.

choices.label: D
choices.text: only findings with no random variation would ever be confirmed.

explanation: The passage states that a real but small effect may not produce statistically significant results in every replication. Therefore, requiring confirmation in every replication attempt would discard many genuine findings with small effects.

passage.text: As temperatures rise, many mountain plants shift their ranges upslope to stay within their climate tolerance. On one mountain range, botanists calculated the elevation gain that would restore a typical summer temperature for each major species by 2080. The required gain was substantial for species now confined to the coolest summits but modest for species found mainly in the lower valleys. Since a summit offers no higher ground, the botanists were led to conclude that ______.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the summit plant species face a greater threat from rising temperatures than the lower-elevation species do.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the lower-elevation plant species will eventually be forced off the mountain entirely.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the projected upward shift will allow lower-elevation species to coexist with summit species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the lower-elevation species are unlikely to respond to warming because their required upward shift is modest.

explanation: Because summit species need a substantial elevation gain to restore their climate but have no higher ground available, they are more at risk from warming than species in lower valleys, which have more room to shift upward.

passage.text: Ancient written sources such as tax rolls and land registers give a misleading impression of the size of past populations, because they count only the people whom the state needed to track. To correct this bias, historians sometimes count the floor areas of excavated houses and multiply by an assumed number of residents per room. However, in many regions the majority of ancient houses were made of timber and have entirely decayed, leaving only more durable stone structures for excavators to find. Counting only excavated house floors can therefore make a region appear ______.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: more urbanized than it actually was if its stone buildings were used only for storage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: less densely populated than it actually was if its ordinary houses were built of wood.

choices.label: C
choices.text: poorer than it actually was if timber was a valuable trade commodity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: more egalitarian than it actually was if wood and stone houses were occupied by different classes.

explanation: If ordinary wooden houses have decayed and only stone structures remain, excavations will reveal fewer dwellings than actually existed, so the region will seem less densely populated than it was.

passage.text: Community-based language archives usually aim to record a language before its last fluent speakers are gone. A persistent obstacle, however, is orthography: speakers often disagree about how to write words that they have only spoken. If archive staff settle such disagreements by imposing an official spelling, many community members may feel that the archive represents one dialect and not their own, and they may withdraw support. Thus the longevity of a digital language archive may be determined less by the quality of its recording equipment than by ______.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: its ability to build consensus around a writing system.

choices.label: B
choices.text: how many words can be recorded before funding runs out.

choices.label: C
choices.text: whether the language has a literary tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the geographic isolation of the speaker community.

explanation: The passage says that imposing an official spelling can cause community members to withdraw support. Thus the archive's survival depends on reaching agreement about orthography, not mainly on equipment or recording capacity.

passage.text: A famous medieval portolan chart is remarkably accurate along coastlines that were heavily trafficked by trading ships, but distorted along coasts that were remote from major routes. One explanation is that the chart was not drawn from a single comprehensive survey, but compiled gradually from sketch maps made by sailors. If this explanation is correct, the portions of a compiled chart that are most trustworthy should be those for which ______.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: independent sketches of the same coast could be compared and reconciled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: a single royal cartographer took personal responsibility for the drawing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: sailors had the strongest incentive to keep their navigational knowledge secret.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the coast had a regular shape that was easy to recall from memory.

explanation: The passage explains that the chart was compiled from sailors' sketch maps, so accuracy should be greatest where many independent sailors' accounts of the same coast were available to be combined.

passage.text: Modern concretes typically weaken as they age because water seeps into microscopic cracks. Roman marine concrete, by contrast, has remained strong for two millennia. For decades, engineers assumed the Romans had found a superior recipe, perhaps involving a special volcanic ash. But a 2023 study suggested that the initial recipe alone was not enough. The researchers immersed a modern reproduction of Roman concrete in seawater and another identical slab in fresh water. Only the seawater slab produced a mineral called aluminous tobermorite, which grows inside cracks and binds to the surrounding material. The researchers concluded that the Romans' choice of seawater construction sites was crucial: without seawater, the concrete would not have gained this self-strengthening ability. Therefore, the extraordinary durability of Roman marine concrete is best explained by ______.

stem: Which conclusion most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the unusual minerals in volcanic ash, which were present in the concrete regardless of water exposure

choices.label: B
choices.text: the ability of seawater to promote a mineral that filled the concrete's developing cracks

choices.label: C
choices.text: the absence of fresh water from the Romans' concrete-making process

choices.label: D
choices.text: the use of high temperatures, which caused the mineral to form during the original construction

explanation: The passage reports that seawater, but not fresh water, produced aluminous tobermorite, a mineral that grows in cracks and binds to surrounding material. The best-supported conclusion is therefore that seawater promoted this crack-filling mineral, making the concrete more durable.

passage.text: In the 1980s, amphibian populations in cloud forests high in the tropical Andes experienced sudden crashes, whereas related species in warmer lowland rainforests remained abundant. Biologists found a fungal pathogen, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), in the dead frogs. In laboratory cultures, Bd multiplied well at temperatures between 17 and 23 degrees Celsius, and its growth slowed sharply above 26 degrees Celsius. High-elevation streams average 12 to 18 degrees Celsius, whereas lowland streams average 24 to 28 degrees Celsius. Because Bd becomes lethal to many amphibians when it multiplies rapidly, the lack of crashes in lowland populations is best explained by the fact that ______.

stem: Which conclusion most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: lowland amphibians were exposed to Bd earlier and therefore developed immunity

choices.label: B
choices.text: the species living in lowland rainforests are not susceptible to Bd at any temperature

choices.label: C
choices.text: cooler high-elevation streams slowed the growth of Bd below the point of lethality

choices.label: D
choices.text: temperatures in lowland streams often rise above the range in which Bd multiplies rapidly

explanation: The passage says Bd multiplies well at 17 to 23 degrees Celsius and its growth slows sharply above 26 degrees Celsius. Lowland streams average 24 to 28 degrees Celsius, so their temperatures often exceed the range in which Bd multiplies rapidly, making D the best-supported conclusion.

passage.text: To determine which compass cue young migratory birds prefer when stars and magnetic fields conflict, researchers raised two groups of hand-reared birds in a planetarium. In one group, the projected star pattern was rotated 90 degrees clockwise while the magnetic field remained normal; these birds departed in a direction shifted 90 degrees clockwise from the species' correct route. In the other group, the natural star pattern was shown while the magnetic field was reversed; these birds still departed in the species' correct route. Based on these results, the clockwise shift in the first group cannot be attributed to the magnetic field, because the magnetic field was unchanged. Therefore, when the two cues contradict one another, the birds' migratory orientation is determined by ______.

stem: Which conclusion most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the pattern of stars, not the magnetic field

choices.label: B
choices.text: the magnetic field, not the pattern of stars

choices.label: C
choices.text: the interaction of stars and magnetic field during migration

choices.label: D
choices.text: the bird's innate route, independent of both cues

explanation: When the stars were rotated but the magnetic field was unchanged, the birds shifted direction, showing that the stars influenced their orientation. When the stars remained natural but the magnetic field was reversed, the birds still chose the correct route. Thus the stars, not the magnetic field, determined orientation when the cues conflicted.

passage.text: Students were asked to learn forty new vocabulary words. Half studied the words in a single long session; the other half studied the words in four short sessions spaced two days apart. Both groups spent the same total amount of time studying. One week after the final session, the spaced group recalled significantly more words. Functional brain imaging during the interval between spaced sessions showed increased activity in the hippocampus, a region associated with memory consolidation, whereas the massed group showed no such increase. This suggests that the benefit of spacing is not due to the amount of time spent studying but to ______.

stem: Which conclusion most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the increased repetition of each word within a single study session

choices.label: B
choices.text: the opportunity to use the words in new sentences during the test

choices.label: C
choices.text: memory consolidation occurring between practice sessions

choices.label: D
choices.text: the students' awareness that they would be tested one week later

explanation: Total study time was the same for both groups, and brain imaging showed hippocampal activity between spaced sessions but not during massed practice. This directly supports the conclusion that spacing improves recall by allowing memory consolidation to occur between sessions.

passage.text: Paranthropus, a genus of early hominins, had enormous molars, thick tooth enamel, and flared cheekbones that anchored powerful jaw muscles. For decades, paleoanthropologists viewed these features as adaptations for cracking hard objects such as nuts. However, a recent analysis of microscopic pits and scratches on Paranthropus teeth found almost no pits like those produced by hammering hard foods; instead, the tooth surfaces carried long, parallel scratches typical of grinding tough, abrasive plants. Functional modeling further showed that grinding such vegetation would require large jaw muscles, whereas cracking nuts would demand a different jaw shape. Therefore, the distinctive chewing anatomy of Paranthropus is most plausibly an adaptation to a diet dominated by ______.

stem: Which conclusion most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: D
choices.text: roots and tubers that required high temperatures to soften

explanation: The passage states that Paranthropus teeth show scratches typical of grinding tough, abrasive plants, not pits from cracking hard foods, and that grinding such vegetation would require large jaw muscles. Thus the best-supported conclusion is that its chewing anatomy was adapted to tough, abrasive plant material.

passage.text: Archaeologists examining dental calculus from a coastal settlement found starch grains from a tuber that grows only far inland, as well as microscopic remains of marine fish and seaweed. Because the site had boats and woven nets, some scholars argued that the starch grains prove the inhabitants ate the tuber. However, starch grains can become trapped in dental calculus when plant fibers are used to make or repair nets, not only when plants are eaten. Therefore, the calculus evidence alone ______.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: confirms that the inhabitants traded with inland groups to obtain the tuber

choices.label: B
choices.text: proves that the inhabitants used seaweed fibers to make nets

choices.label: C
choices.text: does not establish that the tuber was a food source, since the starch grains may have come from net-making

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggests that marine foods left no trace in dental calculus

explanation: The passage explicitly states that starch grains can enter dental calculus from non-dietary activities such as net-making, so the evidence alone cannot prove the tuber was eaten. The other choices overstate or contradict the evidence.

passage.text: In the Namib Desert, a species of beetle climbs to the top of a sand dune at night and stands with its head down and abdomen raised. Researchers noticed that when fog rolls in, water droplets form on the beetle's bumpy back and run toward its mouth. In controlled trials, beetles whose backs were artificially smoothed collected about 40 percent less water than normal beetles, and beetles that were prevented from assuming the headstand posture collected almost no water at all. Therefore, the headstand posture is not simply an idle resting position but ______.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: an action essential to the beetle's ability to drink from fog

choices.label: B
choices.text: a defensive display that also happens to expose the back to fog

choices.label: C
choices.text: a posture that allows fog to condense even on smooth backs

choices.label: D
choices.text: a behavior that enables the beetle to collect water regardless of how much fog is present

explanation: Blocking the headstand posture almost eliminated water collection, so the posture is essential for drinking from fog. Smoothing the back reduced but did not eliminate water collection, making C false, and there is no evidence for B or D.

passage.text: Ancient Roman seawater concrete owes its longevity to a mineral called aluminum tobermorite, which forms when seawater reacts with lime and volcanic ash. The mineral can grow inside cracks, sealing them and preventing further damage. In experiments, replicas of Roman concrete showed that the mineral formed faster at higher seawater temperatures, producing a repair material comparable in strength to the original concrete. Thus, Roman harbor structures built in warmer parts of the empire likely ______.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: experienced more frequent cracking than those in colder regions

choices.label: B
choices.text: had cracks sealed more quickly than those in colder regions

choices.label: C
choices.text: contained less aluminum tobermorite than those in colder regions

choices.label: D
choices.text: depended on imported ash to maintain their strength

explanation: The experiments directly show that warmer temperatures speed up the formation of aluminum tobermorite, which seals cracks. Thus warmer structures likely had faster crack-sealing. The other choices contradict or go beyond the evidence.

passage.text: In a sleep study, participants memorized a list of foreign words translated into English. Half then took a 90-minute nap, while the other half stayed awake. During the nap, researchers played another set of foreign words over speakers, and brain responses showed that the sleeping participants heard them. On testing after the nap, the group that napped recalled the earlier words 20 percent more accurately than the awake group, but neither group showed any memory of the words played during sleep. Therefore, sleep seems to strengthen memories formed before sleep, rather than ______.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: B
choices.text: reactivate brain networks used during wakefulness

choices.label: C
choices.text: selectively strengthen memories that will be tested later

choices.label: D
choices.text: take up new verbal information encountered during sleep

explanation: The key finding is that words played during sleep were not remembered later, even though participants heard them. This supports the conclusion that sleep does not encode new verbal information. The other choices do not address the evidence about words presented during sleep.

passage.text: At an archaeological site in the highlands, researchers recovered ancient DNA from a sediment layer dated to the same period as the earliest known farming villages in the region. The sediment contained DNA from barley and from sheep or goats. Because the site lies in a narrow mountain valley, archaeologists propose that its inhabitants were herders who also grew barley. However, DNA from barley can be transported to a site by wind-blown pollen from distant fields, and DNA from sheep and goats can enter sediment through their dung and urine. Thus, without additional evidence, the DNA evidence alone ______.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: supports the claim that the barley was grown at the site because pollen cannot travel far

choices.label: B
choices.text: cannot distinguish between barley grown at the site and barley pollen carried in from elsewhere

choices.label: C
choices.text: proves that the site's inhabitants kept sheep and goats

choices.label: D
choices.text: indicates that the site was a farming village before any other in the region

explanation: The passage gives an alternative route for barley DNA to reach the site: wind-blown pollen. Therefore the DNA alone cannot prove local cultivation. The other choices make stronger claims than the evidence supports or contradict the stated possibility of long-distance pollen transport.

passage.text: Text 1: Many cities have found that adding bike lanes reduces traffic congestion and improves public health. Because these benefits are clear, local governments should install more bike lanes as quickly as possible.
passage.text_b: Text 2: Bike lanes are popular with cyclists, but they often require narrowing car lanes or removing on-street parking, which can frustrate drivers and nearby businesses. A transportation researcher argues that bike lanes are not a universally effective solution and must be evaluated against each city's particular conditions.

stem: Which choice best describes how the author of Text 2 would respond to the recommendation in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By wholeheartedly endorsing the rapid installation of bike lanes in every city

choices.label: B
choices.text: By cautioning that bike lanes may have drawbacks and may not suit every city

choices.label: C
choices.text: By agreeing that bike lanes reduce traffic but denying that they affect public health

choices.label: D
choices.text: By insisting that bike lanes should be removed wherever they are already installed

explanation: Text 2 states that bike lanes are not universally effective and must be evaluated against city conditions, so the author would caution against Text 1's blanket recommendation.

passage.text: Text 1: Remote work agreements consistently increase productivity and employee satisfaction. Companies that want to succeed in the modern economy should therefore allow employees to work from home whenever possible.
passage.text_b: Text 2: Although many employees enjoy remote work, the evidence on productivity is mixed. In particular, remote work can weaken collaboration, reduce spontaneous mentoring, and make it harder for new employees to learn from experienced colleagues.

stem: How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Text 1's claim that remote work consistently increases productivity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By questioning that claim and pointing out that remote work can weaken collaboration and mentoring

choices.label: B
choices.text: By agreeing that productivity increases while adding that collaboration is unimportant

choices.label: C
choices.text: By arguing that remote work should be banned in all industries

choices.label: D
choices.text: By claiming that employee satisfaction is the only factor companies should consider

explanation: Text 2 directly challenges the idea that productivity consistently increases, noting mixed evidence and negative effects on collaboration and mentoring.

passage.text: Text 1: Public libraries have become obsolete because nearly all books and reference materials can be accessed online. Spending tax money on physical library buildings is no longer justified.
passage.text_b: Text 2: Libraries serve people who lack reliable internet access, offer free meeting spaces, and provide literacy programs. In many communities, they are the only place where residents can get digital training and job-search help. Eliminating them would deepen inequality.

stem: Based on Text 2, the author would most likely view the argument in Text 1 as

choices.label: A
choices.text: Correct, since digital resources have made physical libraries unnecessary

choices.label: B
choices.text: Partly correct, because libraries should charge fees for internet use

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incorrect, because libraries perform important social and digital-access functions beyond lending books

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unimportant, since public spending on libraries is too small to matter

explanation: Text 2 argues that libraries provide essential services such as internet access, meeting spaces, and training, so the author would reject the claim that libraries are obsolete.

passage.text: Text 1: School uniforms improve student discipline and reduce social pressure caused by clothing choices. Therefore, all public schools should adopt uniform policies.
passage.text_b: Text 2: A recent review of school uniform policies found little evidence that uniforms improve grades or behavior. The same review noted that uniforms can limit students' freedom of expression and do not eliminate bullying based on clothing.

stem: Which choice best describes how the author of Text 2 would respond to Text 1's recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By endorsing uniforms as a proven way to raise grades and improve behavior

choices.label: B
choices.text: By agreeing that uniforms reduce social pressure but denying that they affect discipline

choices.label: C
choices.text: By supporting uniforms only for high school students, not elementary students

choices.label: D
choices.text: By rejecting the recommendation on the grounds that evidence does not support it

explanation: Text 2 says there is little evidence that uniforms improve grades or behavior, so the author would reject the recommendation in Text 1.

passage.text: Text 1: Banning single-use plastics is the single most effective strategy for reducing ocean pollution. Governments around the world should implement such bans immediately.
passage.text_b: Text 2: Ocean pollution is a complex problem caused by poor waste management, manufacturing choices, and consumer behavior. Plastic bans alone can be ineffective or even harmful if they lead to greater use of other disposable materials without fixing the underlying waste system.

stem: How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that banning single-use plastics is the single most effective strategy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By agreeing that plastic bans are the best and most complete solution

choices.label: B
choices.text: By arguing that plastic bans are only one part of a broader solution and may have drawbacks

choices.label: C
choices.text: By stating that ocean pollution is caused entirely by consumer behavior

choices.label: D
choices.text: By proposing that plastic bans should be delayed until more plastics are produced

explanation: Text 2 presents ocean pollution as a complex problem and warns that plastic bans alone can be ineffective or harmful, so the author would see bans as only part of a broader solution.

passage.text: During the review, each of the proposed solutions _____ a distinct set of technical and ethical challenges, so the panel must weigh them carefully before voting.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of the verb is the singular pronoun "each," so the present-tense verb must be "presents." The plural noun "solutions" is inside a prepositional phrase and does not determine the verb's number.

passage.text: The cluster of observations from the first expedition, along with the more recent satellite data, _____ to be reconciled before the team can issue a definitive statement about sea-level rise.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "cluster," which is singular, so the verb must be the singular "needs." The intervening phrase "along with the more recent satellite data" does not change the number of the subject, and "needing" is not a finite verb.

passage.text: Before the invention of photographic reproduction, botanical illustrators _____ the minute structure of each plant by hand, a process that could take weeks for a single plate.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The time phrase "Before the invention" and the later past-tense verb "could take" establish a past context, so the simple past "recorded" is the correct choice. "Had recorded" would require a later past event, and "have recorded" cannot be used with a completed past time.

passage.text: Among the many factors that determine whether a coastal town will survive the next century _____ the rate of sea-level rise and the elevation of its storm-surge defenses.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The sentence is inverted: the verb comes before the compound subject "the rate of sea-level rise and the elevation of its storm-surge defenses." Because that subject is plural, the correct verb is "are."

passage.text: The repertory orchestra, whose members have studied under several distinguished conductors, builds its season around pieces that showcase _____ ability to shift from delicate chamber textures to full ensemble climaxes.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The antecedent is the singular noun "orchestra," so the possessive pronoun must be singular: "its." "Their" is plural, "there" is an adverb, and "it's" is a contraction of "it is."

passage.text:
Text 1
The promise of vertical farming in cities is belied by basic physics. Replacing sunlight with LEDs requires enormous electricity, and in most regions that electricity comes from fossil fuels. The carbon footprint of a head of lettuce grown in a skyscraper can exceed that of field-grown lettuce shipped across a continent. Until energy production is decarbonized, vertical farms remain an expensive, high-emission indulgence.
passage.text_b:
Text 2
Critics of vertical farming often compare current LED systems with sunlight and conclude that the enterprise is hopeless. This overlooks the trajectory of technology. The efficiency of horticultural LEDs has doubled roughly every few years, and as lighting costs fall, the location advantages of indoor farming—no pesticides, minimal water use, proximity to consumers—become decisive. The relevant question is not whether vertical farms make sense today, but whether they will in the decade in which the first generation of large-scale facilities is being built.

stem: Which of the following best characterizes how the author of Text 2 would respond to the argument in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By suggesting that Text 1's criticism applies mainly to today's technology and is therefore shortsighted about future efficiency gains.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By disputing Text 1's claim about energy use with new data about recent LED efficiency improvements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By arguing that proximity to consumers already makes vertical farming environmentally superior to field farming.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By claiming that field-grown lettuce also has hidden transportation costs that Text 1 fails to mention.

Text 1
A public library's mission is to provide information, not to serve as a building.
