passage.text: A psychologist claims that social media's effect on loneliness depends on the mode of use. She predicts that using platforms to communicate with close ties will reduce loneliness, whereas passively reading the posts of others will increase it.

stem: Which finding would most directly support this prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A survey finds that people who spend more than three hours per day passively browsing social media report lower loneliness than those who never use social media.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In a four-week study, participants instructed to send several personal messages to friends each day reported lower loneliness at the end of the study, while participants instructed to scroll through their feeds without interacting reported higher loneliness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A national survey finds that loneliness has increased over the same period that social media use has become more widespread.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who were already lonely spent more time sending messages to friends and also spent more time browsing social media.

explanation: Choice B directly tests the proposed distinction: active messaging reduces loneliness while passive browsing increases it. The other choices either contradict the prediction, fail to distinguish modes of use, or suggest loneliness causes social media use.

passage.text: An archaeologist argues that pottery was first invented in multiple separate regions rather than spread from a single point of origin. The archaeologist points out that early pottery traditions in East Asia and the Middle East are separated by thousands of years and show few stylistic similarities.

stem: Which archaeological discovery, if true, would most directly support this argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Radiometric dating shows that the oldest known pottery fragments in East Asia are much older than any pottery found in the Middle East, and there is no evidence of contact between the two regions at that time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Potsherds from the earliest sites in the Middle East contain temper materials that have been chemically traced to a clay source in East Asia.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The earliest pottery from both East Asia and the Middle East occurs at sites where people also cultivated millet and wheat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A single pottery type with identical decorative stamps is found in a continuous arc from East Asia to the Middle East, with progressively younger dates toward the west.

explanation: Choice A supports independent invention by showing that pottery appeared much earlier in one region than the other with no apparent contact. Choices B and D suggest diffusion between regions, and C is irrelevant to whether pottery was independently invented.

passage.text: A cognitive scientist proposes that hearing information during sleep can strengthen memories formed while awake, but cannot create new memories from information never studied. She calls this the “rehearsal-only” account.

stem: Which experimental result, if true, would most directly support this account?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants tested after hearing a list of foreign words for the first time during sleep remembered some of those words the next morning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants who heard recordings of their own voices summarizing a topic they had studied remembered more of that topic than participants who heard the same recording while awake.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants who slept with soft music playing recalled fewer studied items than participants who slept in silence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who studied a set of word pairs before sleep recalled more of those pairs when the same pairs were played during sleep, but participants who heard a different, unstudied set of word pairs during sleep showed no recall of the unstudied set.

explanation: Choice D directly confirms both parts of the rehearsal-only account: replay of studied material strengthens existing memories, while replay of unstudied material creates no new memories. Choice A contradicts the account, and the others are indirect or irrelevant.

passage.text: A political scientist argues that a country's path to democracy depends less on how rich it becomes than on whether it developed representative institutions before economic growth. On this view, inclusive early institutions create the rules and interest groups that later make democratization likely.

stem: Which historical finding, if true, would most directly support this argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several oil-exporting countries became extremely wealthy while ruled by autocratic monarchies and never developed democratic institutions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most countries that adopted democratic constitutions in the nineteenth century had lower incomes than their neighbors but caught up economically over the next century.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Among countries that underwent rapid industrialization in the twentieth century, those with preindustrial parliamentary assemblies were much more likely to become democracies than those without such assemblies, regardless of their final income levels.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Countries that democratized before industrialization generally did so after popular uprisings, not because of gradual institutional development.

explanation: Choice C directly ties democratic outcomes to early representative institutions while controlling for income, which is exactly the comparison the argument depends on. The other choices either reverse the historical sequence, omit the role of early institutions, or emphasize wealth without addressing institutions.

stem: The graph of \(f(x)=x^2\) is translated 4 units to the right and 1 unit up to produce the graph of \(g\). Which equation defines \(g\)?
explanation: Shifting right 4 units replaces \(x\) with \(x-4\), and shifting up 1 unit adds 1 outside the square: \(g(x)=(x-4)^2+1\).

stem: Function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=(x-5)^2+2\). What is the vertex of the graph of \(f\)?
explanation: In vertex form \(f(x)=(x-h)^2+k\), the vertex is \((h,k)\). Here \(h=5\) and \(k=2\), so the vertex is \((5,2)\).

stem: Let \(f(x)=x^2\). The graph of \(g\) is obtained by shifting the graph of \(f\) 3 units downward. Which equation defines \(g\)?
explanation: A vertical shift down by 3 subtracts 3 from the entire function: \(g(x)=x^2-3\).

stem: Which equation has a graph with vertex at \((-1,2)\) and opens upward?
explanation: Vertex form with vertex \((-1,2)\) is \(y=(x+1)^2+2\). Since the coefficient of the squared term is positive, the parabola opens upward.

passage.text: Night-blooming flowers of the desert cactus Echinocereus open within minutes after sunset. Some botanists have hypothesized that the trigger is the sharp drop in air temperature after dark, not the simultaneous increase in humidity, because the cactus is adapted to arid conditions and would not benefit from waiting for humidity. To test this hypothesis, researchers placed flowering cacti in climate-controlled chambers and independently manipulated temperature and humidity around dusk.

stem: Which finding from the experiment would most directly support the botanists' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When the temperature was held constant but the humidity was lowered, the flowers opened at their normal time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When the humidity was held constant but the temperature was lowered, the flowers opened earlier than usual.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When both temperature and humidity were held constant, the flowers failed to open.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When both temperature and humidity were lowered at the same time, the flowers opened later than usual.

explanation: The hypothesis says that a temperature drop, not humidity change, triggers opening. Choice B directly supports this by showing that lowering temperature alone causes earlier opening, while the other choices either weaken the hypothesis or fail to isolate temperature as the trigger.

passage.text: At an ancient workshop site in the Taurus Mountains, archaeologists found clay storage jars with a distinctive red slip. Some scholars argue that the jars were imported from a coastal city 300 kilometers away, where identical red-slip wares were mass-produced. A research team counters that the jars were made locally at the Taurus site, citing the presence of the mineral talc in the jar fabric, a substance common in local clay deposits.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the research team's counterargument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The coastal city's workshop clay also contains talc, though in slightly different proportions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excavations at the Taurus site have revealed many artifacts but no kilns or pottery-making tools.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chemical analysis shows that the talc in the jars matches the signature of local Taurus clay deposits and differs from clay used at the coastal workshop.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The red slip on the Taurus jars is identical in color and thickness to the red slip on jars known to have been made in the coastal city.

explanation: The research team argues for local production because the jars contain talc, which is common in local clay. Choice C directly supports this by showing the talc is chemically matched to local deposits and not to the coastal workshop's clay, making local production the stronger conclusion.

passage.text: Psychologist Dr. Lena Ortiz hypothesizes that making eye contact during an eyewitness interview reduces the number of sensory details a witness can recall, because eye contact competes with mental imagery for limited cognitive resources. To test this, she has participants watch a video of a minor theft, then asks them to describe the thief while either maintaining eye contact with an interviewer or looking at a blank wall.

stem: Which finding would most directly support Dr. Ortiz's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who made eye contact recalled significantly more sensory details than those who looked at the blank wall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants in the two conditions recalled about the same number of sensory details, but the eye-contact group made fewer false statements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants who looked at the blank wall recalled more sensory details, but they also spent more time silently pausing before answering.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who looked at the blank wall reported significantly more sensory details, and in a separate task eye contact reduced participants' ability to form vivid mental images.

explanation: Dr. Ortiz predicts that eye contact reduces sensory recall because it competes with mental imagery. Choice D supports both parts of the hypothesis: blank-wall participants recalled more sensory details, and eye contact independently impaired vivid mental imagery. The other choices contradict or fail to support the predicted effect.

passage.text: Marine biologists have hypothesized that ocean acidification impairs the ability of juvenile coho salmon to detect predators by smell. Because higher dissolved carbon dioxide lowers the pH of seawater and can interfere with odor-receptor proteins, researchers predicted that salmon raised in high-CO2 conditions would show weaker avoidance responses to water containing predator scent than salmon raised in normal seawater.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the biologists' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Salmon raised in high-CO2 water avoided predator-scented water less often than salmon raised in normal seawater.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Salmon raised in high-CO2 water avoided predator-scented water just as consistently as salmon raised in normal seawater.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Salmon raised in high-CO2 water were less active overall than salmon raised in normal seawater.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Salmon raised in normal seawater showed stronger avoidance when both predator scent and visual cues were present.

explanation: The hypothesis predicts that high-CO2 salmon will avoid predator scent less. Choice B shows no difference in avoidance between high-CO2 and normal salmon, directly contradicting that prediction and therefore weakening the hypothesis.

passage.text: In a recent book, a historian argues that lead poisoning from Roman water pipes and cooking vessels was a major cause of the decline of the Roman Empire. She points to Roman medical writings describing colic, anemia, and neurological disorders, and notes that lead was widely used throughout the empire.

stem: Which archaeological finding, if true, would most directly weaken the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Analysis of well-preserved skeletal remains from imperial Rome shows average bone lead levels far below the threshold associated with serious health effects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lead levels in Roman-era skeletons are higher than those in skeletons from earlier Italian cultures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some Roman elites replaced lead pipes with clay pipes after complaining about the taste of the water.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ancient Roman texts report that lead vessels were used mainly for storing wine and olive oil.

explanation: The historian's argument depends on Romans being exposed to harmful levels of lead. Choice A directly undermines this by showing that actual imperial Roman skeletons had lead levels far below the threshold for serious health effects. The other choices either support lead exposure or only show limited awareness of the issue.

passage.text: Paleontologists proposed that the ancient fish species *Altipectes* used its paired fins to walk along the bottom of shallow seas, rather than using them mainly for swimming. To test this, they analyzed newly discovered trackways preserved in rock of the same age. If *Altipectes* walked with its fins, the trackways should show something different from the marks left by a fish that swam close to the seafloor or rested on its belly.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the paleontologists' proposal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The trackways contain a series of evenly spaced, alternating impressions matching the shape and size of *Altipectes*' fins, with no continuous groove from a dragging tail.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The trackways are accompanied by ripple marks indicating the water was shallow, but no skeletal remains of *Altipectes* are preserved in the same layer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The spacing between fin impressions is irregular and variable, and some impressions overlap as if the animal had been pushed along by a current.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Computer simulations suggest that *Altipectes*' fins were poorly suited for supporting its body on the seafloor.

explanation: The alternating, evenly spaced fin impressions with no tail-drag groove indicate the fish moved in a stepping pattern, directly supporting walking over swimming or belly-sliding.

passage.text: A team of educational researchers hypothesized that labeling a diagram directly next to its parts improves students' ability to learn the material because it eliminates the extra effort of searching for labels in a separate key. According to this "integrated labels" hypothesis, splitting attention between diagram and key impairs understanding, so any benefit of a separate key should not occur.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly challenge the integrated-labels hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When students studied a diagram with direct labels, they reported that the page looked less cluttered than when they studied a diagram with a separate key.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students who used the separate key spent more time looking at the diagram and less time looking at the key than students who used direct labels.

choices.label: C
choices.text: On a delayed test, students who studied with a separate key remembered significantly more details than students who studied with direct labels.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students who used direct labels completed the study session in less time than students who used a separate key.

explanation: If separate-key students remembered more details, the prediction that direct integrated labels improve learning is contradicted.

passage.text: City planners hypothesized that increasing the density of street trees reduces neighborhood crime rates because trees signal that a public space is cared for, which encourages residents to use it and discourages criminal activity. To test this, researchers compared crime statistics across 50 neighborhoods over ten years, taking into account income, population density, and the number of police patrols.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the city planners' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the ten-year period, neighborhoods that gained street trees also experienced a sharp increase in the number of new businesses opening.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neighborhoods with higher street-tree density had significantly lower rates of property crime, even after adjusting for income, population density, and police patrols.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residents of high-tree neighborhoods reported that they felt less safe walking at night than residents of low-tree neighborhoods did.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Police records showed that patrol frequency was positively correlated with tree density across the fifty neighborhoods.

explanation: The finding links greater tree density to lower crime after controlling for confounding factors, directly supporting the hypothesis.

passage.text: Psycholinguists hypothesized that readers process passive-voice sentences more slowly than active-voice sentences because the initial grammatical analysis must be revised when the subject is revealed to be the recipient of the action. They recorded eye movements as participants read sentences that were identical in meaning but differed in voice.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the psycholinguists' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants rated passive-voice sentences as more formal than active-voice sentences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reading times for active-voice sentences were longer when they appeared later in a passage than when they appeared in the first sentence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eye-tracking showed that participants briefly looked back to the beginning of passive-voice sentences immediately after reading the verb, while no such lookbacks occurred for active-voice sentences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants recalled the gist of active-voice sentences more accurately than passive-voice sentences in a later memory test.

explanation: The lookback to the start after the verb is direct evidence of the reanalysis the hypothesis predicts.

passage.text: Some climate historians attribute the Little Ice Age (roughly 1300–1850) primarily to decreased solar radiation. Others argue that a cluster of large volcanic eruptions in the mid-thirteenth century triggered the initial cooling, with solar changes playing a secondary role. To test the volcanic triggering hypothesis, a team analyzed ice-core records that preserve annual markers of past eruptions and climate indicators.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the volcanic triggering hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ice cores show that the largest mid-thirteenth-century eruption was followed by a decade of cooler summers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tree-ring records show a drop in temperatures in the thirteenth century that is significantly larger than drops associated with known eruptions alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ice-core record shows that temperatures began to decline at least 50 years before the earliest large eruption in the volcanic cluster, during a period of unusually low solar activity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eruptions in the thirteenth century were recorded in ice cores from both Greenland and Antarctica, suggesting they had global effects.

explanation: Cooling that began before the first major eruption and coincides with low solar activity undermines the claim that the eruptions triggered the cooling.

stem: The graph of function \(f\) is shown in the xy-plane. Which of the following equations defines \(f\)?
explanation: The vertex is at \((3,-2)\), so \(f(x)=a(x-3)^2-2\). Since the graph passes through \((5,2)\), \(2=a(2)^2-2\), so \(a=1\). Thus \(f(x)=(x-3)^2-2\).

stem: The graph of function \(g\) in the xy-plane is the result of shifting the graph of \(f(x)=x^2\) two units to the right and three units up. Which equation defines \(g\)?
explanation: A shift 2 units right replaces \(x\) with \(x-2\), and a shift 3 units up adds 3 to the output. Therefore \(g(x)=(x-2)^2+3\).

stem: The graph of function \(f\) is shown in the xy-plane. Which of the following equations defines \(f\)?
explanation: The vertex is at \((-1,4)\), so \(f(x)=a(x+1)^2+4\). Since the graph passes through \((1,0)\), \(0=a(2)^2+4\), so \(a=-1\). Thus \(f(x)=-(x+1)^2+4\).

stem: The graph of function \(f\) is shown in the xy-plane. Which of the following equations defines \(f\)?
explanation: The vertex is at \((-3,2)\), so \(f(x)=a(x+3)^2+2\). Since the graph passes through \((-1,6)\), \(6=a(2)^2+2\), so \(a=1\). Thus \(f(x)=(x+3)^2+2\).

stem: The graph of function \(g\) is shown in the xy-plane. Which of the following equations defines \(g\)?
explanation: The vertex is at \((-3,-1)\), so \(g(x)=a(x+3)^2-1\). The graph also passes through \((0,8)\), and \(8=a(3)^2-1\) gives \(a=1\). Thus \(g(x)=(x+3)^2-1\).

stem: The dot plot above shows the number of goals scored by each player on a soccer team during a season. What is the median number of goals scored?
explanation: There are 12 data values, so the median is the average of the 6th and 7th values. The 6th value is 7 and the 7th value is 8, so the median is \(\frac{7+8}{2}=7.5\).

stem: The dot plot above shows the number of pets owned by each student in a class. What is the mean number of pets per student?
explanation: The data set is \(2,2,3,3,3,4,4,4,4,5\). The sum is \(34\), and there are 10 values, so the mean is \(34 \div 10 = 3.4\).

stem: The dot plot above shows the ages of participants in a chess tournament. What is the range of the ages?
explanation: The greatest age shown is 22 and the least age shown is 10, so the range is \(22 - 10 = 12\).

stem: The dot plot above shows the number of books read by each member of a book club over the summer. What is the mode of the data set?
explanation: The value 4 appears 4 times, more than any other value, so the mode is 4.

visual.title: Books Read by Book Club Members

stem: The dot plot above shows the number of hours a group of volunteers spent at a community center last week. What is the median number of hours?
explanation: There are 15 data values, so the median is the 8th value. Counting up from the smallest value, the 8th value is 9, so the median is 9.

stem: A music teacher recorded the number of hours students practiced during a week and their scores on a short performance test. The scatterplot shows the data and the line of best fit. Based on the line of best fit, what score is predicted for a student who practiced for 4 hours?
explanation: The line of best fit passes through about \((2,30)\) and \((6,70)\), so its equation is approximately \(y=10x+10\). At \(x=4\), \(y=10(4)+10=50\).

stem: A lemonade stand recorded the number of cups of lemonade sold each day and the daily high temperature. The scatterplot shows the data and the line of best fit. Based on the line of best fit, how many cups of lemonade are predicted to be sold when the daily high temperature is \(75^\circ\)F?
explanation: The line of best fit passes through about \((60,120)\) and \((80,200)\), so its equation is approximately \(y=4x-120\). At \(x=75\), \(y=4(75)-120=180\).

visual.title: Lemonade sales vs. daily high temperature

stem: A patient’s medication amount in the blood was measured over time. The scatterplot shows the number of milligrams of medication remaining and the number of hours since the dose. The line of best fit is shown. What is the slope of the line of best fit?
explanation: The line of best fit decreases by 40 milligrams over 8 hours, from about \((0,80)\) to \((8,40)\). Thus the slope is \((40-80)/(8-0)=-5\) milligrams per hour.

stem: A gardener measured the height of a tomato plant each week after planting. The scatterplot shows the height of the plant and the number of weeks since planting, with the line of best fit. Based on the line of best fit, what is the predicted height of the plant at week 5?
explanation: The line of best fit passes through about \((1,6)\) and \((7,18)\), so its equation is approximately \(y=2x+4\). At \(x=5\), \(y=2(5)+4=14\) inches.

visual.title: Tomato plant height vs. weeks since planting

stem: A small bakery tracks the number of birthday cakes made each day and the total production cost in dollars. The scatterplot shows the data and the line of best fit. Based on the line of best fit, what is the predicted total production cost for making 10 birthday cakes?
explanation: The line of best fit passes through about \((5,75)\) and \((10,135)\), so its equation is approximately \(y=12x+15\). At \(x=10\), \(y=12(10)+15=135\) dollars.

visual.title: Production cost vs. birthday cakes made

stem: The table above summarizes responses from 200 customers about their order method and whether they were satisfied. If one customer who chose pickup is selected at random, what is the probability that the customer was satisfied?
explanation: Among the 140 pickup customers, 84 were satisfied. The probability is \(\frac{84}{140}=\frac{3}{5}=0.60\).

stem: The table above shows the results of a tutoring program for 200 students. If a student who passed the exam is selected at random, what is the probability that the student attended tutoring?
explanation: Among the 124 students who passed, 72 attended tutoring. The probability is \(\frac{72}{124}=\frac{18}{31}\).

stem: The table above shows whether 200 surveyed customers own a dog or a cat. If a customer who owns a dog is selected at random, what is the probability that the customer also owns a cat?
explanation: Among the 90 customers who own a dog, 18 also own a cat. The probability is \(\frac{18}{90}=\frac{1}{5}\).

stem: The table above summarizes 200 customers by shopping method and whether they returned an item. If a customer who returned an item is selected at random, what is the probability that the customer shopped online?
explanation: Among the 40 customers who returned an item, 28 shopped online. The probability is \(\frac{28}{40}=\frac{7}{10}\).

stem: The table above shows the preferred class type among 150 surveyed adults. If an adult who prefers art class is selected at random, what is the probability that the adult is female?
explanation: Among the 30 adults who prefer art, 20 are female. The probability is \(\frac{20}{30}=\frac{2}{3}\).

stem: A high school surveyed 200 students about their participation in a school club and in a sport. The results are shown in the table below. If a randomly selected student participates in a school club, what is the probability that the student also plays a sport?
explanation: The condition is that the student participates in a school club, so use the club total: 60 students. Of those, 45 also play a sport. Thus the probability is \(45/60 = 3/4\).

headers: Does Not Participate in a Club

stem: A tutoring center recorded pass/fail results for 200 students in two math review programs. The results are shown in the table below. If a randomly selected student passed the review, what is the probability that the student used Program A?
explanation: The condition is that the student passed, so use the pass total: 102 students. Of those, 54 used Program A. Thus \(54/102 = 9/17\).

stem: A city surveyed 400 randomly selected residents about whether they support a new library. The overall proportion of supporters in the sample was \(53\%\), with a margin of error of 5 percentage points. The results by age group are shown in the table below. Based on the sample and the margin of error, which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is plausible that the true proportion of all residents who support the library is between \(48\%\) and \(58\%\).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because \(53\%\) of the sample supports the library, more than half of all residents certainly support it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because residents aged 50 and older are more likely to oppose the library, the true proportion of all residents who support it is less than \(50\%\).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exactly \(68\%\) of the city's 18–34-year-old residents support the library.

explanation: The sample proportion is \(53\%\). Adding and subtracting the margin of error gives \(53\% \pm 5\%\), or \(48\%\) to \(58\%\). This interval describes a range of plausible values for the true proportion of all residents.

stem: A nutrition survey asked 500 adults whether they exercise regularly and whether they eat vegetables daily. The results are shown in the table below. If a randomly selected adult eats vegetables daily, what is the probability that the adult also exercises regularly?
explanation: The condition is that the adult eats vegetables daily, so use that column total: 150 adults. Of those, 105 exercise regularly. Thus \(105/150 = 7/10\).

stem: A high school recorded how 390 students arrived at school and whether they were late. The results are shown in the table below. If a randomly selected student was late, what is the probability that the student took the bus?
explanation: The condition is that the student was late, so use the late total: 64 students. Of those, 28 took the bus. Thus \(28/64 = 7/16\).

stem: The table above summarizes enrollment in Advanced Placement courses by grade level at a high school. If one student is chosen at random from the 11th grade, what is the probability that the student is enrolled in an AP course?
explanation: Because the student is chosen from the 11th grade, the denominator is the total number of 11th-grade students, 75. There are 30 11th-grade students enrolled in an AP course, so the probability is \(\frac{30}{75}=\frac{2}{5}\).

stem: The table above shows the results of a survey of adults who were asked whether they floss daily, categorized by age. If one adult is selected at random from those who floss daily, what is the probability that the adult is under 40 years old?
explanation: There are 120 adults who floss daily. Of those, 36 are under 40 years old. Thus the probability is \(\frac{36}{120}=\frac{3}{10}\).

stem: The table above shows whether students at a school took the bus and whether they completed a homework assignment. If one student is selected at random from those who completed the assignment, what is the probability that the student took the bus?
explanation: There are 117 students who completed the assignment. Of these, 54 took the bus. Therefore, the probability is \(\frac{54}{117}=\frac{6}{13}\).

stem: The table above shows whether students at a school participate in a sport and whether they are in the band. If one student is selected at random from those in the band, what is the probability that the student participates in a sport?
explanation: There are 70 students in the band. Of those, 28 participate in a sport. Thus, the probability is \(\frac{28}{70}=\frac{2}{5}\).

rows: Does not participate in a sport

stem: The table above shows whether residents in a neighborhood received a flyer about a community event and whether they participated in the event. If one resident is selected at random from those who received a flyer, what is the probability that the resident participated in the event?
explanation: There are 100 residents who received a flyer. Of those, 80 participated in the event, so the probability is \(\frac{80}{100}=\frac{4}{5}\).

stem: The table above shows whether students in two grades ride a bike to school. If a randomly selected student is in 10th grade, what is the probability that the student rides a bike to school?
explanation: There are 120 students in 10th grade, and 42 of them ride a bike. So the probability is \(\frac{42}{120} = \frac{7}{20}\).

stem: The table above shows the exercise preferences of adults in two age groups. Given that a randomly selected adult prefers running, what is the probability that the adult is 18–34 years old?
explanation: Of the 175 adults who prefer running, 75 are in the 18–34 age group. Thus the probability is \(\frac{75}{175} = \frac{3}{7}\).

stem: The table above shows lunch and dinner orders at a food truck. Given that an order was placed for dinner, what is the probability that the customer ordered a burrito?
explanation: There were 100 dinner orders, and 30 of them were burritos. So the probability is \(\frac{30}{100} = \frac{3}{10}\).

stem: The table above shows the number of students in two grades who belong to each club. A student is chosen at random from the Art Club. What is the probability that the student is in Grade 12?
explanation: There are 105 students in the Art Club, and 70 of them are in Grade 12. Thus the probability is \(\frac{70}{105} = \frac{2}{3}\).

stem: The table above shows how voters in two regions responded to a ballot measure. If a randomly selected voter is from the city, what is the probability that the voter disapproves of the measure?
explanation: There are 200 city voters, and 120 of them disapprove. So the probability is \(\frac{120}{200} = \frac{3}{5}\).

stem: A circle in the \(xy\)-plane has center \((3,-2)\) and passes through the point \((-1,1)\). Which of the following is an equation of the circle?
explanation: The radius is the distance from \((3,-2)\) to \((-1,1)\): \(\sqrt{(-1-3)^2+(1-(-2))^2}=\sqrt{16+9}=5\). Thus the equation is \((x-3)^2+(y+2)^2=25\).

stem: The midpoint of segment \(\overline{AB}\) is \((2,-3)\). If point \(A\) has coordinates \((-4,1)\), what are the coordinates of point \(B\)?
explanation: The midpoint formula gives \((2,-3)=((x_B-4)/2,(y_B+1)/2)\). Solving: \(x_B=2(2)+4=8\) and \(y_B=2(-3)-1=-7\).

stem: A circle in the \(xy\)-plane has endpoints of a diameter at \((2,5)\) and \((-4,-3)\). Which of the following is an equation of the circle?
explanation: The center is the midpoint \((\frac{2+(-4)}{2},\frac{5+(-3)}{2})=(-1,1)\). The diameter length is \(\sqrt{(2-(-4))^2+(5-(-3))^2}=10\), so the radius is \(5\). Therefore the equation is \((x+1)^2+(y-1)^2=25\).

stem: The distance between the points \((k,3)\) and \((-2,7)\) is \(5\). If \(k>0\), what is the value of \(k\)?
The equation of a circle in the \(xy\)-plane is \(x^2+y^2-6x+4y=12\). What are the center and radius of the circle?
explanation: Complete the square: \(x^2-6x+9+y^2+4y+4=12+13\), so \((x-3)^2+(y+2)^2=25\). The center is \((3,-2)\) and the radius is \(5\).

stem: The table below shows the results of a survey of 200 high school students about their preferred learning format, classified by class level. If a student is chosen at random from the upperclassmen, what is the probability that the student prefers remote learning?
explanation: There are 75 upperclassmen total, and 55 of them prefer remote learning. Therefore, the probability is \(\frac{55}{75}=\frac{11}{15}\).

stem: The table below shows the results of a survey of 500 residents about a proposed parking policy, classified by area of residence. Given that a randomly selected resident lives in the suburbs, what is the probability that the resident opposes the proposed policy?
explanation: There are 300 suburban residents, and 120 of them oppose the policy. Thus, the probability is \(\frac{120}{300}=\frac{2}{5}\).

stem: The table below shows the foreign language enrollment of ninth-grade and tenth-grade students at a small high school. If a randomly selected student is enrolled in Spanish, what is the probability that the student is in the ninth grade?
explanation: There are 90 students enrolled in Spanish, and 50 of them are ninth graders. Therefore, the probability is \(\frac{50}{90}=\frac{5}{9}\).

stem: The table below shows the results of a poll of 1,200 registered voters about their preference in a mayoral race, classified by age group. If a randomly selected respondent is aged 35–54, what is the probability that the respondent supports Candidate A?
explanation: There are 500 respondents aged 35–54, and 210 of them support Candidate A. Therefore, the probability is \(\frac{210}{500}=\frac{21}{50}\).

stem: A circle has endpoints of a diameter at \(A(2,-3)\) and \(B(10,5)\). Which of the following is the equation of the circle?
explanation: The center is the midpoint of the diameter: \(((2+10)/2,(-3+5)/2)=(6,1)\). The radius squared is the squared distance from the center to \(A\): \((2-6)^2+(-3-1)^2=16+16=32\). Thus the equation is \((x-6)^2+(y-1)^2=32\).

stem: A circle has center \((-2,4)\) and passes through the point \((1,0)\). Which of the following points also lies on the circle?
explanation: The radius is the distance from the center to \((1,0)\): \(\sqrt{(1-(-2))^2+(0-4)^2}=\sqrt{9+16}=5\). The circle equation is \((x+2)^2+(y-4)^2=25\). Testing \((-5,0)\): \((-3)^2+(-4)^2=9+16=25\), so it lies on the circle.

stem: The midpoint of \(\overline{AB}\) is \(M(-1,3)\). If point \(A\) is \((4,-2)\), what are the coordinates of point \(B\)?
explanation: Using the midpoint formula, \(B=2M-A\). So \(x_B=2(-1)-4=-6\) and \(y_B=2(3)-(-2)=8\). Therefore \(B=(-6,8)\).

stem: The circle \(x^2+y^2+6x-8y=56\) has center \((h,k)\) and radius \(r\). What is the value of \(h+k+r\)?
The midpoint of \(\overline{AB}\) is \((4,2)\). If \(A\) has coordinates \((2a+1,3b-2)\) and \(B\) has coordinates \((-3a+5,b+4)\), what is the value of \(a+b\)?
A circle in the \(xy\)-plane has endpoints of a diameter at \((-1, 4)\) and \((5, -8)\). Which of the following equations represents the circle?
explanation: The center is the midpoint of the diameter: \(\left(\frac{-1+5}{2}, \frac{4+(-8)}{2}\right)=(2,-2)\). The diameter length is \(\sqrt{(5-(-1))^2+(-8-4)^2}=\sqrt{180}=6\sqrt{5}\), so the radius is \(3\sqrt{5}\) and \(r^2=45\). Thus the equation is \((x-2)^2+(y+2)^2=45\).

stem: In the \(xy\)-plane, the midpoint of segment \(AB\) is \((4, 3)\). If point \(A\) has coordinates \((a - 2, 2a + 1)\) and point \(B\) has coordinates \((2a + 1, -a + 2)\), what is the value of \(a\)?
explanation: Using the midpoint formula: \(\frac{(a-2)+(2a+1)}{2}=4\), so \(3a-1=8\) and \(a=3\). Checking the y-coordinate: \(\frac{(2a+1)+(-a+2)}{2}=3\), so \(a+3=6\), which also gives \(a=3\).

stem: A circle in the \(xy\)-plane has center \((4, -1)\) and passes through \((2, 3)\). The point \((a, -3)\) also lies on the circle and \(a > 0\). What is the value of \(a\)?
explanation: The radius squared is \((2-4)^2+(3-(-1))^2=4+16=20\). For \((a,-3)\), the circle equation gives \((a-4)^2+(-3+1)^2=20\), so \((a-4)^2+4=20\), hence \((a-4)^2=16\). This gives \(a=0\) or \(a=8\). Since \(a>0\), the value is \(8\).

stem: In the \(xy\)-plane, the graph of \(x^2 + y^2 - 10x + 6y = c\) is a circle with radius 7. What is the value of \(c\)?
In the \(xy\)-plane, point \((a, b)\) is equidistant from \((-1, 2)\) and \((3, 6)\). Which equation must be true?
explanation: Equidistance gives \((a+1)^2+(b-2)^2=(a-3)^2+(b-6)^2\). Expanding and simplifying: \(2a-4b+5=-6a-12b+45\), so \(8a+8b=40\), and therefore \(a+b=5\).

stem: A circle in the \(xy\)-plane is given by \(x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 8y = 56\). If a square is inscribed in the circle, what is the area of the square?
explanation: Complete the square: \((x-3)^2 + (y+4)^2 = 81\), so the radius is 9 and the diameter is 18. An inscribed square has diagonal 18, so its side is \(18/\sqrt{2} = 9\sqrt{2}\), giving area \((9\sqrt{2})^2 = 162\).

stem: The midpoint of segment \(\overline{AB}\) is \(M(4,-1)\). If \(A=(2,3)\), what is the length of segment \(\overline{AB}\)?
A circle in the \(xy\)-plane has center \((1,-2)\) and passes through the point \((4,2)\). Which of the following points also lies on the circle?
explanation: The radius is the distance from \((1,-2)\) to \((4,2)\): \(\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5\). For \((-2,2)\), the distance from the center is \(\sqrt{(-3)^2+4^2}=5\), so it lies on the circle. The other points have distances \(\sqrt{50}\), \(\sqrt{13}\), and \(\sqrt{73}\), respectively.

stem: Circle 1 has equation \((x-1)^2+(y+2)^2=25\). Circle 2 has equation \((x+3)^2+(y-1)^2=16\). What is the greatest possible distance between a point on Circle 1 and a point on Circle 2?
explanation: Circle 1 has center \((1,-2)\) and radius 5. Circle 2 has center \((-3,1)\) and radius 4. The distance between centers is \(\sqrt{(1+3)^2+(-2-1)^2}=\sqrt{16+9}=5\). The greatest distance between a point on one circle and a point on the other is the center distance plus both radii: \(5+5+4=14\).

stem: In the \(xy\)-plane, the midpoint of segment \(\overline{AB}\), where \(A=(2m,\;3m-1)\) and \(B=(-2,\;5)\), lies on the line \(y=x+2\). What is the value of \(m\)?
explanation: The midpoint is \(\left(\frac{2m-2}{2},\frac{3m-1+5}{2}\right) = \left(m-1,\frac{3m+4}{2}\right)\). Since it lies on \(y=x+2\), set \(\frac{3m+4}{2} = (m-1)+2 = m+1\). Solving gives \(3m+4 = 2m+2\), so \(m=-2\).

stem: If a student is selected at random from the music club, what is the probability that the student is in the 11th grade?
explanation: There are 100 students in the music club, and 40 of them are in the 11th grade. Thus the probability is \(\frac{40}{100}=\frac{2}{5}\).

stem: Given that a randomly selected survey respondent opposed the measure, what is the probability that the respondent is age 55 or older?
explanation: A total of 200 respondents opposed the measure, and 90 of them were age 55 or older. Therefore the probability is \(\frac{90}{200}=\frac{9}{20}\).

stem: If a defective item is selected at random, what is the probability that it was produced on the night shift, given that it has a mechanical defect?
explanation: There are 100 items with mechanical defects, and 46 of those were produced on the night shift. Thus the probability is \(\frac{46}{100}=\frac{23}{50}\).

visual.title: Defective Items by Shift and Defect Type

stem: If a student from the sample is selected at random and is interested in studying abroad, what is the probability that the student is a sophomore?
explanation: A total of 200 students are interested in studying abroad, and 40 of them are sophomores. Therefore the probability is \(\frac{40}{200}=\frac{1}{5}\).

visual.title: Interest in Studying Abroad by Class Year

stem: Given that a randomly selected voter opposed the measure, what is the probability that the voter is an Independent?
explanation: A total of 250 voters opposed the measure, and 60 of them were Independent. Thus the probability is \(\frac{60}{250}=\frac{6}{25}\).

stem: A teacher recorded the number of hours each student spent reviewing and that student's test score. The scatterplot and line of best fit show the data. Based on the line of best fit, what score is predicted for a student who spent 3 hours reviewing?
explanation: The line of best fit has equation \(y = 54 + 9x\). For \(x = 3\), \(y = 54 + 9(3) = 81\).

stem: A fitness trainer recorded the number of hours per week clients spent on sedentary screen time and the average number of daily push-ups those clients could do. The scatterplot and line of best fit show the data. According to the line of best fit, each additional hour of weekly screen time is associated with how large a decrease in predicted daily push-ups?
explanation: The line of best fit is \(y = 40 - 5x\). Its slope is \(-5\), so the predicted number of daily push-ups decreases by 5 for each additional hour of screen time.

stem: A student council tracked the number of cups of hot chocolate sold at a fundraiser and the temperature at noon. The scatterplot and line of best fit show the data. Based on the line of best fit, how many cups of hot chocolate would be predicted when the noon temperature is 25°F?
explanation: The line of best fit has equation \(y = 110 - 2x\). For \(x = 25\), \(y = 110 - 2(25) = 60\).

visual.title: Noon Temperature vs. Hot Chocolate Sales

stem: The scatterplot shows the number of visitors in a science museum and the number of hours since the museum opened. The line of best fit is also shown. Based on the line of best fit, what is the predicted number of visitors 3 hours after opening?

A used-car dealership recorded the age and selling price of several cars of the same model. The scatterplot and line of best fit show the data. Based on the line of best fit, what is the predicted selling price of a car that is 4 years old?
A circle in the \(xy\)-plane has center \((-4, 1)\) and passes through the origin. Which of the following is an equation of the circle?
explanation: The radius is the distance from \((-4,1)\) to \((0,0)\): \(\sqrt{(0+4)^2+(0-1)^2}=\sqrt{17}\). Thus the circle equation is \((x+4)^2+(y-1)^2=17\).

stem: In the \(xy\)-plane, the endpoints of a diameter of a circle are \((-3,2)\) and \((5,8)\). Which of the following is an equation of the circle?
explanation: The center is the midpoint \(\left(\frac{-3+5}{2},\frac{2+8}{2}\right)=(1,5)\). The diameter length is \(\sqrt{(5+3)^2+(8-2)^2}=10\), so the radius is 5 and \(r^2=25\). The equation is \((x-1)^2+(y-5)^2=25\).

stem: Points \(P(-2,1)\) and \(Q(10,7)\) are endpoints of segment \(\overline{PQ}\). Point \(R\) lies on \(\overline{PQ}\) and is twice as far from \(P\) as from \(Q\). What are the coordinates of \(R\)?
explanation: Since \(PR=2\,RQ\), the ratio is \(PR:RQ=2:1\), so \(R\) is \(\frac{2}{3}\) of the way from \(P\) to \(Q\). The displacement from \(P\) to \(Q\) is \((12,6)\), so \(R=(-2,1)+\frac{2}{3}(12,6)=(6,5)\).

stem: In the \(xy\)-plane, a circle has center \((3,-2)\) and is tangent to the line \(y=4\). Which of the following is an equation of the circle?
explanation: The distance from the center \((3,-2)\) to the horizontal line \(y=4\) is \(|4-(-2)|=6\), so the radius is 6 and \(r^2=36\). The circle equation is \((x-3)^2+(y+2)^2=36\).

stem: A point \(P(x,y)\) in the \(xy\)-plane is equidistant from \(A(-2,1)\) and \(B(4,-3)\). Which of the following equations must be true?
explanation: Equating squared distances gives \((x+2)^2+(y-1)^2=(x-4)^2+(y+3)^2\). Expanding and simplifying yields \(4x-2y+5=-8x+6y+25\), so \(12x-8y-20=0\), or \(3x-2y=5\).

stem: A circle in the \(xy\)-plane has equation \(x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 10y = 2\). What is the radius of the circle?
explanation: Complete the square: \(x^2 - 6x + y^2 + 10y = 2\). This becomes \((x-3)^2 + (y+5)^2 = 36\), so \(r^2 = 36\) and \(r = 6\).

stem: In the \(xy\)-plane, the midpoint of segment \(AB\) is \(M(3, -2)\). If \(A = (7, -5)\), what is the length of \(AB\)?
A circle in the \(xy\)-plane has center \((-2, 3)\) and passes through the point \((1, -1)\). Which of the following is an equation of the circle?
explanation: The radius is the distance from \((-2, 3)\) to \((1, -1)\): \(\sqrt{(1+2)^2 + (-1-3)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5\). Thus the equation is \((x+2)^2 + (y-3)^2 = 25\).

stem: In the \(xy\)-plane, the endpoints of a diameter of a circle are \((-2, 5)\) and \((4, -1)\). Which of the following is an equation of the circle?
explanation: The center is the midpoint of the diameter: \((1, 2)\). The radius squared is \((4-1)^2 + (-1-2)^2 = 9 + 9 = 18\). Therefore the equation is \((x-1)^2 + (y-2)^2 = 18\).

stem: In the \(xy\)-plane, the distance between the points \(P(k, 4)\) and \(Q(3, -2)\) is \(2\sqrt{13}\). If \(k > 3\), what is the value of \(k\)?
A circle in the \(xy\)-plane has center \((2,-3)\) and passes through the point \((5,1)\). Which of the following is an equation of the circle?
explanation: The radius squared is \((5-2)^2+(1-(-3))^2=9+16=25\). Thus the equation is \((x-2)^2+(y+3)^2=25\).

stem: Points \(A(-1,4)\) and \(B(5,-2)\) are the endpoints of a diameter of a circle. What is the area of the circle?
explanation: The distance between \(A\) and \(B\) is \(\sqrt{(5+1)^2+(-2-4)^2}=\sqrt{72}=6\sqrt{2}\). The radius is half of that, or \(3\sqrt{2}\). Therefore the area is \(\pi(3\sqrt{2})^2=18\pi\).

stem: Point \(M(3,-1)\) is the midpoint of segment \(\overline{AB}\). If point \(A\) has coordinates \((7,2)\), what are the coordinates of point \(B\)?
The center of a circle lies on the line \(y=x-1\). The circle passes through the points \((1,4)\) and \((7,2)\). What is the radius of the circle?
explanation: Let the center be \((a,a-1)\). Equating squared distances to the two given points gives \((a-1)^2+(a-5)^2=(a-7)^2+(a-3)^2\). Solving gives \(a=4\), so the center is \((4,3)\). The radius is \(\sqrt{(4-1)^2+(3-4)^2}=\sqrt{10}\).

stem: A circle in the \(xy\)-plane passes through the points \((0,0)\), \((4,0)\), and \((0,6)\). Which of the following is an equation of the circle?
explanation: The perpendicular bisector of the segment from \((0,0)\) to \((4,0)\) is \(x=2\), and the perpendicular bisector of the segment from \((0,0)\) to \((0,6)\) is \(y=3\). Thus the center is \((2,3)\), and the radius squared is \(2^2+3^2=13\). The equation is \((x-2)^2+(y-3)^2=13\).

stem: A city surveyed 300 residents about whether they support a new library tax. The table shows the results by whether the resident had visited the library in the past month. If a randomly selected survey respondent had visited the library in the past month, what is the probability that the respondent supports the library tax?
explanation: There were 100 respondents who had visited the library, and 60 of them support the tax. Thus the probability is \(\frac{60}{100}=\frac{3}{5}\).

stem: A high school surveyed 500 students about whether they are enrolled in at least one AP class and whether they have a private tutor. The results are shown in the table. If a randomly selected student has no private tutor, what is the probability that the student is enrolled in at least one AP class?
explanation: There are 375 students with no private tutor. Among them, 225 are enrolled in an AP class, so the probability is \(\frac{225}{375}=\frac{3}{5}\).

stem: A phone company surveyed 240 customers about whether they upgraded their plan last year and whether they use an installment plan or pay upfront. The results are shown in the table. If a randomly selected customer paid upfront, what is the probability that the customer upgraded their plan?
explanation: There are 72 customers who paid upfront, and 24 of them upgraded. Therefore the probability is \(\frac{24}{72}=\frac{1}{3}\).

stem: A school recorded how 330 students arrived at school and whether they were late today. The results are shown in the table. If a randomly selected student arrived late today, what is the probability that the student took the bus to school?
explanation: There are 60 students who arrived late, and 30 of them took the bus. Thus the probability is \(\frac{30}{60}=\frac{1}{2}\).

stem: A poll of 300 registered voters classified respondents by age group and by which of two candidates they prefer. The results are shown in the table. If a randomly selected respondent prefers Candidate X, what is the probability that the respondent is under 40?
explanation: There are 140 respondents who prefer Candidate X, and 84 of them are under 40. Therefore the probability is \(\frac{84}{140}=\frac{3}{5}\).

passage.text: Text 1: Electric scooters have become a hazard on city sidewalks. Riders weave around pedestrians at high speed, and accidents have increased sharply. The safest solution is to ban e-scooters from sidewalks entirely; they belong only in bike lanes or not at all.
passage.text_b: Text 2: Critics who call for banning e-scooters ignore their benefits. E-scooters reduce car trips and emissions. The real problem is a lack of sensible rules. Cities that set low speed limits, require designated parking areas, and educate riders have found that e-scooters and pedestrians can coexist safely.

stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that e-scooters are a sidewalk hazard by saying that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the hazard can be substantially reduced through well-enforced regulations rather than a ban.

choices.label: B
choices.text: sidewalks are actually more dangerous for pedestrians now than they were before e-scooters appeared.

choices.label: C
choices.text: bike lanes should also be closed to e-scooters to protect all users.

choices.label: D
choices.text: e-scooters cause fewer accidents than cars do, so the data in Text 1 must be mistaken.

explanation: Text 2 argues that irresponsible scooter use can be managed through rules such as speed limits and parking requirements. Therefore, the author would reject a total ban and instead say that regulation can reduce the danger.

passage.text: Text 1: Taking notes by hand improves learning. Because handwriting is slower, students must summarize and process ideas rather than transcribe every word. This deeper mental work creates stronger memory for the material.
passage.text_b: Text 2: Typed notes are more complete and easier to review. Research suggests that when students later review their notes, typing offers at least as much learning as handwriting. The key variable is not the note-taking tool but whether students revisit and reflect on what they wrote.

stem: Based on the passages, the author of Text 2 would most likely respond to Text 1's assertion that handwriting is necessary for learning by saying that

choices.label: A
choices.text: handwriting is slower, so it is a waste of class time compared with typing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: students who type should be required to write summaries by hand.

choices.label: C
choices.text: reviewing typed notes can produce learning equal to that from handwritten notes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: memory is strengthened only when students transcribe the teacher's words verbatim.

explanation: Text 2 explicitly says that when notes are reviewed, typed notes can produce at least as much learning as handwritten notes. Thus, the author would not agree that handwriting is required for learning.

passage.text: Text 1: Remote work weakens a company because innovation depends on casual conversations and spontaneous meetings. When employees work from home, they miss the exchange of ideas that happens naturally at an office, and collaboration suffers as a result.
passage.text_b: Text 2: Remote work can actually strengthen collaboration. Online tools allow employees from different locations to contribute more easily, and many teams use structured virtual meetings to ensure every voice is heard. Flexibility also lets people work when they are most focused, leading to better collective outcomes.

stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that remote work undermines collaboration by arguing that

choices.label: A
choices.text: spontaneous office conversations are the only reliable source of innovation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: online tools and intentionally designed meetings can support or even improve collaboration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: workers should be required to return to the office at least three days a week.

choices.label: D
choices.text: innovation does not matter as much as employee comfort.

explanation: Text 2 directly challenges Text 1 by claiming that remote work can improve collaboration through online tools and structured virtual meetings, so the author would point to those methods as supporting evidence.

passage.text: Text 1: Adolescents naturally go to sleep later and need about eight to ten hours of sleep. Starting school at 8:30 or later aligns classes with students' internal clocks, and districts that made the change report better attendance and higher grades. Later start times are therefore a clear win.
passage.text_b: Text 2: Moving school start times later is not as simple as it sounds. It can disrupt bus schedules, after-school jobs, sports, and family routines. Moreover, if students still stay up late using screens, a later school bell may not increase total sleep. Districts need to weigh these practical problems before making such a change.

stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely characterize Text 1's claim that later start times are "a clear win" as

choices.label: A
choices.text: correct because better attendance and higher grades leave no reason for doubt.

choices.label: B
choices.text: too cautious because the benefits outweigh any scheduling concerns.

choices.label: C
choices.text: incomplete because practical consequences and student behavior must be considered.

choices.label: D
choices.text: unsupported because the studies mentioned by Text 1 are not published.

explanation: Text 2 argues that a later start time has important downsides and may not increase sleep if students continue staying up late. Thus, the author would reject calling the change a clear win without weighing those problems.

passage.text: Text 1: Space exploration is not a luxury. Technologies developed for space missions have led to improvements in medicine, materials, and communications. The sense of wonder it creates also encourages young people to study science. These benefits justify the cost.
passage.text_b: Text 2: Every dollar spent on space is a dollar not spent on urgent earthly needs, such as immunization, clean water, and climate adaptation. The thrilling discoveries of space travel may be inspiring, but inspiration does not feed a child or stop a flood. Public funds should address immediate crises first.

stem: The author of Text 2 would most likely respond to Text 1's claim that space exploration produces valuable technological benefits by saying that

choices.label: A
choices.text: those benefits are usually invented by scientists to win public support.

choices.label: B
choices.text: even if the benefits are real, they come at the cost of addressing pressing needs on Earth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: technological benefits are valuable but not as valuable as fostering wonder.

choices.label: D
choices.text: private companies will eventually provide technological benefits without government spending.

explanation: Text 2 focuses on opportunity cost: public spending on space comes at the expense of urgent problems on Earth. The author would therefore grant that benefits may exist but argue they are not worth the trade-off.

passage.text: Entomologists proposed that the boom in urban beekeeping is harming native wild bees. They argued that large numbers of managed honeybees deplete the limited nectar and pollen in small city habitats, making wild bees less likely to visit flowers and reproduce. To test this, researchers monitored flowering vacant lots across one city for two summers, comparing lots within 100 meters of large apiaries to otherwise similar lots farther away.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the entomologists' hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In lots near apiaries, overall flower abundance was higher because of pollination by honeybees, and wild bee species richness was about the same as in distant lots.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Wild bees in lots near apiaries visited flowers less often and spent more time interacting with honeybees, and these lots contained significantly less nectar than distant lots.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Distant lots had more of the flowering plant species wild bees prefer, while lots near apiaries were dominated by grasses and nonnative weeds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Honeybees in urban lots produced more honey per hive than honeybees in rural areas, indicating that city flowers were not a limited resource.

explanation: Choice B directly supports the hypothesis by linking proximity to honeybee hives with lower nectar availability and reduced wild bee foraging, consistent with competition for limited floral resources.

passage.text: A psychologist hypothesized that the memory boost of a brief daytime nap is caused by slow-wave sleep, which strengthens hippocampal connections. If this hypothesis is correct, then selectively disrupting slow-wave sleep should eliminate the nap's memory benefit, whereas disrupting REM sleep should not.

stem: Which result, if true, would most directly support the psychologist's hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Participants who napped with slow-wave sleep disrupted performed no better than participants who stayed awake, whereas participants who napped with REM sleep disrupted performed just as well as undisturbed nappers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants who stayed awake but listened to white noise reported feeling as rested as nappers, but their recall of word pairs was significantly worse.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When nappers were allowed to sleep 20 minutes longer, their recall improved regardless of whether the extra time contained slow-wave or REM sleep.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Participants who dreamed vividly during REM sleep remembered more emotional images, while slow-wave sleep had no effect on emotional memory.

explanation: Choice A isolates slow-wave sleep as essential: disrupting it removes the memory benefit, while disrupting REM sleep leaves the benefit intact, exactly matching the hypothesis.

passage.text: A city council member has argued that funding neighborhood public-art initiatives reduces crime more effectively than increasing police foot patrols. The council member reasons that public art builds community cohesion, leading residents to informally discourage disorder. A criminal-justice research team examined data from cities that implemented one or both strategies.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the council member's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neighborhoods that chose public-art projects reported higher resident satisfaction and more block parties than neighborhoods that chose patrols.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In comparable cities, increased police patrols were associated with a 12 percent reduction in property crime, while public-art initiatives were associated with only a 2 percent reduction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residents in public-art neighborhoods said they felt more attached to their streets, and property values rose over a five-year period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cities that funded public art completed an average of 14 murals per year, while cities with increased patrols employed 40 additional officers.

explanation: Choice B weakens the council member's claim by showing that increased patrols were associated with a much larger crime reduction than public-art initiatives were.

passage.text: A marine biologist proposed that the main danger microplastics pose to fish is chemical, not physical. She argued that toxic additives such as phthalates leach from the particles into tissues and disrupt endocrine function, while the mere presence of particles in the digestive tract is relatively harmless. To test this, her lab exposed fish to microplastic particles that either contained additives or had been processed to remove all additives.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the biologist's proposal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fish fed microplastic particles from which all additives had been removed showed severe intestinal blockages and weight loss, while fish exposed only to the particles' chemical extract showed normal feeding and growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fish fed intact microplastic particles had higher concentrations of phthalates in their blood and lower egg production than fish fed additive-free particles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When microplastic particles were absent from the tank, fish exposed to phthalates alone still showed disrupted hormone levels.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fish fed additive-free particles had the same survival rates as fish fed untreated particles, but untreated particles increased hormone disruptors.

explanation: Choice A weakens the chemical hypothesis by showing that additive-free particles caused physical harm and that chemical extract alone had no harmful effect.

passage.text: A linguist argues that the English word “okay” did not arise from an American newspaper abbreviation in the 1830s but instead came into English from the West African language Wolof, in which an approving phrase sounds similar. She maintains that written uses of “okay” in American English should therefore appear earliest in documents that had contact with Wolof-speaking people, especially in ports where transatlantic ships called.

stem: Which piece of evidence, if true, would most directly support the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A well-known 1840 New York essay used “o.k.” as an abbreviation for “oll korrect,” a humorous misspelling popularized by the Democratic Party.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 1902 memoir recalls hearing “okay” as a child, but the author admits that the word might have been popularized by the “oll korrect” joke.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A 1796 ship's log kept by a Wolof-speaking trader in Charleston contains the entry “we okay” to mean “we have agreed,” and the phrase closely resembles an approving expression in Wolof.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Early American dictionaries published before 1830 list the word “okay” as obsolete slang of unknown origin, with no reference to West African languages.

explanation: Choice C supports the linguist's argument by providing an earlier American use of “okay” in a context involving a Wolof-speaking person, consistent with a West African origin rather than an 1830s abbreviation.

passage.text: Text 1: Some educators argue that assigning daily homework is essential for reinforcing classroom learning. They claim that regular practice improves retention and builds academic discipline, and students who complete homework consistently tend to score higher on standardized tests.
passage.text_b: Text 2: A researcher observes that homework can widen the achievement gap. Students from well-resourced homes get help and quiet spaces, whereas students without those advantages fall further behind. This researcher concludes that schools should focus on in-class assignments instead of requiring homework at home.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the researcher in Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that daily homework reinforces learning and builds discipline?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By agreeing that regular practice improves retention but arguing that the costs to disadvantaged students outweigh the benefits

choices.label: B
choices.text: By questioning whether standardized tests are an accurate measure of academic discipline

choices.label: C
choices.text: By insisting that homework can be designed so that it does not require quiet space or parental help

choices.label: D
choices.text: By denying that students who complete homework consistently score higher on standardized tests

explanation: The researcher in Text 2 focuses on how homework disadvantages students without resources. Thus, the researcher would likely accept the general value of practice but argue that the unequal burdens of homework outweigh those benefits.

passage.text: Text 1: Public libraries should remain open on weekends because working families rely on them for internet access, children need safe spaces, and weekend programs draw community members together.
passage.text_b: Text 2: City officials argue that extending library hours would require additional staff and utilities, and the same funds could instead be used to upgrade outdated computer systems in schools. With limited budgets, each dollar should support services that reach the greatest number of residents.

stem: How would the city officials in Text 2 most likely respond to the argument in Text 1 that libraries should remain open on weekends?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By claiming that weekend library programs have little community support

choices.label: B
choices.text: By acknowledging the benefits of weekend libraries but arguing that budget constraints make the proposal impractical

choices.label: C
choices.text: By stating that working families do not actually need weekend internet access

choices.label: D
choices.text: By proposing to close schools on weekends instead

explanation: The city officials in Text 2 do not deny the benefits of weekend library service; instead, they argue that the required spending is not justified given limited budgets and competing needs.

passage.text: Text 1: A local museum's director says charging admission is necessary to cover conservation costs. Without ticket revenue, fragile paintings and historical artifacts cannot be properly preserved.
passage.text_b: Text 2: A community organizer argues that museums are public institutions and should be free. She notes that many other countries fund museums through taxes, and that charging fees keeps low-income visitors from accessing their own heritage.

stem: How would the community organizer in Text 2 most likely respond to the museum director's statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By denying that fragile paintings and historical artifacts need to be preserved

choices.label: B
choices.text: By suggesting that only low-income visitors should be exempt from admission fees

choices.label: C
choices.text: By agreeing that preservation is important but insisting that public funding, not admission fees, should pay for it

choices.label: D
choices.text: By claiming that museums should focus on profit rather than public access

explanation: The community organizer in Text 2 supports free access and cites tax-funded museums as an alternative. She would therefore agree on the importance of preservation but reject admission fees as the right funding method.

passage.text: Text 1: A nutritionist claims that the best way to reduce sugar consumption is to ban sugary drinks in schools. She argues that removing these options will help students form healthier habits and improve concentration in class.
passage.text_b: Text 2: A school administrator opposes the ban, saying students will simply buy sugary drinks off campus or hide them in their backpacks. He believes the policy would be difficult to enforce and would not actually change students' diets.

stem: The administrator in Text 2 would most likely respond to the nutritionist's proposal by doing which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By agreeing that sugar consumption is not a serious problem in schools

choices.label: B
choices.text: By proposing even stricter rules, such as searching students' backpacks

choices.label: C
choices.text: By supporting the ban if it is announced to parents well in advance

choices.label: D
choices.text: By questioning its effectiveness because students would find ways around the ban

explanation: The administrator in Text 2 argues that the ban would be difficult to enforce and that students would still obtain sugary drinks. He would therefore question whether the nutritionist's proposal would actually work.

passage.text: Text 1: A city's transit director says building more highway lanes is the quickest way to reduce traffic congestion during rush hour. Wider roads, he argues, allow more cars to move through at once and shorten commute times.
passage.text_b: Text 2: An urban planner argues that expanding highways actually increases congestion over time. By making driving easier, she observes, highways encourage more people to drive, so the new lanes fill up quickly and traffic returns.

stem: How would the urban planner in Text 2 most likely respond to the transit director's claim that wider roads are the quickest way to reduce congestion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By agreeing that wider roads reduce congestion but insisting they should include bicycle lanes

choices.label: B
choices.text: By arguing that commute times are less important than air quality

choices.label: C
choices.text: By countering that easier driving attracts more drivers, so the congestion reduction would be temporary at best

choices.label: D
choices.text: By stating that no new roads should ever be built under any circumstances

explanation: The urban planner in Text 2 directly challenges the transit director's reasoning: expanding highways makes driving easier, which draws more drivers and causes congestion to return. She would thus view the claimed reduction as temporary.

passage.text: Dr. Aiko Yamamoto ___ will deliver the keynote address at the national botany conference.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that the underlined?

choices.label: A
choices.text: whose research on desert plants has transformed agricultural practices,

choices.label: B
choices.text: , whose research on desert plants has transformed agricultural practices

choices.label: C
choices.text: , whose research on desert plants has transformed agricultural practices,

choices.label: D
choices.text: whose research on desert plants; has transformed agricultural practices;

explanation: The phrase 'whose research on desert plants has transformed agricultural practices' is a nonessential modifier describing Dr. Yamamoto, so it must be set off by commas both before and after. Choice C supplies both needed commas.

passage.text: The old lighthouse ___ has been converted into a small maritime museum.

stem: Which choice completes the text with correct punctuation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: built in 1892 by a crew of local stonemasons

choices.label: B
choices.text: built in 1892 by a crew of local stonemasons,

choices.label: C
choices.text: , built in 1892 by a crew of local stonemasons

choices.label: D
choices.text: , built in 1892 by a crew of local stonemasons,

explanation: The phrase 'built in 1892 by a crew of local stonemasons' is a nonessential modifier describing the lighthouse, so it must be set off by commas on both sides. Choice D provides the required opening and closing commas.

passage.text: The novel's protagonist ___ faces a series of moral dilemmas that test her loyalty and courage.

stem: Which choice completes the text with correct punctuation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: , a former detective haunted by her past,

choices.label: B
choices.text: a former detective haunted by her past,

choices.label: C
choices.text: , a former detective haunted by her past

choices.label: D
choices.text: a former detective haunted by her past

explanation: The appositive phrase 'a former detective haunted by her past' gives extra information about the protagonist and is not essential to the sentence, so it must be set off by commas on both sides. Choice A is the only option that does this correctly.
